Vistas of Algebraic Probability, Quantum Computation and Information
Antonio Falcó, Hermann G. Matthies

Abstract
Kolmogorov’s foundation of probability takes measure spaces, σ \sigma -algebras, and probability measures as the foundation of probability theory. It is widely recognised that the classical Kolmogorovean view on probability is inadequate to deal with random phenomena involving quantum effects, or more widely with quantum-like situations. Thus one might look for a wider, more encompassing view. Such a formulation can be achieved by what may be termed an algebraic point of view. This starts with algebras of random variables with a distinguished linear functional, the state, which is interpreted as expectation. Incidentally, this may be seen as a modern interpretation of the framework used by the early practitioners of probability like the Bernoullis. The algebraic view, in its modern form emanating from and extensively used in quantum physics, offers the potential to deal with both the classical and quantum-like behaviours, but is not much appreciated in classical probability and uncertainty quantification, although even here it may lead to new vistas and illuminate different aspects. This origin gives a physics flavour to the language, but the subject is purely probability. The key difference between classical and quantum-like probabilistic behaviour turns out to be commutativity, the lack of which leads to the effects encountered in quantum-like situations. The advent of quantum computers is one example which may make it necessary even for classical practitioners of computational sciences to deal with quantum-like behaviour. Here we endeavour to show the purely algebraic part of this approach. By concentrating on finite dimensional algebras one can avoid many difficult analytical questions, but at the same time still show the main flavour and ideas of the algebraic point of view in classical probability, and how this extends to quantum-like behaviour, and is actually applicable to quantum computing. Keywords: algebraic probability, non-Kolmogorovean probability, non-commuting random variables, quantum-like behaviour, quantum channels and information, quantum computation MSC2020 Classification: 46L53, 47L90, 46K10, 81R05, 81S25, 46N50, 46L89, 81P68, 60A99



Probability is the most important concept in modern science,
especially as nobody has the slightest notion what it means.

Bertrand Russell, 1929

1
Introduction

The classical probabilistic framework based on Kolmogorov’s axioms

[
91
,
92
]

(see also e.g.
[
137
]
) is typically
used when performing uncertainty quantification (UQ). It starts from
sample spaces,
\sigma
-algebras of subsets of events and
probability measures, and can be used to define
algebras of random variables (RVs) as measurable functions on these measure
spaces, and the expectation operator as integral of these RVs w.r.t. the
probability measure. A different view is offered by an alternative route,
where one uses
as fundamental concepts algebras of RVs, in physics lingo also called “observables”, together
with the expectation operator (e.g.
[
124
]
) as a positive linear
functional. More to the point, the expectation is an example of a “state”
(of the system under consideration), mathematically an element of the dual of
the algebra of RVs and what will take the rôle of probability distributions
in classical probability. The necessity of this algebraic view arose from the
needs to describe quantum phenomena, or, to put it more generally, to describe
quantum-like behaviour (QLB), where the sequential order of observations matters.
As it turns out, it is this property of non-commutativity or commutativity
in the algebra of RVs which describes the difference between QLB and the classical case.
The algebraic view allows a unified picture of both classical and QLB. And
this view does not distinguish between isomorphic objects resp. faithful representations, so that
much of the description and discussion can be done in an abstract framework,
which hence focuses on the essentials. But it allows one also to switch to some
of the isomorphic concrete mathematical representations, if so desired.
This also allows one to infer properties in the abstract setting from well known
facts in one of the faithful representations.
Although a number of terms, like “state” or “observable”, originate
from quantum physics, it will hopefully become clear that algebraic
probability is a purely mathematical theory, no physics is needed,
and when restricted to finite dimensional algebras it is actually just
part of (multi-)linear algebra.

In case the algebra of RVs is Abelian or commutative, one essentially
recovers equivalence with classical Kolomogorovean probability.
Notably, the algebraic approach allows for non-commutative algebras of RVs,
developed along with quantum theory, and is also important in order to deal
with e.g. random matrices (e.g.
[
103
]
), random fields of tensors, and
quantum-like behaviour (QLB) (e.g.
[
18
,
80
,
154
,
89
,
21
,
38
,
39
,
72
,
135
,
14
,
155
,
108
,
22
,
19
,
106
,
90
]
), also outside of quantum theory.
Here we also show how this nicely applies to
quantum computing (QC) (e.g.
[
107
]
), and quantum channels and
information (QI) (e.g.
[
150
,
23
,
151
]
),
which incidentally is also an application of the theory in the simplest setting,
when the algebras of RVs may be taken as finite dimensional
(e.g.
[
28
,
71
]
). For the sake of simplicity and brevity
we shall limit ourselves here to the finite dimensional setting and show the key concepts
by concentrating on the algebraic aspects. As will become clear very quickly,
such probability algebras can be represented as algebras of linear maps on the algebra itself,
which can be equipped with the structure of a pre-Hilbert space.
Here the “real”, or actually observable, or self-adjoint RVs correspond to self-adjoint maps.
Thus, in the case of finite dimensional algebras, a faithful representation
can be provided by a matrix algebra. Although the focus here will be finite
dimensional algebras, the presentation will still be kept
in the more abstract setting, as it brings out the algebraic content independently
of any representation. The motivation for this kind of description is that it
turned out that the specific realisation of the algebra does not matter, it is
the intrinsic algebraic properties which hold the probabilistic information,
whereas the concrete realisations or representations can be used as desired
for specific purposes. In addition, this way offers the reader a smooth transition
to approach the algebraic view also when dealing with continuous random variables.

As will be shown later, the possible observations or samples of an observable or random
variable are values in its spectrum, and thus the self-adjoint RVs have real valued samples.
As the spectrum of self-adjoint linear maps on finite dimensional spaces is a discrete
and finite subset of the real numbers, in order
to describe continuous RVs one has to deal with infinite dimensional algebras, so that linear
maps may have a continuous spectrum. And to represent unbounded RVs, one has to deal
with unbounded self-adjoint maps.
Thus the concentration on finite dimensional algebras avoids the analytical difficulties
which otherwise appear when dealing with — possibly unbounded — linear operators
on infinite dimensional spaces, while still occasionally offering a glimpse on
how this may be extended in the infinite dimensional case.
But we would like to point out that the algebraic view can naturally deal
with systems with infinitely many degrees of freedom
(e.g.
[
116
]
, where the different types of von Neumann algebras are
investigated in this respect), stochastic processes, and random fields, or more
generally with RVs with values in infinite dimensional spaces more directly; topics which can be
treated with classical probabilistic methods only in a somewhat circumlocutory fashion.

The treatment of QLB phenomena is not possible within the Kolomogorovean
view — which is equivalent to using only commutative algebras —
as it turns out that in the non-commutative case one can not define a global
\sigma
-algebra
of events with consistently assigned probabilities,
a notion which is at the basis of classical probability.
This is due to the fact that for QLB phenomena not all observables or RVs are

compatible
, i.e. they can not be realised or observed simultaneously — in the
same state of the system under consideration. The possible probability assignments
depend on the “context”, i.e. which other random variables (RVs) are observed
simultaneously. Mathematically this is expressed by the
question of whether these RVs commute or not, and the Boolean algebra of events
is replaced by a weaker notion, the lattice of projections.
As it turns out, there is no global “sample space”, this is a
“pointless” probability theory. This leads to consequences
which are “strange” or not possible from a classical point of view. This is evidenced in
the theory in the violation of the Bell inequalities and by the connected Kochen-Specker
theorem — which we shall see is a purely probabilistic result —
two of the so-called “no-go” theorems of quantum theory.
To wit, the 2022 Nobel prize in physics was awarded for
“…, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities
and pioneering quantum information science …”,
the experimental confirmation of this fact. But what looks strange in the
light of classical probability is exactly what is being harnessed in quantum information
and quantum computing. The point of view taken here though is that the (non-commutative)
algebraic view is a
probability theory
, and not only a description of the physics of
quantum-physical phenomena.

Looking back at the historical development of probability (e.g.
[
10
]
),
its mathematical treatment began
by considering games of chance, and traces back to early work by Cardano, and further
seminal contributions in the 17th century by
Fermat, Pascal, Huygens, and the Bernoullis in the early 18th century, culminating in
Jacob Bernoulli’s (1713) “Ars Conjectandi”, for two modern appraisals
of its significance see
[
133
,
122
]
.
Starting with Huygens, Jacob Bernoulli and his nephew Daniel Bernoulli,
among others, clarified the meaning of probability and expectation.
These early probabilists may be seen
[
124
]
as
early proponents of the algebraic approach in their way of operating with RVs
algebraically like numbers according to certain intuitive rules, which were,
however, never explicitly stated.
Incidentally, what is mostly called probability today
was called “chance” then, and what was considered “probable” then, today would be called
a kind of Bayesian interpretation of probability
[
133
]
. There is
even today a multitude of opinions of what probability actually “is”
in the real world, not dissimilar to analogous discussion about the
interpretation of quantum theory (e.g.
[
47
]
). In both areas there is agreement
on how to use the formal machinery, but the interpretations of what this “is” differ.
The formalisation and analysis
of classical probability theory gained momentum with the works of Gauss and others,
and was brilliantly displayed with Laplace’s analytical treatment of
probability
[
95
]
.

At the dawn of the new century in 1900 Hilbert announced a list of mathematical problems
which await a solution, and the 6th problem was to establish an axiomatic basis for
probability and mechanics — incidentally this was the same year when Planck announced
his discovery of energy quanta, and which marked the start of quantum theory, which was
to bring such changes to our understanding of probability, leading to quantum
probability
[
11
]
. For classical probability, such an axiomatic
basis, started by von Mises
[
146
]
in 1928,
was provided by Kolmogorov in 1933 with his so-called “Grundbegriffe” monograph

[
91
,
92
]
. It put classical probability on a firm axiomatic
footing based on measure theory — which emanated from the geometric problem of measuring
lengths, areas, volumes, etc., and had been brought to a mathematical maturation
in the preceding decades — and defined RVs as derived objects, namely as measurable
functions, and expectation as the integral w.r.t. a probability measure.

When Kolmogorov published his “Grundbegriffe” in 1933, he, in his own words,
expressed what many mathematicians were thinking about the formalisation of probability.
But the “new” probability in the form of quantum probability
[
10
,
11
]

had already been formulated in its essential lines through contributions from Heisenberg

[
73
]
, who in 1925 noted the non-commutativity of quantum observables, and this was
immediately extended by his colleagues in Göttingen, Born and Jordan
[
32
]
,
and by all three together
[
31
]
. While Heisenberg regarded the
non-commutativity more as a nuisance
[
144
]
, it was Dirac
[
50
,
51
]

who may be credited with recognising its fundamental importance first. Further contributions
in this direction came from Hilbert
[
76
]
together with von Neumann and
Nordheim. Von Neumann shortly afterwords worked out the Hilbert space formulation

[
147
,
148
]
, where the RVs are self-adjoint operators. This was one
way to capture the non-commutative properties, stemming from the fact that it mattered in
which temporal order RVs were observed or measured.

All this happened before the publication date of Kolmogorov’s “Grundbegriffe”, and von
Neumann’s work indicated a possibility on how to build an axiomatic basis for both
classical and quantum probability, but this seems to have evaded Kolmogorov at the time.
As Accardi rightly states
[
10
,
11
]
,
there is a difference between describing the mathematical construction and deriving
it from a set of axioms. And in the late 1920’s and early 1930’s the algebraic path
seemed far too weak to use as an axiomatic foundation. This was about to change
in the next decade.

It was Jordan
[
85
]
already in the late 20’s,
and later together with Wigner and von Neumann,
who had started in the 1930’s considering algebraic approaches
[
84
]

to quantum theory. This was followed by von Neumann, who in the late 1930’s and early 1940’s
together with Murray started developing the algebraic method, all nicely summarised
in his collected works
[
149
]
. This algebraic view of random variables,
in the form of algebras of observables with the expectation resp. state as
a linear functional, pioneered by von Neumann and Murray with their work on “rings
of operators” (in
[
149
]
), now provided a powerful framework for analysing
quantum systems as well as classical ones.
Subsequent developments, including the work of Gel’fand and Neumark (Naĭmark)

[
63
]
and Segal
[
131
]
, led to the GNS-construction
(GNS for Gel’fand, Neumark, and Segal) and established the connection of abstract algebras
with the earlier Hilbert space approach used in quantum physics.

Although there have been several proposals on how to answer Hilbert’s call for
axiomatisation in his 6th problem, starting from von Neumann himself (cf. again

[
149
]
), as well as e.g.
[
125
,
101
,
56
,
99
,
100
,
11
,
118
]

to name but a few, we shall take a humbler path and approach the algebraic view on RVs
in an “operational” manner, by saying a bit informally what to do with RVs, not what
they are. This is then by design an abstract approach to establish rules for a mathematical
structure, and the usual ways of dealing both with classical (RVs are measurable functions,
i.e. a commutative or Abelian algebra) and QLB (RVs resp. observables are self-adjoint
Hilbert space operators) appear as
representations
.
This operational approach is very similar to what the early probabilists like the
Bernoullis implicitly used, and actually most practically working statisticians do
today, where the underlying measure spaces rarely appear, if at all, and the real work is
with random variables and their distributions.

Our aim here is to give an appetiser of the view on the algebraic structure of
probability theories, without delving too deep in algebraic theory,
but which may even in the Abelian case shed a different light
on the subject. We hope to show that the study of different representations
of probability may bring out different traits.
This algebraic approach is also connected with a very geometric view, and it leads naturally
to the consideration of non-commutative algebras, which are a natural framework
to consider QLB phenomena, or combinations of classical and QLB phenomena.
We want to refrain from an attempt to
re-create probability theory (even only for the Abelian case) from axioms,
and will develop the starting point more leisurely;
for such axiomatic attempts see
[
85
,
76
,
51
,
147
,
148
,
149
,
84
,
125
,
101
,
56
,
99
,
100
,
9
,
11
,
12
]
,
mostly trying to develop quantum probability theory.
It is also not intended to take a puristic view and try to dispense with the
notions of probability or
\sigma
-algebras,
but to embed this into a more general and deeper structure, and hence results
from measure and integration theory will be used where appropriate.
The algebraic theory has also been developed into a more detailed and deeper
analysis and understanding of what the “value” of a RV is, and what the formal
description of an observation, measurement, or sample of a RV is.

Our approach in this paper is twofold. Firstly, we aim to elucidate the algebraic
view of probability in its simplest setting, emphasising its geometric and
operational aspects. Secondly, we touch on the implications of this framework by
applying it to quantum computing (QC) and quantum information (QI), highlighting its
potential to accommodate quantum-like behaviour (QLB). Our approach
tries to minimise the use of technicalities and generalities, albeit staying
mostly on an abstract level, trying to make statements simple and not the most general.

No attempt has been made to be complete in any way, not with respect to
the history of the subject, neither w.r.t. the selection of the associated topics,
nor in the selection of references, where obviously many
undoubtedly important contributions are not mentioned.
Indeed, there are so many different aspects — and open problems about them — that
a complete survey seems impossible, or at least extremely difficult, at the present time.
Examples of similar efforts are
[
26
,
104
,
96
,
28
,
71
]
.
But we hope that this article may convince the reader that it is worthwhile to have different
ways of looking at the subject, and perhaps inspire her or him to consult
the literature further, and possibly even pursue the concept in their own research.
We claim no originality, except for what has been left out from the presentation.
The treatment in this paper is intended to be more descriptive than rigorous,
focusing on key concepts and insights rather than technical details and proofs,
which are typically relegated to the references. Although these “vistas” are
distinctly mathematical — without diminishing the contribution originating
and coming from physics —
the aim is to avoid mathematical scaffolding, and make the exposition suitable
for readers with diverse backgrounds in mathematics and computer science, the
natural sciences, and engineering.

The plan of the paper is as follows.
We begin by elucidating the algebraic view on random variables (RVs) in Section
2
,
highlighting its importance in dealing with non-commutative phenomena.
This perspective allows for the representation of RVs as linear maps or
operators, especially when a Hilbert space structure provided by the expectation
is added to the picture. This leads to the description of properties of W*-algebras
and the structure of finite dimensional algebras.
In Section
3
, after considering the important topic on how to formally
describe observations, and connecting this with the question of whether it is
possible to assign probabilities to events independent of observations — which
is given a negative answer by the Bell-Kochen-Specker Theorem — the focus shifts
to generalised observations or
positive operator valued measures
(POVMs)
and the important topic of completely positive
maps and channels, which is the general description of information transmission.
A further example of the algebraic point of view is the connections with Krylov subspaces,
orthogonal polynomials, and even the ladder operators from quantum mechanics (QM),
including creation and annihilation operators and the (interacting) Fock space,
which again will be explored in its simplest setting of analysing just one
RV. Quantum computing (QC) and quantum information (QI) emerge as important subjects which
can be approached within this framework in its simplest purely algebraic setting in
Section
4
. Here the important points from the previous development are collected
and used to define a
quantum processing unit
(QPU) in an abstract way, and
to show how a program for such a QPU is formulated. As an example, the
Grover algorithm is described in this abstract setting in detail.
We conclude with Section
5
.

\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}:2^{X}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.31248pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
with

\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}(X)=I_{\mathcal{H}}
and countable additivity (finite here);
writing
\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}(\{i\})=E_{i}
, one has
E_{i}\succeq 0
and
\sum_{i}E_{i}=I_{\mathcal{H}}
.
A PVM
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{\mathcal{H}}
is the projection-valued special case.

\mathscr{F}:\mathcal{C}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.87498pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})

The (linear)
observation channel
associated with a POVM:
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}=(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\in\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathbb{C}^{n}
,

\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=\sum_{i}f_{i}E_{i}
.

Dirac notation

\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal{H}
,
\bra{\psi}:=\ket{\psi}^{\dagger}
,
rank-one operators
\ket{\psi}\bra{\phi}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
.

n
qubits

\mathcal{H}_{1}\simeq\mathbb{C}^{2}
with computational basis
\{\ket{0},\ket{1}\}
.
For
n
qubits:
\mathcal{H}_{n}:=(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}
and
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{n})\simeq M_{2^{n}}(\mathbb{C})
.

Standing convention.
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, we work in
finite dimensions, so that states admit density (trace) representations and all traces
(partial traces, where used) are well-defined.

2
Algebraic Formulation of Probability

In the sequel we shall be mainly be concerned with numerical random variables (RVs),
as other RVs can be treated in terms of these.
Starting with the algebraic ideas on probability by focusing on random variables
and expectation / states, we first describe the basics of this algebraic language
and give some examples. The first observation is that the algebra may be represented
by an algebra of linear maps — the regular representation. The expectation allows
one to introduce an inner product and a norm based on it. Now one has linear maps
on a Hilbert space — the GNS-construction alluded to in Section
1
—
and one may employ the spectral calculus of self-adjoint maps.
This leads to further representations, as well as new norms and the
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-spaces.
Additionally, correlation and independence, notions central
to probability, are given a geometrical interpretation.

Taking a closer look at the expectation entails examining the entire set of
possible states.
Observations or measurements naturally lead to non-commutative phenomena such as
Heisenberg’s uncertainty relation and the Bell-Kochen–Specker theorem.
All of these ideas converge on the notion of a duality between states and effects.

Observations or samples of a random variable (RV) will turn out to be elements of
the dual space, specifically with values in the suitably defined spectrum of the RV.
The algebraic structure also encompasses the idea of forming polynomials of RVs, so a
key question is whether and how to extend polynomial operations to more general
functional operations on RVs. In a representation of probability algebras as linear
maps on Hilbert spaces, real RVs — viewed as the “true” observables — correspond
to self-adjoint operators, and the problem of computing functions of these RVs is
then one of spectral calculus.

In infinite dimensional contexts, requiring the probability algebra to be a Banach or
C*-algebra (see, for example,
[
119
,
105
,
13
,
53
,
124
,
138
,
54
,
34
,
45
,
46
,
87
,
29
]
)
enables holomorphic and continuous versions of the spectral calculus; for von Neumann or
W*-algebras, one can also employ a Borel-measurable spectral calculus. However, restricting
our attention to finite dimensional algebras means each RV can only attain finitely many
(spectral) values. Since any function on a finite set of real points can be interpolated
by a polynomial, the polynomial functional calculus is fully adequate here, and more
advanced constructions can remain in the background. Basic information on algebras
in the context of finite dimensional linear algebra can be found in
[
64
]
.
A standard reference on finite dimensional associative algebras is
[
55
]
,
and focusing on matrix algebras, one should mention
[
75
]
.

We also look at how to combine probabilistic systems by looking at probability algebras
in direct sums resp. direct products as well as tensor products.
Finally, the general structure of such finite dimensional algebras is given
— concretely as a faithful representation in a direct sum of matrix algebras.

2.1
Basics

As mentioned in Section
1
, the Bernoullis may be seen as early proponents
of an algebraic approach to probability. They implicitly handled random variables
(RVs) like numbers; specifically, RVs could be added to each other, and they could
be multiplied by numbers and with each other following the usual rules of arithmetic.

Introduction to Probability Algebras:

In modern mathematical language
[
127
,
124
]
, the Bernoullis’
random variables (RVs) can be viewed as elements of a vector space
\mathcal{A}
.
Moreover, these elements can be multiplied by one another — denoted
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}

for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, but mostly, and also in the following except for these
first few remarks, just denoted as a juxtaposition:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
—
and in the classical Bernoulli setting, this multiplication
is commutative (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
). Constants, i.e. ordinary numbers,
appear as a degenerate kind of random variable. In contemporary terms, this means

\mathcal{A}
is not only a vector space, but also an associative, distributive,
commutative (Abelian) algebra, whose unit element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
represents the
multiplicative identity:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\cdot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
.

The underlying idea is that if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
are random variables, then
expressions such as
2\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
, and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
are themselves valid
random variables. If

\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
are subsets of elements of
\mathcal{A}
, then

\mathcal{S}\mathcal{T}:=\mathcal{S}\cdot\mathcal{T}:=\{\sum_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{s}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{s}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{s}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{s}}_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{t}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{t}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{t}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{t}}_{j}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{s}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{s}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{s}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{s}}_{j}\in\mathcal{S},\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{t}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{t}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{t}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{t}}_{j}\in\mathcal{T}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
is a shorthand for the set of all sums of products where the first
factor is in
\mathcal{S}
and the second one in
\mathcal{T}
.

Historically, the Bernoullis worked with what in modern terms would be called

expectation
, an
averaging
procedure or
mean
,
that Laplace famously called “mathematical hope.” In more recent physics
terminology, it is often referred to as a
state
. Mathematically,
this expectation is a linear functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
on
\mathcal{A}
, i.e. an element of the dual space
\mathcal{A}^{\star}
.

Just as numbers themselves can be “positive,” random variables admit a partial
order
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
, with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
and squares
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{2}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}

being positive by definition. If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is positive,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
is
non-negative, and therefore it is a
positive
functional;
moreover,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
takes the unit
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\in\mathcal{A}
to
1\in\mathbb{R}
,
making
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
a
normalised state
.
Note that one should really say that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is
non-negative
or

positive semi-definite
, but just as in the case of matrices and operators,
or general elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
of an abstract algebra
\mathcal{A}
,
we are lazy and just say positive. If one these really has to be positive and
not just non-negative, we say
positive definite
.

Random variables also have — at least in the commutative setting — a
value
,
that can be observed, measured, or sampled. Mathematically, such an observation is
again a linear functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}
, in fact it has reasonably to
satisfy all requirements from above to be a state. One may regard the observational
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
as the “state of the world” at the time of observation.
Crucially,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
also satisfies
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
, meaning
that the observed value of a product
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
is the product of the observations of

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
. For now, no distinction is made between a random variable’s
“true” value and the uncertainty involved in measuring it; that refinement appears later.

In modern language, these conditions mean that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
is a non-zero algebra homomorphism
from
\mathcal{A}
into the base field, also called a
character
or
pure state
.
Under reasonable conditions, such characters exist — particularly in finite dimensional
algebras. As both
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
are elements of
\mathcal{A}^{\star}
, one sometimes writes

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle,

and one may also write
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}):=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle
to emphasise classical sampling notation.

The Bernoullis used the real numbers as their underlying number field. While imaginary
and complex numbers were already known (with Cardano having used them in solving
polynomial equations), it is possible to formalise Abelian probability algebras over
the real field alone
[
127
]
. Yet, in keeping with the maxim of Painlevé
and Hadamard — that the shortest path between two truths in the real domain passes through
the complex domain — one often extends a real algebra
\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
to a complex
one
\mathcal{A}
. Usually one sets

\mathcal{A}:=\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}},

with elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
, for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
and imaginary
unit
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\in\mathbb{C}
, and the usual rules of complex arithmetic.
This extension allows states and observations to be extended by complex linearity
and also paves the way for non-commutative probability, as to deal with quantum-like behaviour
(QLB) with non-commutative algebras, it is usually deemed necessary to consider complex algebras.
The real observables of primary
interest (with real samples) are precisely the
self-adjoint
elements of
\mathcal{A}
,
while the other elements can be seen as a convenient “algebraic completion” that
makes the theory more elegant.

To accommodate complex conjugation
\mathbb{C}\ni z\mapsto z^{*}
, one needs an analogous
operation in
\mathcal{A}
. Thus we require an
adjunction
or
involution

\star:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
, satisfying

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})^{\star}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\quad(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})^{\star}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star},\quad(z\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})^{\star}=z^{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star},

(2.1)

for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
and
z\in\mathbb{C}
. An algebra with this structure is
called an
involutive algebra
or *-algebra. In many familiar cases
(e.g. real matrix algebras), a natural involution exists (the transpose in the
real matrix case) — which for the
moment will be denoted by
\natural:\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\natural}
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
— but one may also
have trivial involutions like the identity. If no non-trivial involution exists on

\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
, one may define
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\natural}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{R}}
.
Taking care of the natural involution, one then defines

\bigl(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\bigr)^{\star}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\natural}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\natural}.

(2.2)

The second identity in Eq.(
2.1
) is already formulated in such a way that
it can also be used for non-commutative algebras. Elements which satisfy

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
are called

or

,
whereas if they satisfy
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
, they are called
skew-adjoint
or

. The constants
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
are self-adjoint, and every
element of the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
or
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
is self-adjoint.
For observations and states one requires *-linearity:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{*}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{*}
,
ensuring real values on self-adjoint elements.

Definition 2.1

(State, Expectation)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a unital associative *-algebra (not necessarily commutative).
A linear functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}
is called a
state
if it is

Positive:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\geq 0
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
, and

Hermitean (self-adjoint):

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{*}
.

If additionally
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is
normalised
.
A state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is
faithful
when
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=0

iff

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.
If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is
called a
tracial
state or a
trace
.

The set of all normalised states is denoted by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
.
For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
, its
expectation
under the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is denoted as

\mathbb{E}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\;:=\;\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\;:=\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\;=\;\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle.

Remark 2.2
.

In finite dimensional algebras
\mathcal{A}
(and more generally
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebras),
requiring
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
already ensures
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is Hermitean and positive.

Now we are able to define:

Definition 2.3

(Probability Algebra)
.

A
probability algebra
is a complex, associative, distributive, and unital
*-algebra
\mathcal{A}
(not necessarily commutative), equipped with a normalised state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
. This will be denoted as the tuple
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
.

One must distinguish between the elements of a probability algebra —
which are random variables (RVs) having expectations and thus constituting a probability
law — and the actual observables, which can be measured in different states. As noted,
only self-adjoint observables and random variables can truly be observed to yield real values.
To formalise this distinction, we first specify what is meant by a *-homomorphism:

Definition 2.4

(*-Homomorphism)
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{A}
be two complex unital *-algebras. A
linear
map

\Phi:\mathcal{B}\;\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\;\mathcal{A}
is called a
*-homomorphism
if it is:

Multiplicative:

\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\;=\;\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})

for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
.

Involution-Preserving:

\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})\;=\;\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{\star}

for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{B}
.

With this in hand, one may define random variables abstractly:

Definition 2.5

(Random Variable (RV))
.

A random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{R}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{R}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{R}}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
is defined to be a *-homomorphism from an associative, distributive, and unital *-algebra
\mathcal{B}
into a probability
algebra
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
, cf. Definition
2.3
.

The elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
— at least the self-adjoint ones — may thus be called

observables
. This separates the observables
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
from the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
, which determines the probability law (see Definition
2.27
).
In particular, the state can change — for example, when measurement or sampling
(Definition
2.6
) occurs, or when it is updated due to new information,
see Example
21
and Example
22
.
Formally, such a change modifies the probability algebra
from
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
to
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}})
. However, the observables

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
remain the same, even though the state and thus the probability law has changed.

Often, the random variable is just the identity map
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{R}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{R}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
.
In that situation, one may identify the observable with the RV itself and treat both
as an element of
\mathcal{A}
. This identification is the most common scenario in the examples here.

Definition 2.6

(Sample, Observation, Character)
.

A
sample
or
observation

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}

is a
character
, i.e. a non-zero *-homomorphism from
\mathcal{A}
into
\mathbb{C}
,
cf. Definition
2.4
.
Equivalently, it is a multiplicative state (and necessarily normalised).
Denote the set of all characters by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
.
In general, for a given
\mathcal{B}
, it may happen that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})=\emptyset
,
i.e. there are no characters.
For an Abelian *-algebra
\mathcal{A}
, the set of all characters
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{A})
is also
called the
spectrum
of
\mathcal{A}
.

The notion of spectrum is pivotal in non-commutative probability. We will return
to it later, but for now we introduce the spectrum of a single random variable:

Definition 2.7

(Spectrum)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a unital algebra.
For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
, the
spectrum
of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is defined as

\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\;\mid\;(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\lambda\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})\,\text{ is not invertible in }\,\mathcal{A}\}.

(For the definition of the inverse
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{-1}
of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{-1}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{-1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, see Definition
2.12
.)
The number
\varrho(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\sup\{\left|\lambda\right|\mid\,\lambda\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\}

is called the
spectral radius

If
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]
denotes the algebra generated by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
(all complex coefficient
polynomials in
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
), we immediately get:

Proposition 2.8

(Spectrum and Sample)
.

If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
is a non-zero *-character (i.e. an observation or sample, cf. Definition
2.6
),
then no element of the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
is invertible. Hence, for any

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}])
, one has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
.

Proof.

If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}
is invertible, we have
1=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{-1})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{-1})
. Thus,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\neq 0
. But for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
one
has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=0
.
Hence,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
cannot be invertible, implying
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
.
∎

What is seen here in Proposition
2.8
is an important point, namely that the
values of observations like
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
have to be elements of the spectrum
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})

of the observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
.

Definition 2.9

(Commutator, Lie Algebra)
.

For an associative algebra
\mathcal{A}
, the
commutator
of two elements is

[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\quad\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}.

This mapping
[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
is antisymmetric and
non-associative, but is linear in each argument, i.e. it is a product.
The vector space
\mathcal{A}
with this product is a
Lie algebra
.
If
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
, then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
commute.

Having laid out the underlying motivation and definitions, we turn to examples
— focusing first on commutative algebras. As Paul Halmos advised, one should gather
as many examples as possible; following David Hilbert, we start with the simplest ones.

Example 1
.

Consider
\mathbb{C}
as a complex algebra over itself, with involution given by complex
conjugation. Define a state by the identity functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{C}}(z)=z
.
This yields a commutative probability algebra. A sample or observation
(i.e. a character) is simply the identity map
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{\mathbb{C}}(z)=z
.

Allthough this algebra is “trivial” in the sense that its elements are not really random,
it shows that the framework is not dealing with the empty set.

Example 2

(Hadamard Algebra)
.

Consider
\mathbb{C}^{n}
with entry-wise complex conjugation as the involution.
Define the multiplication
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}\odot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}
of two vectors
