\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}

component-wise (this is called the
Hadamard
product, although apparently
it goes back to
Schur

[
70
]
):

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}\odot\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}})_{j}:=y_{j}z_{j};\;j=1,\dots,n.

The multiplicative identity is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}=(1,1,\dots,1)
. Note that this is also an
inner product space — a finite dimensional Hilbert space — with canonical inner product

\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\right\rangle_{c}:=\sum_{j}y^{*}_{j}z_{j}
. Thus, for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
, every
linear functional on
\mathbb{C}^{n}
has the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\mapsto\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{r}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\right\rangle_{c}
for some

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{r}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
. One can define the
canonical state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{c}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathbb{C}^{n})
by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}})={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\right\rangle_{c}
. This is a commutative probability algebra corresponding to a uniform distribution on the index set

[n]:=\{j\in\mathbb{N}\mid j\leq n\}
; the vector
{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}
can be called a

density
or a (uniform) discrete
probability distribution
on
[n]
.

More generally, any discrete probability distribution or density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}=(\rho_{i})
on
[n]

(
\rho_{i}\geq 0
,
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}\right\rangle_{c}=1
) defines a state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\right\rangle_{c}
.
The set of samples or observations (characters) is given by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{i}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}})=z_{i}=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}\right\rangle_{c}
, using the standard basis vectors
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i}
.

An alternative viewpoint is to take a finite set
\mathcal{X}
of cardinality
n
.
The
algebra of functions

\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C})
under point-wise operations is isomorphic
to
\mathbb{C}^{n}
via any enumeration
\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}=\mathcal{X}
. The function algebra

\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C})
may also be seen as the
algebra of continuous functions

\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C})
when
\mathcal{X}
carries the discrete topology.

Clearly, Example
1
is just the
n=1
version of the above.

Example 3

(Polynomial *-Algebra)
.

Let
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}]
be the algebra of polynomials in one indeterminate
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}
with
complex coefficients, where the involution on
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}})=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}^{k}
is

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}})^{*}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}^{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}^{k}
. Define a state by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}))=\alpha_{0}
, often written as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(0)
.
This is a commutative probability algebra.

Example 4

(Diagonal Matrix Algebra)
.

Let
\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{C})\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be the algebra of diagonal matrices over
\mathbb{C}
.
The involution is entry-wise complex conjugation plus transpose
(\cdot)^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
.
Recall that any linear functional on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
has the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}\mapsto\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}})

for some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, due to the fact that
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}\right\rangle_{F}:=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}})

defines the
Frobenius
or
Hilbert-Schmidt
inner product on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
,
making
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
into a finite dimensional Hilbert space with subspace
(in fact *-sub-algebra)
\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.

A
canonical
or
Frobenius
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))

is given by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}})={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}\right\rangle_{F}
, a kind of uniform
distribution with
density matrix

{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
.
This is a tracial state, cf. Definition
2.1
.
For a density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\diag(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}})
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
a discrete
probability distribution, define a state by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}\right\rangle_{F}
.
Observations (characters) take the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{i}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{D}})=D_{ii}
.
This algebra is isomorphic to the component-wise or Hadamard algebra in Example
2
.

Example 5

(Projection Algebra)
.

Let
R=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}\}_{j=1,\dots,m}
be a set of commuting orthogonal
projections in
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, including the identity
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
.
Thus
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}^{2}
, and

[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}
. Using the same Frobenius
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}
as in Example
4
, then
\mathbb{C}[R]

forms a finite dimensional commutative probability algebra. Note that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i})={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}\right\rangle_{F}={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\rank\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}.

In case that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}
is positive (semi-definite), denote this as

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}
. This is a partial order on
\mathbb{C}[R]
(and on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
).
A non-zero projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}<\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\in\mathbb{C}[R]
is called
minimal
,
if for any other projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}\in\mathbb{C}[R]
such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}
, it holds
that either
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}
or
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}
.

If both
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}\in\mathbb{C}[R]
are
projections, then so is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}
, and one has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}
as
well as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}
. It is easily seen that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{P}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}})
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{Q}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}})
are also projections,
that they are orthogonal:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{P}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{Q}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}
, and that they are orthogonal to

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}
:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{P}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{Q}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}
. Observe that the sum of these

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{P}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{Q}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}
is again a projection. Using
the notation from Proposition
2.19
, this may be written as

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\sqcap\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}},\;\text{ and }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}\sqcup\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{P}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{Q}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}.

Note that in such a way one can find minimal projections

\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{1},\dots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{d}\}=:B\subseteq\mathbb{C}[R]
,
mutually orthogonal to each other (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{j}=\updelta_{kj}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}
) —
where
\updelta_{ij}
is the
Kronecker
-
\updelta
— with

d=\dim(\mathbb{C}[R])
, which form a basis for
\mathbb{C}[R]
, and

partition of unity
:
\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
.

Example 6

(Commutative Matrix Algebra)
.

If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})_{sa}
is self-adjoint, consider the commutative *-algebra

\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}]\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
generated by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
.
With the Frobenius state from Example
4
, this is a commutative
probability algebra.

Remark 2.10
.

Any self-adjoint
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}
can be diagonalised:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\in\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{R})
,
for some unitary
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
.
Thus any function
f(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}})
(particularly polynomials)
shares the same diagonalising unitary. Indeed,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}
has a spectral decomposition

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
with
\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}})\subset\mathbb{R}
and with
orthogonal projections
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
onto the eigenspace of
\lambda_{k}
.
The
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
are a
partition of unity

(cf. Example
5
).
Then
f(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}})=\sum_{k}f(\lambda_{k})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
, and
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}]=\mathbb{C}[\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\}]=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\}
,
cf. Example
6
.

In his influential monograph
[
91
,
92
]
, Kolmogorov begins
with finite sample spaces and random variables taking finitely many values.
The examples above reflect precisely this setting, and we remain mostly at that
level here — particularly when venturing into non-commutative territory —
although we sometimes peek at infinite dimensional cases.

Commutative or Abelian algebras are essentially function algebras, and the
following Example
7
is an extension of the Hadamard algebra
described at the end of Example
2
:

Example 7

(Function Algebra)
.

For any non-empty set
\mathcal{X}
,
consider
\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C})
, the vector space of complex-valued functions on
\mathcal{X}
.
Point-wise multiplication and complex conjugation form a commutative *-algebra
structure with point-wise operations. The algebraic unit is the
function
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{X}}\equiv 1
. If the cardinality of
\mathcal{X}
is finite,
this is the Hadamard algebra of Example
2
, otherwise
this is an infinite dimensional algebra.

States may be added to this in various ways, often by requiring possibly extra conditions
like measurability or continuity of the functions, like in the more specialised
examples to follow.

The main importance of the next
Example
8
is to show that classical Kolmogorovean probability may be
subsumed into the algebraic framework.

Example 8

(Algebra of Simple Functions)
.

Let
(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
be a classical probability space with sample
space
\Omega
,
\sigma
-algebra
\mathfrak{F}
, and probability measure

\mathbb{P}
. For each
\mathcal{E}\in\mathfrak{F}
, let
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{E}}
be the indicator
function. Identify indicators that differ only on a nullset.
Define
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{P}}({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{E}})=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})
.
Extend
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{P}}
linearly to

\mathrm{L}_{0s}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{E}}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathfrak{F}\}
.
As in Example
7
, with point-wise operations this is a commutative *-algebra,
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{P}}
is a state. Thus
\mathrm{L}_{0s}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
is a
commutative probability *-algebra.

This is essentially the infinite dimensional analogue of Example
5
,
where
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{E}}
acts like a projection. If
\Omega
has finite cardinality
and
\mathfrak{F}=2^{\Omega}
is the power set, this is the special case Example
2

of Example
7
. Similarly, for any non-empty set
\Omega
,
if
\mathfrak{F}
has finite cardinality,
this reduces to Example
2
, as
\mathrm{L}_{0s}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})

is finite dimensional.
Normally one would take completions of this algebra to obtain
mathematically more convenient structures, like in

Example 9

(Bounded RV Algebra)
.

Similarly, in the same measurable setting as Example
8
,

\mathrm{L}_{\infty}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
— the algebra of essentially bounded
measurable complex functions — has point-wise algebraic operations and involution by
conjugation as in Example
7
, with state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{P}}(f)=\int_{\Omega}f(\omega)\,\mathbb{P}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\omega).

This is a commutative probability algebra, the completion of Example
8
in the

\mathrm{L}_{\infty}
-norm.

Of course,
\mathrm{L}_{0}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
— the *-algebra of all
measurable complex functions, resp. the *-algebra of all classical random
variables (RVs) on
\Omega
— is larger still, but here not every element has a
finite integral. A practical intermediate is:

Example 10

(All-Moments RV Algebra)
.

Define

\mathrm{L}_{\infty-}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})=\bigcap_{p\in\mathbb{N}}\mathrm{L}_{p}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P}),

i.e. those random variables with finite moments of every order.
Here
\mathrm{L}_{p}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
is the completion of Example
8
in
the
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-norm, the
Banach
space of RVs with finite moments up to order
p
.
This is again a commutative *-algebra under point-wise operations and conjugation
as in Example
7
, with the same state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathbb{P}}
as in
Example
9
. Hence
\mathrm{L}_{\infty-}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})
is also a
commutative probability algebra. One thus has the chain of inclusions of *-algebras

\mathrm{L}_{0s}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{L}_{\infty}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{L}_{\infty-}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P})\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{L}_{0}(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},\mathbb{P}),

with equality everywhere in the finite dimensional case.

A further important setting arises when
\mathcal{G}
is a compact topological space:

Example 11

(Uniform Algebra)
.

Let
\mathcal{G}
be compact and
\mu
a finite Radon measure supported on

\mathcal{G}
. Consider
\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})
, the algebra of continuous complex
functions on
\mathcal{G}
. Under point-wise operations and conjugation as in
Example
7
, and with the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mu}(\varphi)=\frac{1}{\mu(\mathcal{G})}\,\int_{\mathcal{G}}\varphi(x)\,\mu(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x),

this is a commutative probability algebra. A sample at
x\in\mathcal{G}
is

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{x}(\varphi)=\varphi(x)
. This is a sub-algebra of
\mathrm{L}_{\infty}(\mathcal{G},\mathfrak{B},\mu)
,
where
\mathfrak{B}
is the Borel
\sigma
-algebra. If
\mathcal{G}
has finite cardinality,
this reduces to Example
2
.

Finally, we introduce a commutative sub-algebra that resides in any algebra:

Definition 2.11

(Centre of an Algebra)
.

The
centre
of an algebra
\mathcal{A}
is

\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A}):=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\mid[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\;\text{for all}\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}\}.

In a unital algebra, we always have
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]\subseteq\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
, where

\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]
denotes the scalar multiples of the identity.

Example 12

(Algebra Centre)
.

For any probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
, the centre
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
is itself a
commutative probability algebra. If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
is self-adjoint, the
sub-algebra
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]\subseteq\mathcal{A}
(all complex polynomials in
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
) is also
commutative (cf. Remark
2.10
).

The smallest commutative sub-algebra is
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]
, which is isomorphic to
\mathbb{C}

(Example
1
); in this sense,
\mathbb{C}
is naturally embedded in every unital algebra.

Non-Commutative Probability Algebra:

We now extend the foregoing ideas to the non-commutative setting

[
51
,
148
,
131
,
125
,
126
,
128
,
129
,
130
,
105
,
56
,
124
,
65
,
45
,
102
,
104
,
89
,
107
,
28
,
11
]
.
Recall from Eq.(
2.1
) that the involution was defined in a way suitable for
non-commutative algebras. In this setting — often associated with quantum-like behaviour (QLB)
— the product of random variables (RVs) requires special attention. Note that
sometimes we will call a commutative or Abelian algebra a “classical algebra”, and a
non-commutative one a “QLB-algebra” (QLB — Quantum Like Behaviour).

Following
[
11
]
, one can motivate the product of two RVs
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}

by interpreting
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
as a temporal ordering in which
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is observed before

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
. When
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
, the observables
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
are

compatible
, implying that their order of observation does not matter and that
they can effectively be measured simultaneously. The involution corresponds to a time
reversal (Eq.(
2.1
)), so if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is self-adjoint (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
),
the measurement has no further “reverse” aspect —– such RVs represent the
elementary observables of interest.

In this non-commutative setting, characters (i.e. non-zero *-homomorphisms into
\mathbb{C}
)
typically fail to exist on the entire algebra unless it is commutative. As we will see
(cf. the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, Theorem
3.3
), non-commuting elements

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
(with
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]\neq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
) are incompatible and cannot be jointly
observed or measured.

To speak about non-commutative algebras, some concepts and terminology are needed,
and most of them are familiar from matrix algebras.
Below is a concise summary of standard definitions and nomenclature:

Definition 2.12

(Basic Definitions)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a complex associative unital *-algebra with involution
\star
,
and let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}\in\mathcal{A}
. We use the following
notation and terminology.

Unit and zero element.

The multiplicative unit is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, and the zero element is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.

Powers.

For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
and
n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
, define recursively

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{0}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}},\qquad\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{n}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{(n-1)}\quad\text{for }n>0.

Clearly,
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{n},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{m}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
for any
m,n\in\mathbb{N}
.

Algebra generated by elements.

\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]\subset\mathcal{A}
denotes the
commutative
sub-algebra generated by
all powers of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
. If
R=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{j}:j\in J\}
is a set of not necessarily
commuting elements,

\mathbb{C}\langle R\rangle\;=\;\mathbb{C}\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{j}:j\in J\rangle\;\subset\;\mathcal{A}

is the (possibly non-commutative) sub-algebra of all polynomials in the
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{j}
,
respecting the order of arguments. If the
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{j}

do
commute pairwise,
the commutative sub-algebra they generate is written
\mathbb{C}[R]\subset\mathcal{A}
.

Unital Sub-Algebra.

Let
\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{A}
be a sub-algebra, i.e.
\mathcal{B}

is a subspace and for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{B}
it holds that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{B}
.
If there is an element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathcal{B}
which acts as an identity
on
\mathcal{B}
(
\forall\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}:\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
),
then
\mathcal{B}
is called a
unital sub-algebra
. Note that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathcal{B}

can be different from
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\in\mathcal{A}
.

Ideal.

A *-sub-algebra
\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
is called a
left ideal

iff

\mathcal{A}\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{J}
, a
right ideal

iff

\mathcal{J}\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{J}
,
and a
two-sided ideal
or just plain
ideal
iff it is both a left
and right ideal. An algebra
\mathcal{A}
is called
simple
, iff it has no non-trivial
ideals (ideals other than
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
and
\mathcal{A}
) and
\mathcal{A}^{2}:=\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}\neq\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
.

Commutant.

For a sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
, its
commutant

\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
is
the sub-algebra

\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\;:=\;\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}:[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\ \text{ for all }\ \mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}\}.

In a unital algebra,
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
.
Moreover,
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
always, where
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
is the centre of

\mathcal{A}
, cf. Definition
2.11
.
Note that
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{B}
, whereas the algebra

\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
itself is generally
not
a sub-algebra of
\mathcal{B}
.
Observe that
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime}:=(\mathcal{B}^{\prime})^{\prime}
.

MASA — Maximal Abelian Sub-Algebra.

The commutative resp. Abelian *-sub-algebra

\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
is a
maximal Abelian sub-algebra (MASA)

iff
it holds
that for an Abelian *-sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
with
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{B}
, it
follows that
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{C}
. Thus also
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
.

Mean and fluctuating part.

Given a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\colon\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}
, define the
mean
of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
by

\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}},\quad\text{ and the \emph{fluctuating part} by }\quad\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}.

Hence
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}+\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
. The algebra of scalar multiples of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}

is
\,\overline{\!{\mathcal{A}}}:=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]
, and
\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}:=\ker\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is the vector space of all
zero-mean elements. Consequently,
\mathcal{A}=\,\overline{\!{\mathcal{A}}}\oplus\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}
.
Viewing
\mathbb{C}
embedded in
\mathcal{A}
via
z\mapsto z\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
,
one can identify
\,\overline{\!{\mathcal{A}}}\cong\mathbb{C}
.

Normal, self-adjoint, and skew-adjoint.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
is
normal
iff
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.
It is
self-adjoint
or
Hermitean
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
,
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}
is
skew-adjoint
or
skew-Hermitean

iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}=-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{\star}
. With
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
self-adjoint,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is skew-adjoint.
Let
\mathcal{A}_{sa}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
denote the real vector space
of self-adjoint elements. Observe that the real and imaginary part

\Re(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\;:=\;\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\bigr),\quad\Im(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\;:=\;\frac{1}{2\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}}\bigl(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\bigr)

are self-adjoint, hence any element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
decomposes as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\Re(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,\Im(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
.
Thus
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{sa}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,\mathcal{A}_{sa}=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}(\mathcal{A}_{sa})
.

Invertible elements.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is
invertible
iff there is an element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
with

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
.
In that case,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{-1}
is the
inverse
.
The multiplicative group of all invertible elements is denoted as
\mathcal{A}^{\times}
.
Clearly, the unit
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
is invertible (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}^{-1}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
), whereas
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
is not.

Unitary elements.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}
is
unitary
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{-1}
. In other words,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
. All unitary elements are normal,
and the multiplicative sub-group of all unitary elements is denoted by

\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\times}
.

Positive elements.

A self-adjoint element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is
positive
, written
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
,
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
can be expressed as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\sum_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{j}^{\star}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{j}
.
The convex cone of positive elements is denoted as
\mathcal{A}_{+}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{sa}
.
This defines a partial order:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.

Effects.

A positive element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}
is called an
effect
iff
0\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
.
Hence
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}
is self-adjoint and the set of all effects is denoted

\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{+}
.

Idempotents and projections.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}\in\mathcal{A}
is an
idempotent
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}^{2}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}
. If additionally
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}

is self-adjoint (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}^{\star}
), it is called a
projection
. The set of
projections is
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{+}
. Two projections

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{2}
are
orthogonal
iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{2}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.
For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}^{\perp}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
is again a projection,
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}^{\perp}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.

Minimal projections.

A projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
is
minimal
in some subset
\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}>\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
and there is no strictly
smaller nonzero projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\in\mathcal{P}
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}<\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}<\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
. Similarly to
Example
5
, this may be rephrased as saying that if there is
another projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\in\mathcal{P}
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
, then either
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}

or
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
.

Isometries and Partial Isometries.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}\in\mathcal{A}
is called an
isometry
, iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}

and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{v}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{v}}^{\star}
is a projection.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}\in\mathcal{A}
is called a
partial isometry
, iff

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
is a projection.
In that case,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{f}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{f}}^{\star}
is also a projection.

Bounded random variables.

An element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
is called
bounded
if there exists a constant

C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}>0
such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\bigl(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\bigr)\;\leq\;C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}^{2}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\bigl(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\bigr)\quad\text{ for all }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}.

The set of all bounded RVs is
\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})\subseteq\mathcal{A}
, which is itself a probability
sub-algebra. One always has
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]\subseteq\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})
. In the finite dimensional case,

\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})=\mathcal{A}
, so all elements are bounded.

Internal automorphisms.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\times}\subset\mathcal{A}
be a unitary,
then
\Psi:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, defined by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}
, is a

*-isomorphism
, an invertible *-homomorphism (Definition
2.4
)
of the algebra onto itself, i.e. a
*-automorphism
.
As
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}
is formed completely by expressions internal to the *-algebra,
this is also called an
internal
*-automorphism.

An easy implication of the definitions is

Proposition 2.13
.

For any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
one has
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}]=2\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\,[\Im(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}),\Re(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})]
, and thus

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is normal
iff

\Re(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
and
\Im(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
commute.
Thus for a self-adjoint
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
,
any
