\tau_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}})=\int_{-C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}^{C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(x)\,\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x).

(2.12)

This allows one to extend the map
\tau_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
from polynomials to the continuous functions
on the interval
[-C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}},C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}]
,
\,\overline{\!{\tau}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}:\mathrm{C}([-C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}},C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}],\mathbb{C})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}

via continuity, by defining for a continuous function
\varphi
:

\,\overline{\!{\tau}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\varphi)=\int_{-C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}^{C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}\varphi(x)\,\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)
.

The proof of this theorem (e.g.
[
104
]
) follows from the
Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem and the
Stone-Weierstrass theorem. Together with Proposition
2.28
one sees that
this is the Hausdorff moment problem, which has the unique measure
\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
as solution.

As here the focus is on finite dimensional algebras, all RVs from such an algebra
are not only automatically bounded, but, as seen in Remark
2.20
in connection
with the upcoming Proposition
2.49
, the values
of such a RV are in a finite subset in
[-C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}},C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}]
; and on finite sets any
distribution can be interpolated by a polynomial, and so no approximation is needed at all.

Definition 2.30

(Convergence of RVs in Law or Distribution)
.

Let
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}\}
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
be a sequence of RVs. They
converge in law

resp.
converge in distribution
to a RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}

iff

\tau_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}})
converges
to
\tau_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}})
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}\in\mathbb{C}[X]
.

The following is implied directly by linearity:

Proposition 2.31

(Moments and Convergence in Distribution)
.

The sequence
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}\}
converges in law resp. distribution to a RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}

iff

for all
m\in\mathbb{N}
one has that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{M}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{M}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{M}}_{m}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n})
converges to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{M}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{M}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{M}}_{m}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
as
n\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\infty
.

Now is the time for some non-commutative examples of probability algebras. A very general
example is:

Example 13

(Commutant)
.

Given a probability sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
of a probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
,
its
commutant

\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
, cf. Definition
2.12
, is a possibly non-commutative
probability sub-algebra,
\mathcal{B}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
.

Observe that the elements in the commutant
\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
commute only with all elements
in
\mathcal{B}
, but not necessarily with each other.

Example 14

(Matrix Algebra)
.

Let
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be the algebra of matrices with complex entries. With
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}=(M_{ij})\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, as involution take the Hermitean transpose
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=(M_{ij})^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}:=(M_{ij}^{*})^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}=(M_{ji}^{*})
, cf. Example
4
. And as
already noted in Example
4
, any linear functional
can be written as a trace:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}\mapsto\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}})
for some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.
The induces the
Frobenius
or
Hilbert-Schmidt
inner product
(and corresponding norm)
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\right\rangle_{F}=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}})
,
turning
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
into a finite dimensional Hilbert space.

On
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
one has a canonical
Frobenius
state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}})={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}
as in Remark
2.20
,
where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
. This is the
unique tracial state

on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, cf. Definition
2.1
. It corresponds to the uniform distribution.
This non-commutative probability algebra has in general no characters when
n>1
,
i.e. no samples or observations defined on
the whole algebra —
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))=\emptyset
.

For a self-adjoint
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})_{sa}
,
the sub-algebra
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}]\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
considered in Remark
2.20

is a commutative sub-algebra of the full matrix algebra. And on this commutative sub-algebra
there are characters, samples, or observations, i.e.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}])\neq\emptyset
. They
are pure states in the form of vector states like in Definition
2.23
, such that the
state vector is a normalised eigenvector of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}
.

This is a typical example of a finite dimensional non-commutative probability algebra.
As will be seen later, any finite dimensional algebra is isomorphic to a direct sum
of such algebras. And as the algebraic view does not distinguish between isomorphic
representations, sometimes arguments are carried out directly on this kind of
faithful representation.

Remark 2.32

(Matrix Schatten Norm)
.

When considering Example
14
, recall from linear algebra
that each matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
has a
singular value decomposition

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
, where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
are unitaries
(
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}
) and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{S}}=\diag(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}})
is the
diagonal self-adjoint matrix of non-negative
singular values

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\varsigma}}=(\varsigma_{1},\dots,\varsigma_{n})
,
\varsigma_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}
. Then for any
p\geq 1

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{Sp}:=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varsigma_{j}^{p}\right)^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}}=\left(\tr\left[(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}})^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}\right]\right)^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}}

(2.13)

is a unitarily invariant
norm
on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, the
Schatten
p
-norm
.
Extend this to
p=\infty
by setting
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{S\infty}:=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{\infty}=\max\{\varsigma_{j}\mid 1\leq j\leq n\}
, i.e. the
operator norm
of

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{n})
when
\mathbb{C}^{n}
is equipped with its canonical inner product
(cf. Example
2
).

Note that the Schatten-2-norm
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{S2}=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{F}

is equal to the
Frobenius
norm, and comes from the
Hilbert-Schmidt
inner
product which makes
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
into a
Hilbert space
.
The norm
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{S1}
is also called the
trace norm
or
nuclear norm
.
As
Banach spaces
,
(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}),\left\|\cdot\right\|_{Sp})
and
(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}),\left\|\cdot\right\|_{Sq})
,
with
{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}+{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle q$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle q$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle q$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle q$}}}}}}}}=1
(extended to
p=1,q=\infty
), are
dual
to
each other. The operator- or Schatten-
\infty
-norm satisfies

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\right\|_{\infty}\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{B}}\right\|_{\infty}
, and with it

(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}),\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty})
is a
Banach algebra
(cf. Definition
2.60
).

Proposition 2.33

(Density Matrix as Element of Matrix Algebra)
.

If
\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
is a unital *-sub-algebra, with states from
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})

restricted to
\mathcal{C}
it becomes a probability algebra. At the same time
\mathcal{C}
is a closed
subspace of the finite dimensional Hilbert space
(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}),\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{F})
;
hence there is an orthogonal decomposition
\mathcal{C}\oplus\mathcal{C}^{\perp}=\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
,
and
\mathcal{C}
is a Hilbert space in its own right. Thus any linear functional

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}\in\mathcal{C}^{\star}
can be written as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\right\rangle_{F}
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\in\mathcal{C}

with some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\in\mathcal{C}
.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
be a density matrix or mixed state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}
as in
Definition
2.23
, defining a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}):=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}})
on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.
Then there is a decomposition
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{C}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{\perp}\in\mathcal{C}\oplus\mathcal{C}^{\perp}
, so that

\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{\perp}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\right\rangle_{F}=0
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\in\mathcal{C}
.
This means that for any state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
resp. any density matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
, there is a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{C}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{\perp}\in\mathcal{C}
, such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}|_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{C}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\right\rangle_{F}=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{C}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}})
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}\in\mathcal{C}
.
Thus the density matrix can be always taken as an element of the sub-algebra, i.e.
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{C})\subset\mathcal{C}
.

The next example is similar to Example
14
,
and also typical of a possibly infinite dimensional
non-commutative probability algebra.

Example 15

(Bounded Operator Algebra)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a complex Hilbert space with inner product
\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
,
and
\xi\in\mathcal{H}
a unit vector. For
A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
, a bounded linear map,
define a conjugation as the Hilbert space adjoint
A^{\dagger}
, i.e.
\left\langle\phi\mid A\psi\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\left\langle A^{\dagger}\phi\mid\psi\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
.
With this involution,
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
becomes a unital *-algebra.
Recall that with the
operator norm

\left\|A\right\|_{\infty}
, which satisfies

\left\|AB\right\|_{\infty}\leq\left\|A\right\|_{\infty}\left\|B\right\|_{\infty}
and
\left\|A^{\dagger}A\right\|_{\infty}=\left\|A\right\|_{\infty}^{2}
,
the
Banach space

(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}),\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty})
is a

Banach algebra
(cf. Definition
2.60
).

Let
\mathcal{A}_{\xi}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
be a possibly non-commutative unital
complex sub-algebra closed under adjoints, and
\xi\in\mathcal{H}
a unit vector.
Then, for
A\in\mathcal{A}_{\xi}
, one may define a state to be

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\xi}(A):=\left\langle\xi\mid A\xi\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
. This is a possibly non-commutative probability
algebra, and the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\xi}
is an example of what is called a vector state,
i.e. a pure state (cf. Remark
2.20
and Proposition
2.48
).
The vector
\xi
is usually called
the state(-vector) — typically of some system whose observables are described by
\mathcal{A}_{\xi}

— which is the original use of the designation “state”.
In case
\xi
is a unit eigenvector of a self-adjoint
H\in\mathcal{A}_{\xi}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{\xi}(A):=\left\langle\xi\mid A\xi\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
is a character on the commutative
sub-algebra
\mathbb{C}[H]\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{\xi}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
. Later, in the
GNS-construction Theorem
2.53
, it will be seen that any state can be made to
look like a vector state.

Proposition 2.34

(Trace)
.

In case the space
\mathcal{H}
is finite dimensional, it is possible to define a unique
kind of canonical faithful state. Recall from linear algebra (e.g.
[
64
]
)
that in the finite dimensional case on the algebra of linear maps
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})=\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
, there is a linear functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})^{*}
, such that for

A,B\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
one has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(AB)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(BA)
, unique up to a scalar factor.
It is automatically invariant under unitaries or internal automorphisms (cf. Definition
2.12
, just like the usual trace on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
),
as for a unitary
U\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))

one has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(U^{\dagger}AU)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(UU^{\dagger}A)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(A)
.

If this functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}
is normalised for the identity
I\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
to
\dim\mathcal{H}
,
then it is called the trace
\tr I:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\tau}}(I)=\dim\mathcal{H}
. The inner product it
induces on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
is
\left\langle A\mid B\right\rangle_{HS}:=\tr(A^{\dagger}B)
, the
Hilbert-Schmidt

inner product. With it one may define a faithful normalised state on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
,
which we shall call the
Frobenius
or
canonical
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}
in analogy to
Example
14
, i.e.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{F}(A):={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\tr A={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,\left\langle I\mid A\right\rangle_{HS}
.
It is the
unique tracial state
(cf. Definition
2.1
), and represents a kind
of uniform distribution, with density operator
{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle n$}}}}}}}}\,I
.

Remark 2.35

(Matrix Representation)
.

Recall from linear algebra (e.g.
[

]
)
that in the finite dimensional Hilbert space case with
\dim\mathcal{H}=n
, one
may take an ortho-normal basis

and define a

unitary
map

Remark 2.36

(Operator Schatten Norms)
.

In case
\mathcal{H}
is a finite dimensional Hilbert space, for each operator

B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
and any
p\geq 1
one may define
the unitarily invariant
Schatten-
p
-norm

\left\|B\right\|_{Sp}:=\left(\tr\left[(B^{\dagger}B)^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}\right]\right)^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}},

(2.14)

where
(B^{\dagger}B)^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}
has to be computed via functional calculus
(cf. Proposition
2.77
).

Extend this to

by setting

,
i.e. the

Note that the Schatten-2-norm

The norm

And as

,

and

on a finite dimensional Hilbert space.
Without spelling everything out in detail, the main points are collected in:

Corollary 2.37

(Density Operators and Projection Lattice)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a finite dimensional Hilbert space with
\dim\mathcal{H}=n
,
and consider the unital *-algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})=\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
.
As
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
is a Hilbert space with the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product, any state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{R}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
can be represented by a

density operator
or
density matrix

R\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))=\{R\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})_{+}\;\mid\;\tr R=1\}
by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{R}(A)=\left\langle R\mid A\right\rangle_{HS}=\tr(RA)
, which are in a
bijective correspondence with the set of states.

Recalling the rank of an operator
A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, which is given by

\rank A=\dim A(\mathcal{H})=\dim(\im A)
, and denoting
the density operators of rank
r
by
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{r}
,
one has the
disjoint union

\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))=\biguplus_{r=1}^{n}\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{r}.

The extreme points of
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
are the rank one operators

\mathrm{ext}(\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})))=\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{1}=\{\left\langle x\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,x\mid x\in\mathcal{H},\left\langle x\mid x\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=1\},

where

\bigl(\left\langle x\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,x\bigr):\;\mathcal{H}\ni y\mapsto\left\langle x\mid y\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,x\in\mathcal{H}
.
They are also called
pure
or
vector states
, all other states are called

mixed states
, and according to the Krein-Milman theorem they are
a convex combination of vector or pure states. Again, often the unit vector

x\in\mathcal{H}
is called the “state” or “state vector”,
this is actually the original usage of the term.

The pure states
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{1}\subset\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
are orthogonal
projections of unit rank, and are the atoms in the projection lattice

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})))
of
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, cf. Proposition
2.25
.
Every projection of rank
m\leq n
can be expressed as the sum of
m
projections
/ pure states in
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{1}
.

And any Abelian sub-*-algebra
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
(e.g. PVM-generated)
can be embedded in or extended to a
maximal Abelian sub-algebra
(MASA).
Such an Abelian sub-*-algebra
\mathcal{C}
is a MASA
iff
it is unitarily equivalent
to the algebra of diagonal matrices
\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{C})\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
from
Example
4
, i.e. there is a unitary
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}:\mathcal{H}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}^{n}
such
that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}\,\mathcal{C}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{V}}^{\dagger}=\mathbb{D}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.

Before entering the subject of representations in the upcoming Section
2.2
, a
first taste of which was provided by Remark
2.35
, it is worthwhile to
look at some more examples of constructions of unital *-algebras using other mathematical
constructs like groups and tensor products.

Example 16

(Group Algebra)
.

Let
G
be a discrete group with group operation
g\boxtimes h\in G
for
g,h\in G
.
Consider the free vector space
\mathbb{C}G
over
G
, i.e. the set of all formal finite linear
combinations with complex coefficients with the group elements
g_{j}\in G
as basis,
with generic elements like
\phi=\sum_{j=1}^{k}z_{j}g_{j}
, with
z_{j}\in\mathbb{C}
and
g_{j}\in G
.
As involution
\natural
on this vector space define for such
\phi
the expression

\phi^{\natural}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}z^{*}_{j}g^{-1}_{j}
, and as product for
\phi_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}z_{1i}g_{i},\phi_{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}z_{2j}g_{j}\in\mathbb{C}G
set

\phi_{1}\phi_{2}:=\sum_{i=1,j=1}^{k,\ell}z_{1i}z_{2j}(g_{i}\boxtimes g_{j}).

which makes
\mathbb{C}G
into the
group algebra
of the group
G
. Observe
that the product can also be written in the form of a
convolution
.
Both the complex numbers
\mathbb{C}
and the group
G
are naturally embedded in
\mathbb{C}G
.
The unit of the algebra is the same as the group unit
e\in G
, and as state one may
take
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{G}(\phi)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{G}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}z_{j}g_{j})=\sum_{g_{j}=e}z_{j}
.
Then this is a probability algebra.

This is an algebra of bounded RVs.
For a finite group
G
, this is a finite dimensional algebra, and for a commutative
group
G
, this is a commutative algebra.

Example 17

(Tensor Matrix Algebra)
.

Let
(\mathcal{A}_{c},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c})
be any probability algebra with involution denoted by
\sharp

— the probability algebra for the components.
Now consider
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})
, the set of matrices with entries from
\mathcal{A}_{c}
. Define addition and
multiplication by complex scalars component-wise in the obvious fashion.
Multiplication of two elements is done following the rules of matrix multiplication
for the algebra of matrices with complex entries: Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}_{ik}),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}_{kj})\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}_{ik},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}_{kj}\in\mathcal{A}_{c}
,
i,j,k=1\dots n
, then their product is

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{X}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Y}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{ij})=(\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{X}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{X}}_{ik}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Y}}_{kj}),

where the ordering of the factors in the summands matters if
\mathcal{A}_{c}
is not commutative.
Observe that this construction can also be denoted as
\mathcal{A}_{c}\otimes\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
,
a tensor product algebra, as will be explained later in Definition
2.71
.
A general element in this view has the representation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{k}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}_{k}
,
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{c}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}_{k}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.

As involution
\flat
on
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})
take for a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})

\flat:\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{ij})\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}^{\flat}:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}^{\sharp}_{ji})\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c}),

this is very similar to what was done in Example
4
to define the
conjugation
{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
, but here using
\sharp
instead of complex conjugation
*
.

Towards defining a state, observe that one may form a “matrix of means”,
i.e. for a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{ij})\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})
compute

\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}}:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{ij}))\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, a “reduced state” or
“partial trace”. In the representation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{k}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{c}\otimes\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
from above, this partial trace is

\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{Z}}_{k})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{Z}}_{k}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
.

As in Example
14
, let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be a self-adjoint positive definite
matrix with unit trace.
Then, for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{c})
, one may define a state to be

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c})}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}):=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{V}}}(\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Z}}}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}})
.
This is a non-commutative probability algebra.
It has in general no characters when
n>1
, i.e. no samples or observations.
For
n=1
this is just the component algebra
\mathcal{A}_{c}
, and for
\mathcal{A}_{c}=\mathbb{C}

this is Example
14
.

This example is essentially a tensor product of some not specified algebra
\mathcal{A}_{c}

with
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
. Another frequent construction is to take one of the “function algebras”
Example
2
or Examples
7
–
11
, denoted by

(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{X}),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{F}})
,
and take the tensor product with some unspecified probability algebra
(\mathcal{A}_{v},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v})

(cf. Definition
2.71
), this gives vectors resp. functions with values in
\mathcal{A}_{v}
.
In the examples alluded to above, the probability algebra
\mathcal{A}_{v}
is
\mathbb{C}

(cf. Example
1
).

Example 18

(Random Fields of Algebras)
.

Here we take e.g. the commutative algebra from Example
11
,
\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})
,
and define the new algebra
\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{A}_{v})
of continuous functions with values in

\mathcal{A}_{v}
, with the algebraic operations performed point-wise. If
\mathcal{A}_{v}
is commutative,
this is an Abelian algebra, otherwise it is not. The multiplicative unit is the function
with constant values
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}_{v}}
, and the involution is also defined by using
the involution from
\mathcal{A}_{v}
point-wise as well as complex conjugation.
Just as in Example
17
a matrix of
means or mean matrix was introduced, so one can define here a “mean function”.
With a typical element
\varphi\in\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{A}_{v})
written as
\varphi:\mathcal{G}\ni x\mapsto\varphi(x)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}(x)\in\mathcal{A}_{v}
, the “mean function” is again just applying a
reduced state:
\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}}:\mathcal{G}\ni x\mapsto\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}(x))=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}(x))\in\mathbb{C}
.
This means that in case
\mathcal{G}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}
is some spatial domain, one may interpret

\varphi\in\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{A}_{v})
as a
random field
with values in
\mathcal{A}_{v}
,
and
\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}}\in\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})
as its
mean field
.
The total mean is then computed according
to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{G}}(\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}})=\mu(\mathcal{G})^{-1}\int_{\mathcal{G}}\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}}(x)\,\mu(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)
, cf. Example
11
.

Observe that this construction can also be denoted as
\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathcal{A}_{v}
,
a tensor product algebra, as will be explained later in Definition
2.71
.
A general element then has the representation
\varphi=\sum_{k}\phi_{k}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{k}
,
with
\phi_{k}\in\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{k}\in\mathcal{A}_{v}
, and the partial trace resp. reduced state from above, producing the mean function, is given by

\,\overline{\!{\varphi}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}}=\sum_{k}\phi_{k}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{k})=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{v}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{k})\,\phi_{k}\in\mathrm{C}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{C})
.

Dirac’s Bra-Ket Notation:

Promoted by Dirac in 1939
[
52
]
,
this notation has caught on and is often used in matters related to quantum behaviour,
so it is appropriate to mention it here shortly, as it will also be used later.
Let
\mathcal{V}
be a complex vector space, and
\mathcal{V}^{\star}
its dual space. The duality pairing,
for a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}\in\mathcal{V}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathcal{V}^{*}
has been denoted by
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}\right\rangle:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}})
,
a bilinear form, i.e. linear in both arguments.

Dirac proposed for a vector
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}\in\mathcal{V}
to use a symbol called “ket”,

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}}
, to denote that vector
\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}}\in\mathcal{V}
,
and even just
\ket{}\in\mathcal{V}
for a general vector, although this is rarely used. One nice
feature is that inside the ket one can use an arbitrary label, like
\ket{007},\ket{+},\ket{01},\ket{\%*\&}
, etc., instead of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}_{007},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}_{+},\dots
.
The surrounding ket makes it clear that this is an element of
\mathcal{V}
.

The ket is the last part of the word “bra-c-ket”, and the first part, the “bra” is written
like
\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}}
, and it is a linear form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathcal{V}^{\star}
, i.e.
\mathcal{V}^{\star}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}:=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}}:=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}}(\cdot):=\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}|\cdot}
.
It can be combined with the ket to form a “bra-ket”
\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}}
, similarly to the
the duality pairing above, but with a difference, as the bra as well as the whole
“bra-ket” is anti-linear in the first argument: for
\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}}=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}}

with
\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}}
and
\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}}
from the underlying space
\mathcal{V}
,
one has
\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}}=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{y}}}
, so that

\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{z}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{v}}}
is a sesqui-linear form,
linear in the second and anti-linear in the first argument.
Observe that the vertical bar
is usually only written once when a bra and a ket are combined to a bra-ket.

In case that
\mathcal{H}
is a Hilbert space with a sesqui-linear inner product

\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{H}
, it is clear that

\mathcal{H}
is isometrically isomorphic with its dual
\mathcal{H}^{*}
via the anti-linear
Riesz-map
R:\mathcal{H}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}:=R\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in{\mathcal{H}}^{*}

to form the inner product
\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}:=\left\langle R\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\rangle
.
Thus the bra is a linear map:

R\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}=\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\cdot}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathbb{C})=\mathcal{H}^{*}
.
From this, note that
another useful notation is the tensor product
\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\otimes\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
,
which could be written as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes R\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
, and which is a projection along

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
onto
\spn\{\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\}
:

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}:\mathcal{H}\ni\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}\mapsto\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}\,\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\in\mathcal{H}.

This notation is expanded generally for all kinds of tensor products.
Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{H}
, and
consider the tensor product of
\mathcal{H}
with itself, where
an elementary tensor is often written as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2}
. In Dirac’s notation, this can be just abbreviated to

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}:=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\otimes\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
, and even

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}:=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
. Looking at e.g.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 3}
, this simply becomes

\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}:=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}\in\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 3}
.

Let
A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
be a linear map. Then, for the inner product between

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}=A\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}
, one may write:

\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}}=\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mid A\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}A\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}=\braket{A^{\dagger}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}},

where
A^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
is the adjoint of
A
. For the special case from
above, where
A=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
(with
A^{\dagger}=\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
)
one obtains with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}=A\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}=\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
the following:

\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}}=\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}\;(\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}})\;\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}}=\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}},

showing the versatility and practicality of the notation.

In the finite dimensional complex Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}^{n}
— where one may denote an element

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
also as
\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
— with the canonical inner product

\braket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}}_{c}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}
, the Riesz map can be written as
R:\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
.
The tensor product
\ket{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{b}}}\bra{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{a}}}
is then equivalent to the expression
