).
But one has non-zero elements
\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\neq 0
in the algebra

\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{c})
which may
vanish almost surely (a.s.)
,
as
\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\,\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}^{\dagger}\,\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
may vanish.

On the other hand, if the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
is not faithful and one deliberately takes
the choice
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
in Eq.(
2.17
), this
means the that subspace — actually it is a left ideal in the algebra
\mathcal{A}
—
defined as
\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=0\}\subset\mathcal{A}

is non trivial, i.e.
\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\neq\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
.
In
\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
are the elements which vanish a.s. as just above.
Note in connection with Remark
2.15
and Proposition
2.16
,
where the ideal
\mathcal{I}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\mid\sup_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\neq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}}\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}((\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})\}=0\}

of all elements where the least bounding constant vanished was assumed to be factored
out, that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
; i.e.
\mathcal{I}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\subseteq\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
.

In order to have a Hilbert space where these elements vanishing a.s. are
declared equivalent to zero, one may factor out
\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}

and consider the quotient space
\mathscr{H}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}:=\cl(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}})
instead,
the closure being in the induced quotient norm.
The sesqui-linear form induced on
\mathscr{H}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
now is positive definite
and hence defines an inner product, and the elements in
\mathscr{H}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}

are defined by equality a.s. As
\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
is a left ideal, the multiplication
from the left on
\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
is well defined, hence one may construct a
*-representation via the *-homomorphism
\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}})

induced by the left regular representation (Definition
2.39
) by following further as
in Theorem
2.53
. Observe that the *-representation
\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
is not
injective and thus not faithful, but one may still find a *-isomorphic matrix
representation for
\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathcal{A})
as in Corollary
2.55
.

In the infinite dimensional case there is no trace functional, so there is no
canonical state like
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\phi}}_{c}
in order to achieve a faithful representation.
What helps here is a direct sum
\mathscr{H}:=\bigoplus_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathcal{E}}\mathscr{H}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
, where

\mathcal{E}=\mathrm{ext}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A}))
are the pure states of
\mathcal{A}
— the extreme points of the
set of states — each of which can be shown
[
138
,
94
]
to correspond
to an irreducible GNS-representation on
\mathscr{H}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
(cf. Definition
2.43
)
in order to achieve a faithful *-representation on
\mathscr{H}
.

States and Densities:

The representation based on the GNS-construction depended on the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
,
and produced a pure vector state, whereas the previous representation used the trace as
a generic linear functional, which in this fashion is only possible in finite dimensions.
In this latter case based on the trace, the considered state is represented by a

density matrix
(cf. Definition
2.23
, as well as Proposition
2.24

and Proposition
2.33
) or a density operator (cf. Corollary
2.37
).
The idea of densities can be carried over to the abstract situation in the finite
dimensional case.

In Proposition
2.48
the set of states was characterised as a subset of
\mathcal{A}^{\star}
,
the space of all linear functionals. In finite dimensions one has even
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{H}
,
and the Hilbert space structure allows one to find an equivalent to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
in the algebra
itself.

Corollary 2.56

(Density as Element of Algebra, Set of Densities and State Representation)
.

In case the probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
is finite dimensional, it is equal as a vector space

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{H}
to the Hilbert constructed in Remark
2.51
.

Hence for any linear functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}
, there is an element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}\in\mathcal{A}

such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\rangle_{c}=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
for
all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, using the trace based canonical inner product introduced on

\mathcal{A}
in Remark
2.51
.

Define the density elements in
\mathcal{A}
as

\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\in\mathcal{A}_{+}\;\mid\;\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}=1\}
,
they may be called algebraic densities. And any state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})

can be written as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
.
The statements from Corollary
2.37
can now be translated very easily to this
abstract situation, so that there is no need spell them out in detail here.

The states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{+}\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
are in one-to-one
correspondence with the densities
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{+}\subset\mathcal{A}

(cf. Corollary
2.56
):

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}}

\displaystyle\leftrightarrow\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})

\displaystyle\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}:\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})

\displaystyle=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}).

The characterisation of the convex set of states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
in Proposition
2.48

can now easily be translated for the set of densities; it is a compact convex set, the
intersection
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})=\mathcal{A}_{+}\cap\mathcal{S}
of the closed convex cone
\mathcal{A}_{+}
and
the hyperplane
\mathcal{S}=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}\mid\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}=1\}
.

As it is obvious how to reformulate Corollary
2.56
for concrete unital
*-sub-algebras
\mathcal{B}\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
or
\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, and has
partly already been exposed (cf. Definition
2.23
, as well as Proposition
2.24

and Proposition
2.33
, or Corollary
2.37
), there is no
need to repeat it here.
The statement in Corollary
2.56
can be viewed from another angle, in an
argument simplified to the present situation of finite dimensional algebras from

[
65
]
:

Corollary 2.57

(Radon-Nikodým for Functionals)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital *-algebra, and let

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{A}^{+}\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
be self-adjoint and positive definite,
i.e. a faithful unnormalised state. Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}

be an arbitrary functional. Then there is a
B\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
,
such that for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
it holds that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(B\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
.

B
is called the
Radon-Nikodým
derivative of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}
w.r.t.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
,
also denoted by
B=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}/\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
.

In case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}
is self-adjoint and positive (definite), so is
B
. If in addition

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}
is normalised (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
, and thus
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is a state),
one has that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(B\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
, i.e. that
B
is a density for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
.

The trace
\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{A}^{+}
is such a self-adjoint and positive definite functional,
so that for a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
the Radon-Nikodým derivative

R=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}/\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
is a
density
, such that
for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
one has
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(R\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
.
Note that one may write this in a symmetric form as

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(R^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}R^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}})
.

The last result concerning the density was
already stated in Corollary
2.56
. So, in this case of the trace on a
finite dimensional algebra
\mathcal{A}
, the Corollary
2.57
is just another way of
looking at a well known fact. Thus,
as in the finite dimensional case any state can be represented through densities, this
is often the preferred method of dealing with states, especially when working with concrete
representations such as sub-algebras of
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
or
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
.

Remark 2.58

(Radon-Nikodým theorems)
.

This result from Corollary
2.57
can be extended to the case of infinite dimensional
algebras
[
65
]
, but the functional
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\beta}}
has to be absolutely
continuous in a certain sense (not to be defined here) w.r.t.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
. This connects
Corollary
2.57
with the classical Radon-Nikodým theorem
(e.g.
[
30
]
). This one may see as a result translating
the relation between measures / functionals in the convex positive cone of the dual
space (cf. Proposition
2.48
) into positive functions / operators resp. elements of the algebra, i.e. elements in the convex positive cone of the original space.

Convergence:

Starting from these Hilbert representations, the inner product

\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{2}
on
\mathscr{H}:=\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
— which is the completion of
\mathcal{A}

if the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
is faithful, and the completion of
\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{J}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}

otherwise — induces the norm
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}
, with which
one may define a stronger notion of convergence for RVs than considered up to now:

Definition 2.59

(Convergence in Mean Square)
.

Given a sequence
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}\}
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
in
\mathscr{H}
,
one says that it
converges in mean square
— or
in
root mean square
(RMS) — to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathscr{H}

iff

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\|_{2}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>0
.

Later this will be extended to other powers than 2.

Before proceeding to to define the uniform norm on
\mathcal{A}
,
now is the time for few definitions concerning normed algebras, e.g. cf.
[
105
,
124
,
13
,
45
,
46
,
87
,
86
,
34
,
35
,
120
,
138
,
139
,
140
,
29
,
152
,
94
]
:

Definition 2.60

(Normed Algebras)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a *-algebra with a norm defined on the vector space
\mathcal{A}
.

•

In case the norm
\left\|\cdot\right\|
satisfies

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|\leq\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
,
then the algebra
\mathcal{A}
is a
normed algebra
.
This means that not only the vector space operations, but also the algebra
multiplication is continuous in the norm topology.

•

If in addition
\mathcal{A}
is a Banach space with the norm
\left\|\cdot\right\|
,
it is called a
Banach algebra
.

•

If a Banach algebra
\mathcal{A}
satisfies Eq.(
2.20
) in Proposition
2.61
,
i.e. the so-called
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-equality:

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\right\|\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|^{2}
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
,
it is called a
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebra
.

•

If
\mathcal{A}
satisfies Eq.(
2.20
), its norm-completion is a
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebra
denoted by
\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})
.

•

A unital
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebra, which, as a Banach space, is a dual space,
i.e. there is a Banach space
\mathcal{B}
such that
\mathcal{A}\cong\mathcal{B}^{*}
,
is called a
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
or a
von Neumann
algebra,

Observe that for a finite dimensional normed *-algebra,
one has
\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})
,
and
\mathcal{A}

is a

\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebra as well.

The representation on a Hilbert space leads to

Proposition 2.61

(Uniform Norm on
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
)
.

For the finite dimensional *-algebra
\mathcal{A}
, the faithful Hilbert *-representation
in Theorem
2.53
shows that

\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})=\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{H})
is *-isomorphic to
\mathcal{A}
.

In the finite dimensional case, all linear maps in
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
on the space

\mathcal{H}
are bounded
[
120
]
, thus all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
are
bounded, i.e.
\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})
.
Hence one may take — as in Remark
2.15
— the infimum

\widehat{C}_{ra}
of all possible bounding constants

C_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
in Definition
2.12
, and denote it by
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}
.
This is the
uniform
or operator norm on
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
,
i.e.
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}:=\left\|\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})}
, and it is
thus a norm on
\mathcal{A}
. Observe that

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{S\infty}
, cf. Remark
2.52
.

It follows from these Hilbert *-representations that for

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
one has
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|_{\infty}

as this holds in
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
:

\left\|\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\,\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})}\leq\left\|\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})}\left\|\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})}
. This makes

\mathcal{A}
into a
normed algebra
, cf. Definition
2.60
below.
Moreover, it satisfies also

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}^{2}=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\right\|_{\infty}=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}\,\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\right\|_{\infty},

(2.20)

as this is satisfied for
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
. These results show that multiplication and
conjugation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}
are continuous in the uniform norm.

With the metric defined by
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty}
in Proposition
2.61
,
one may now define an even stronger notion of convergence:

Definition 2.62

(Uniform Convergence)
.

Given a sequence
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}\}
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
in a bounded
Banach probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})
,
one says that it
converges almost uniformly
to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})
iff

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\|_{\infty}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>0
.

From Definition
2.59
and Definition
2.62
one immediately has

Proposition 2.63

(Uniform to RMS Convergence)
.

If a sequence
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{n}\}
,
n\in\mathbb{N}
in a bounded
Banach probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})

converges almost uniformly to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})
,
then it converges also in mean square to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})\subseteq\mathscr{H}
,
cf. Definition
2.59
. For the finite dimensional case, recall that

\mathcal{A}=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})=\mathscr{H}
as sets.

Correlation and Independence:

With the inner product (now just denoted as
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\rangle
)
and Hilbert space
\mathscr{H}=\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathcal{A})
from Proposition
2.50
,
some more quantities known from probability theory can be defined:

Definition 2.64

(Correlation, Covariance)
.

For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, their inner product
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\rangle
is also called
their
correlation
.

Remembering the decomposition in Definition
2.12
and Theorem
2.53
of RVs into their
mean and the zero-mean fluctuating part,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}+\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
, and the associated
direct sum decomposition
\mathscr{H}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{H}}}\oplus\widetilde{\mathscr{H}}
, it is easy to
see that for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathscr{H}
one has
\left\langle\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}\mid\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\right\rangle=0
,
and thus the direct sum decomposition is an
orthogonal direct sum
.
Thus one has Pythagoras’s theorem

\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\left\|\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{2}+\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{2}+\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}),

where the quantity
\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}):=\left\|\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}
is called the
variance

of the RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
(in the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
).
For two RVs
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathscr{H}
, the inner product of their zero-mean parts is
their
covariance
:

\cov_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}):=\left\langle\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\mid\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}-\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}-\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\right\rangle.

(2.21)

Two RVs are
uncorrelated
if
\cov_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=0
; this means geometrically
that
\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
and
\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
are orthogonal, or that the two subspaces

\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}
and
\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}
are orthogonal, also denoted as

\left\langle\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\mid\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\widetilde{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}}\right\rangle=\{0\}
.

Two probability sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}
can not be orthogonal, as
both contain
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. But the relevant idea that their zero-mean parts
are orthogonal is captured by (cf.
[
75
]
)

Definition 2.65

(Complementarity)
.

Let
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}
be probability sub-algebras. They are
complementary

or
quasi-orthogonal
iff for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
it holds that

\cov_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=0
.

Independence is another important notion from probability theory:

Definition 2.66

(Independence)
.

Two RVs
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
are
independent
if they commute
(
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
), and the probability sub-algebras they generate (
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]

and
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]
) are complementary (cf. Definition
2.65
).

More generally, two probability sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}
are independent

iff
they commute (
[\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}]=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
) and are complementary or
quasi-orthogonal (cf. Definition
2.65
).

One may write this in such a way that for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
one has

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}).

(2.22)

This kind of independence is sometimes also called
tensor-independence

[
26
,
27
]
.

This means that for independent factors in Eq.(
2.22
) the state acts
like a multiplicative state resp. character.
It should be obvious how to extend the above Definition
2.66

to more than two RVs resp. sub-algebras.

From the Definition
2.66
of independence follows directly:

Proposition 2.67
.

Assume that the sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}
are independent.
Further let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
.
The relation Eq.(
2.22
) can also be expressed as the statement that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=0\;\text{ and }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=0\quad\text{ implies }\quad\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=0.

(2.23)

For any three RVs
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
one has

\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\mathbb{E}_{2}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}).

(2.24)

Now assume additionally that the probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{C}\left\langle\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\right\rangle

is generated by the independent sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}
.
This implies that the restrictions

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}|_{\mathcal{B}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}|_{\mathcal{C}}
determine the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
.

Sums and Products:

When considering different system which interact in some way, one is lead
to consider the ways on how probability algebras can be combined to yield new
probability algebras, and how to interpret this probabilistically.

Definition 2.68

(Direct Product)
.

Given two probability algebras
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
with states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}

respectively, and involutions
\sharp
and
\flat
, consider
their
direct product

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{C}
. It is a vector space of
elements denoted as
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\in\mathcal{A}
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
.

One now defines a (Hadamard) product as

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1})\odot(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}):=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2})\;\text{ for }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\in\mathcal{B},\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}\in\mathcal{C},

with unit element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}})
and involution
\natural

defined by
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})^{\natural}:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\sharp},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{\flat})
.

For a given
0<\alpha<1
, one may define the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\alpha}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\alpha\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})+(1-\alpha)\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})
,
to obtain a new probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{C}
.

\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are naturally embedded in
\mathcal{A}
as elements
of the form
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{C}})
resp.
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{B}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})
.

It is clear how to extend this to more than two factors.
The Example
2
may be seen as the
n
-fold direct product of Example
1
.

By essentially only changing the notation, the same construction as in Definition
2.68

can be written for the
direct sum

\mathcal{A}_{\oplus}=\mathcal{B}\oplus\mathcal{C}
, as a finite
number of products and a finite number of summands produce isomorphic algebras.

Definition 2.69

(Direct Sum)
.

Given two probability algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
with states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}
,
and involutions
\sharp
and
\flat
, consider
their
direct sum

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\oplus\mathcal{C}
. It is a vector space of
elements denoted as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
.

One now defines a product — written again as juxtaposition — as

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1})(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}):=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2})\;\text{ for }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\in\mathcal{B},\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}\in\mathcal{C},

with unit element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}})
and involution
\natural

defined by
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})^{\natural}:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\sharp}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{\flat})
.

For a given
0<\alpha<1
, one may define the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\alpha}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\alpha\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})+(1-\alpha)\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})
,
to obtain a new probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\oplus\mathcal{C}
.

\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are naturally embedded as elements
of the form
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{C}})
resp.
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{B}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})
.

For a finite number of direct summands, it is obvious that the relation

\mathcal{B}\oplus\mathcal{C}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\mapsto(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\in\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{C}

provides the algebra *-isomorphism alluded to above.
One may note that in both cases (direct product and direct sum)
the two embedded sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
commute, and the
sub-algebras
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are sometimes called the
sectors
of
\mathcal{A}
.
The interpretation of this construction is that of a
mixture
:
with probability
\alpha
one chooses
the algebra
\mathcal{B}
, and with probability
(1-\alpha)
the algebra
\mathcal{C}
.

Considering maps on such direct products and direct sums, it is useful to have:

Definition 2.70

(Direct Sum of Maps)
.

If
B\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B})
and
C\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C})
are linear maps on
\mathcal{B}
resp.
\mathcal{C}
, then
the direct sum
B\oplus C\in(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B})\oplus\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C}))\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{C})

is written as

\displaystyle\text{on }\;\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{C}:\;B\oplus C:

\displaystyle\,(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}B&0\\
0&C\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\\
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\end{bmatrix}=(B\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},C\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\;\text{ or }

(2.25)

\displaystyle\text{on }\;\mathcal{B}\oplus\mathcal{C}:\;B\oplus C:

\displaystyle\,(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\mapsto(B\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\oplus C\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}).

(2.26)

To go beyond the idea of a mixture and express the idea that two combined components are
interacting in one system, one uses the

Definition 2.71

(Tensor Product of Algebras)
.

Given two unital *-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
with
involutions
\sharp
and
\flat
, consider
their
tensor product

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
. It is a vector space of
elements of the form
\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{j}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{j})\in\mathcal{A}
with

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{j}\in\mathcal{B}
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{j}\in\mathcal{C}
, and
z_{j}\in\mathbb{C}
, a linear combination of elementary
tensors of the form
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
.
One now defines a bilinear product (linear in each entry) —
written again as juxtaposition — on elementary tensors as

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1})(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}):=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2})\;\text{ for }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}_{2}\in\mathcal{B},\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}_{2}\in\mathcal{C},

and extends this by linearity.
The unit element is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}
, and the
involution
\natural
on
\mathcal{A}
is
defined by
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})^{\natural}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\sharp}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}^{\flat}
,
and again extended by linearity. This defines a unital *-algebra structure on
\mathcal{A}
.

It is again clear how to extend this to more tensor factors.
The algebras
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
represent the component systems — the elements of
\mathcal{B}

resp.
\mathcal{C}
are the RVs of the separate component systems, and those of

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
are the RVs of the combined compound system.
The component algebras
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are embedded into the compound algebra

\mathcal{A}
by identifying them as the generating and commuting sub-algebras

\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}]
and
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}]\otimes\mathcal{C}
of
\mathcal{A}
,
with elements formed of elementary tensors of the form

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
, respectively.

Definition 2.72

(Tensor States — correlated and entangled)
.

Assume given states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}
on
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
, the components of
the compound system probability algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
.

Given states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}
on the components, one may define a
compound state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}
on
\mathcal{A}
by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}),

(2.27)

and extend this by linearity to all of
\mathcal{A}
. This is called
a
product state
on
\mathcal{A}
. If
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c}
,
the algebras
\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}]
and
\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}]\otimes\mathcal{C}

are
independent
;
and the algebras
