\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are termed
uncorrelated
relative to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}
.

In case

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,j}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,j};\quad 0\leq\alpha_{j}\leq 1;\quad\text{ and }\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}=1,

(2.28)

where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,j}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,j}
are states on
\mathcal{B}
or
\mathcal{C}
respectively
— this is called a
separable state
, a convex combination of product states —
the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is termed
classically correlated
.

Otherwise
the state is called
entangled
.

On the other hand,
let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
be any state on the compound probability algebra

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
. As the algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
are naturally embedded in

\mathcal{A}
as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
, and as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}

for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}
one may, by setting

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,r}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})

\displaystyle:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}),\;\text{ and}

(2.29)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,r}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})

\displaystyle:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{a}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}});

(2.30)

and extending by linearity,
define
reduced
states on
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
respectively.

These states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,r}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})
,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,r}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{C})
, on the components
give rise to what is called a

partial trace
, as linear maps
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})

resp.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{C}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
,
by defining for an elementary tensor
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,r}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C},\quad\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,r}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B},

(2.31)

and extending by linearity to all of
\mathcal{A}
.

Again it is obvious how to extend this to more tensor factors. This is one way how
probabilistic descriptions are extended in the algebraic picture. The interpretation of
the uncorrelated case is: when the two components systems
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
are combined,
they do not interact. Conversely, this means that interacting component systems

can not
have a product state as in Eq.(
2.27
) as a
global compound state. In the classically correlated case Eq.(
2.28
),
it is important that
this is a
convex combination of product states

[
150
,
81
]
.
In fact, if one allows
\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{C}
, any linear form on

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
could be written in that way.
The interpretation is that there is a classical probability
distribution — given by the
\alpha_{j}
— which picks one of the uncorrelated
cases
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{b,j}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{c,j}
. It is worthwhile to note that in case
one of the algebras
\mathcal{B}
or
\mathcal{C}
is Abelian or commutative,
every
state
on the compound algebra
\mathcal{A}
is separable or classically correlated.

It was already remarked in Definition
2.66
that that notion of independence is
closely linked to tensor products, and indeed the tensor product as given in
Definition
2.71
is the prime example of this kind of independence

[
27
]
. In fact, one has

Proposition 2.73
.

In case two (or more) sub-algebras
\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{A}

wich generate
\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{C}\left\langle\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}\right\rangle
are tensor-independent
as in Definition
2.66
, it is possible to find a representation of the
algebra as a tensor product as in Definition
2.71
. This means that
there is a *-isomorphism
\Phi:\,\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{D}
with a probability algebra

\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathcal{F}
, such that
\mathcal{E}
and
\mathcal{F}
are independent,
and additionally it holds that
\Phi(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{E}
and
\Phi(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{F}
.

The property which is most desired is given in
Eq.(
2.22
), or equivalently in Eqs.(
2.23
) and (
2.24
).
But this can also be achieved with another kind of product,
e.g.
[
145
,
74
,
104
,
103
,
136
]
, namely the
free product
.
It is defined by a universal property, similarly to the tensor product.
In this case a property similar to Eq.(
2.22
) for free RVs
then defines
free independence
.
Note that in
[
26
,
27
]
it is shown that
the tensor and the free product are the only two constructions to fulfill
certain requirements regarding the notion of independence.
The free product and connected developments are beyond the scope of this
paper, so we confine ourselves to these few words on this subject.

Now that the one-to-one correspondence between states and densities
together with the trace has been firmly established in Corollary
2.56
,
it may be worthwhile to just touch on the tensor product Definition
2.71

and the topic of partial trace abstractly introduced in Eq.(
2.31
) in
Definition
2.72
.

Remark 2.74

(Compound and Partial Trace:)
.

Consider the tensor product of probability algebras
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}

as in Definition
2.72
, with densities
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{B})
and

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{C})
.
The
compound product
state corresponding to Eq.(
2.27
) is for
an elementary tensor
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
defined as

\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl((\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c})(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\bigr):=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\;\tr_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}),

(2.32)

and then extended by linearity. This product state means that the corresponding density
is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
, a
product density
.

Echoing Eq.(
2.28
), in case a density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
is given by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,j}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,j};\quad 0\leq\alpha_{j}\leq 1;\quad\text{ and }\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}=1,

(2.33)

with densities
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,j}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,j}
on
\mathcal{B}
or
\mathcal{C}
respectively
(a convex combination of product densities),
this is a
separable density
and
\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{C}
called

classically correlated
.
Otherwise
the density is called
entangled
.

On the other hand, given a density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
on the compound probability algebra

\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}
, by analogy to Eqs.(
2.29
) and (
2.30
)
one defines
reduced
densities or
marginals

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,r}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{B})
and

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,r}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{C})
, by requiring for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C}

\displaystyle\tr_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,r}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})

\displaystyle=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}})),\;\text{ and}

(2.34)

\displaystyle\tr_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,r}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})

\displaystyle=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{a}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})).

(2.35)

These reduced densities
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,r}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,r}

on the components give rise to what is called (now truly) a

partial trace
, as linear maps
\tr_{p,\mathcal{B}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C})

resp.
\tr_{p,\mathcal{C}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, by defining, similarly to
Eq.(
2.31
), for elementary tensors:

\displaystyle\tr_{p,\mathcal{B}}:\,\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}

\displaystyle\mapsto\tr_{p,\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{b,r}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{C},\quad\text{ and}

(2.36)

\displaystyle\tr_{p,\mathcal{C}}:\,\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{C}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}

\displaystyle\mapsto\tr_{p,\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}):=\tr_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{c,r}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B},

(2.37)

and then extended by linearity.

Again it is obvious how to reformulate Remark
2.74
for concrete unital
*-sub-algebras of
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
or
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, so this
does not have to be spelt out here.

2.3
Structure of Finite Dimensional Algebras

From Proposition
2.61
we have seen the
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty}
-norm introduced on
\mathcal{A}

as the operator norm of a faithful *-representation. As a finite dimensional
\mathcal{A}

is complete in all Hausdorff vector space topologies
[
120
]
, when
equipped with a norm it becomes a Banach space.
The combination of the norm with the multiplication leads to the various normed algebras

[
105
,
124
,
13
,
45
,
46
,
87
,
86
,
34
,
35
,
120
,
138
,
139
,
140
,
29
]
,
which were already defined in Definition
2.60
. Here we are
primarily interested in
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras.

W*- or von Neumann Algebras:

From Remark
2.52
one may recall that in the finite dimensional case
the operator norm is equal to the Schatten-
\infty
-norm
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{S\infty}
.

Corollary 2.75
.

As a Banach space,
(\mathcal{A},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{S\infty})
is the
dual
of

(\mathcal{A},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{S1})
. According to Definition
2.60
it is thus
a
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra.

Often the name “von Neumann algebra” is reserved for sub-algebras of
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
,
whereas “
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra” is used for the abstract concept. Recall that
\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{H})

is a von Neumann or
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra for any Hilbert space
\mathscr{H}
. And, due to the
faithful Hilbert *-representation
\Upsilon
in Theorem
2.53

and Proposition
2.61
, a finite dimensional probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
is norm
*-isomorphic to a von Neumann sub-algebra
\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
.

The normed algebras are important in general, as they come with an extensive
functional calculus, especially in the form of Banach-,
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-, and
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras.
Especially for self-adjoint elements of the algebra
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
,
one wants to be able to compute
f(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
, where
f
is a possibly complex-valued
function defined on a subset of the real line,
like for example the exponential, the square root, the absolute value, or an
indicator function
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathcal{E}}
for
\mathcal{E}\subset\mathbb{R}
.
This functional calculus allows one to proceed from polynomials on general
and normed algebras to holomorphic functions on Banach algebras, on to
continuous functions on
\mathrm{C}^{*}
-algebras, and finally to Borel-measurable
functions on
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras.

Luckily, as was remarked already several times
(e.g. Remark
2.10
), on finite dimensional algebras this all reduces
to a polynomial calculus, as the spectrum of self-adjoint elements — being equivalent
to a linear map on a finite dimensional space — consists only of a finite number of points,
and on a finite subset of
\mathbb{R}
any function can be written as a polynomial.

Also, now is the point to collect few results which have been hidden in some assumptions
so far, namely Remark
2.15
and Proposition
2.16
, and to see
the significance in the assumption in Proposition
2.49
,
and show their inter-dependencies, cf.
[
153
,
105
]
.

Proposition 2.76

(Semi-Simple Algebra)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital *-algebra; then, given the trace

\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}
as defined in Proposition
2.49
, for each

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
define the functional

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}:\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}):=\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\in\mathbb{C}
. The ideal

\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\;\text{vanishes identically}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

is called the (Jacobson) radical of the algebra. It may also be defined as

[
105
]
:

\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\mid(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\text{ { is invertible
for any }}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}.

In case
\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
,
the algebra
\mathcal{A}
is called
semi-simple
.

The following statements are equivalent:

•

\mathcal{A}
is semi-simple.

•

\mathcal{A}
has a faithful state.

•

\mathcal{A}
is a
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra.

•

The trace
\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{A}^{\star}
is non-degenerate, cf. Remark
2.15
.

•

The normalised trace functional on
\mathcal{A}
is a faithful state,
cf. Proposition
2.16
.

•

\mathcal{A}
has a faithful *-representation on a Hilbert space, cf. Theorem
2.53
.

Hence, only in other words, up to now and also in the sequel, we have assumed that
the algebra
\mathcal{A}
is semi-simple, and Proposition
2.76
notes a few equivalent
properties. As was already stated in Remark
2.15
, in case

\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})\neq\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
, i.e. the algebra
\mathcal{A}
is
not semi-simple, then the quotient unital *-algebra
\mathcal{A}/\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})

is semi-simple. In the sequel, it will again be tacitly assumed that this
quotient is taken in case
\text{rad}(\mathcal{A})
is non-trivial.

Here we collect a number of results for such finite dimensional semi-simple

\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras:

Proposition 2.77

(General finite dimensional
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-Algebras)
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
be a finite dimensional
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-probability algebra
with (uniform) norm
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\infty}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
self-adjoint,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}\in\mathcal{A}
general elements, and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}
normal (cf. Definition
2.12
).
Then

•

for a complex valued function
f
defined on a domain
J\subseteq\mathbb{C}
(
f:J\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}
)
which encompasses the spectrum
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\subseteq J
of a normal element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
, there is a

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}=f(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\in\mathcal{A}
;

•

for such functions there is a
spectral mapping

\sigma(f(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}))=f(\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}))\subset\mathbb{C}
;

•

for such a normal element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}
there is a unique injective *-homomorphism

\Psi:\mathrm{C}(\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}))\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
from the complex continuous functions on the spectrum
into the algebra
\mathcal{A}
, such that
\Psi({\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\in\mathcal{A}

and
\Psi(\mathrm{id}_{\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}
, where
\mathrm{id}_{\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})}:z\mapsto z

is the identity on
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})\subset\mathbb{C}
;

•

in particular it is possible to compute the square root of positive elements,
and the
absolute value
or
modulus
of an arbitrary element:

\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right|:=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}\in\mathcal{A}_{+}\subset\mathcal{A}_{sa}
;

•

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}
implies
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}

for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
,

\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right|\leq\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}\right|
implies
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{y}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{y}}\right\|_{\infty}
, and

0\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}
implies
0\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}^{\beta}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}^{\beta}

for any

;

•

if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}
is invertible and
0<\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}
, then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}
is invertible and

0<\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}^{-1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}^{-1}
;

•

given the absolute value one can define the positive part

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{+}:={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}(\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right|+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
, and the negative part
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{-}:={\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}(\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right|-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
, such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{+}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{-}
, as well as

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{+}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{-}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{-}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{+}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
; this is also called the

Jordan-Hahn
decomposition;

•

given the absolute value, one can find the
polar decomposition

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right|
, where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}\in\mathcal{A}
is a partial isometry (cf. Definition
2.12
);

•

every
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
has a spectral decomposition:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\sum_{\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})}\lambda_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}},

(2.38)

with
\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\subset\mathbb{R}
and a complete set of mutually
orthogonal projections

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\in\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]
(
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{j}}=\updelta_{kj}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}
),
such that
\sum_{\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
— a

partition of unity
. The assignment

\Uppi_{A}:2^{\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})}\ni\{\lambda_{k}\}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

(2.39)

is called an abstract
projection valued measure
(PVM), cf. Definition
2.21
,
Remark
2.22
, Remark
2.90
, and Remark
2.91
.
The algebra
\mathcal{A}
contains all the projections
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
from
the spectral decomposition, in fact they are given explicitly by
Lagrange

, cf. Remark
2.10
:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}=\prod_{j\neq k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\lambda_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})(\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{j})^{-1}
.
Just as in Definition
2.21
, the PVM generates the commutative sub-
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra

\spn\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\mid\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\}=\mathbb{C}[\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\}]=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]
;

•

as any element of the algebra
\mathcal{A}
is the sum of two self-adjoint elements,
it is clear from the above spectral decomposition that the algebra
\mathcal{A}

is generated by its projections
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
:

\mathcal{A}=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\,\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
, and the projections
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
can be
equipped with a lattice structure as in Proposition
2.25
,
which on commutative subsets coincides with the one in Proposition
2.19
.
This lattice is denoted by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}))
.
As
\mathcal{A}
is finite dimensional, from
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
one can extract the
minimal projections (cf. Definition
2.12
)

M=\{p\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})\mid p\text{ is minimal}\}
,
such that
\mathcal{A}=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\,M
. Any PVM-generated commutative sub-
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
can be extended or embedded in a
maximal Abelian sub-algebra
(MASA);

•

Double Commutant Theorem, von Neumann:

the image of the Hilbert *-representation
\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
is a

\mathrm{W}^{*}
-sub-algebra of the
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
, it is its own

double commutant
(cf. Definition
2.12

\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{W}^{*}(\Upsilon(\mathcal{A}))=(\mathrm{W}^{*}(\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})))^{\prime\prime}=(\Upsilon(\mathcal{A}))^{\prime\prime}\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H}).

Given the faithful Hilbert space *-representation in Theorem
2.53
, most
of these statements are just well known facts from linear algebra, which can be transported
to the
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathcal{A}
via the faithful representation; the only exception here may
be the double commutant theorem, cf.

With the absolute value, one can define more norms, and associated metrics:

Definition 2.78

(
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-spaces)
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
be a finite dimensional probability algebra. In case the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is not faithful,

0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}}.

(2.40)

Observe the similarity with the Schatten-
p
-norms, cf. Remark
2.52
.
Define the completion of
\mathcal{A}
in those norms:
\mathrm{L}_{p}(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})=\cl_{p}(\mathcal{A})
,
the
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-Banach spaces. For
p=2
this repeats Definition
2.42
.
For
p=\infty
one sets

\mathrm{L}_{\infty}(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})=\cl_{\infty}(\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{C}^{*}(\mathcal{A})=\mathrm{B}(\mathcal{A})\equiv\mathrm{W}^{*}(\Upsilon(\mathcal{A}))
,
with
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{\infty}
, the operator norm of
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})

(cf. Remark
2.52
); this is an algebra.

Convergence in those norms is called
convergence in the
p
-th mean
.
As in Example
10
one may form

\mathrm{L}_{\infty-}(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})=\bigcap_{p\in\mathbb{N}}\mathrm{L}_{p}(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}),

which is again an algebra.

Note that for integer values of
p
the
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-norm can also be defined
by the last expression in Eq.(
2.40
) without spectral calculus.

In general, one has for
1\leq p\leq 2\leq q\leq\infty
the inclusions (natural
continuous embeddings)

\mathrm{L}_{\infty}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{\infty-}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{q}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{p}(\mathcal{A})\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}_{1}(\mathcal{A}),

and
\mathrm{L}_{q}(\mathcal{A})
is the dual space to
\mathrm{L}_{p}(\mathcal{A})
. This little excursion was to
show how one may introduce these
\mathrm{L}_{p}
-spaces in the non-commutative case.
However, in finite dimensions the spaces
\mathrm{L}_{p}(\mathcal{A})
are all
the same as vector spaces, and equal to
\mathcal{A}
, but they each carry a different norm
or metric. Even so, as all vector space topologies on finite dimensional spaces are
equivalent, all the
p
-th mean convergences are equivalent in that case.

If the algebra is in addition Abelian or commutative, for example as an Abelian
sub-algebra
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
of some possibly non-commutative probability algebra

\mathcal{A}
, a bit more can be said:

Proposition 2.79

(Abelian
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-Algebras)
.

In addition to the assumptions in Proposition
2.77
assume that
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

is a commutative or Abelian but not necessarily a
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-sub-algebra. Then

•

the Abelian or commutative probability sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

can be embedded in a maximal Abelian sub-algebra, a MASA (cf. Definition
2.12
),
and this is in fact its commutant
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
, i.e.
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
,
cf. Proposition
2.77
.
This MASA
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
is a
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-sub-algebra, as it satisfies
von Neumann’s double commutant theorem in Proposition
2.77
;

•

every element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
is normal;

•

the
spectrum

\Omega:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})=\mathrm{ext}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})
is non-empty,

weak-*-compact
, and this
are the
extreme points
(pure states) of the weak-*-compact convex set of states

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})\subset\mathcal{B}^{*}
. Any element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\Omega
is a *-algebra
homomorphism
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}
(a sample);

•

(Krein-Milman) the state set
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})
is the

of the spectrum:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})=\cl\co\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
;

•

for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
one has
\lambda\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
iff there is a

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\Omega:\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})=\lambda
.
Or, in other words, the mapping (by abuse of notation
denoted again by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}
)
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}:\,\Omega\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\subset\mathbb{C}
given by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}:\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})
is continuous and surjective;

•

(Gel’fand-Neumark) one has that
\mathcal{B}\cong\mathrm{C}(\Omega)
, i.e. the algebra is
isomorphic to the algebra of
all continuous
complex-valued functions
on the weak-*-compact Hausdorff space
\Omega=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
.
These kind of algebras are mentioned in Example
11
.
This isomorphism is called the
Gel’fand transform
;

•

two Abelian
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras

are *-isomorphic

the spectra

and
\Omega_{2}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C}_{2})
