•

(Riesz-Markov-Kakutani)
as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})\subset\mathcal{B}^{*}
is a positive continuous functional on

\mathcal{B}\cong\mathrm{C}(\Omega)
, there is a
Radon probability measure

\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\in\mathrm{C}(\Omega)^{*}
such that for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{B}
one has

\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\int_{\Omega}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})\,\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})=\int_{\Omega}\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\rangle\,\mu_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}).

•

Conversly, any Radon probability measure
\nu\in\mathrm{C}(\Omega)^{*}
induces in this way
a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\nu}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})
. This is another way of expressing that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})=\cl\co\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
, and it induces a correspondence between
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{B})

and the Radon probability measures on
\Omega=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
;

•

(von Neumann)
there is an
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{B}_{sa}
such that any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{B}
is a function

f_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}
of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
:
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}=f_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
, and in case
\mathcal{B}
is finite dimensional,
this function can be expressed as a polynomial in
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{B}_{sa}
.
This
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
has a spectral decomposition

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\sum_{\lambda_{j}\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})}\lambda_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{j}}
, where
the
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{j}}
are commuting, mutually orthogonal, minimal projections,
i.e. a PVM;

•

there is a PVM
M=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\}_{(j=1\dots m)}
of mutually orthogonal
minimal projections which are a partition of unity, such that
\mathcal{B}=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}M
.
These projections can be taken as the ones from the

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{B}_{sa}
just above,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{j}}
.

Structure of Finite Dimensional W*-Algebras:

The idea here is to decompose any finite dimensional probability algebra into simpler
pieces, a purely algebraic result which does not use the state. This may be seen as
a version of the Wedderburn–Artin theorem for rings.
These simpler pieces are the
factors
, algebras which have simple resp. trivial centres:

Definition 2.80

(Factor)
.

A
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathcal{A}
is called a
factor
, iff the centre (cf. Definition
2.11
)
is trivial, i.e. it just consists of scalar multiples of the multiplicative unit:

\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]
.

For any Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
, observe that
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
is a factor.
Note that
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
is a factor, indeed a factor of type
\mathrm{I}_{n}
, e.g. cf.
[
87
,
86
,
34
,
35
,
138
,
139
,
140
,
29
]
.
As will become clear shortly, any finite dimensional factor essentially looks like this.
To proceed, the minimal projections in the centre of the algebra will play a decisive role.

Theorem 2.81

(Action of Minimal Projection)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra. Any ideal
\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

in a finite dimensional
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra has the form
\mathcal{I}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}=\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}

for some central projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
, and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\in\mathcal{C}
acts as a
multiplicative unit
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{I}}
on
\mathcal{I}
.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
be a
minimal
projection in the centre of the algebra.
Then the ideal

\mathcal{C}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}=\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}

is a
factor
, and its centre is
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{C})=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\}=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}]
,
cf.
[
138
,
71
]
.
Such a factor
\mathcal{C}
is *-isomorphic to a full matrix algebra
\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})
resp. to

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
with
\dim\mathcal{K}=m
, cf. also Theorem
2.84
. The dimension

m=\dim\mathcal{K}
is the dimension of a MASA (maximal Abelian sub-algebra)

\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
, cf.
[
138
]
, showing that the dimension of the
factor
\mathcal{C}
satisfies
\dim\mathcal{C}=m^{2}=\dim\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})
.

Observe, as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{C})
in Theorem
2.81
is minimal, according
to the first part of the theorem
\mathcal{C}
has no non-trivial sub-ideals, and is thus
simple, cf. Definition
2.12
. Further, those *-isomorphisms in Theorem
2.81

are representations on
\mathbb{C}^{m}
resp.
\mathcal{K}
; and as a full matrix algebra
\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})

resp. the full operator algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
has no non-trivial proper invariant subspaces
(cf. Definition
2.43
), this representation of a factor is
irreducible
.

Theorem 2.82

(Factor Decomposition)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra, with centre
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
.
The spectrum (cf. Definition
2.6
) of this commutative sub-*-algebra,
\Omega=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A}))
,
is a finite set, say
\Omega=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{1},\dots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{K}\}
. For each
k\in 1,\dots,K
,
let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A}))
be the
minimal central projection
such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{j})=\updelta_{kj}
, cf.
[
138
]
.

One has
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, and with
\mathcal{C}_{k}=\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}

the algebra decomposes into factors — in fact simple ideals —
as
\mathcal{A}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{C}_{k}
, cf. Theorem
2.81
.

Each factor
\mathcal{C}_{k}
is *-isomorphic to a full matrix algebra
\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})
,
resp. to
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}_{k})
with
\dim\mathcal{K}_{k}=m_{k}
, cf. Theorem
2.81
.
Hence one has the *-isomorphisms

\mathcal{A}\cong\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})\cong\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}_{k}).

(2.41)

In total these *-isomorphisms are bijective *-representations on
\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}

resp.
\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{K}_{k}
, i.e. a direct sum of irreducible representations
(cf. Definition
2.43
).
Each
\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}
resp.
\mathcal{K}_{k}
is an irreducible invariant subspace, and the
direct sum is an expression of intrinsic symmetries of the algebra.

As we have previously seen in Remark
2.46
that any finite dimensional
algebra can be represented as a matrix sub-algebra, and that a finite dimensional
probability algebra is isomorphic to a von Neumann sub-algebra of
\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})
(cf. Theorem
2.53
) for a finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathscr{H}
, resp. a matrix
sub-algebra on the Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}^{n}
(cf. Corollary
2.55
),
one has to say that the *-isomorphisms and representations in Theorem
2.81

do not come via the GNS-construction, but via so-called
matrix units
,
cf.
[
138
]
.

In Theorem
2.82
the algebra
\mathcal{A}
satisfies

\dim\mathcal{A}=n=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\dim\mathcal{C}_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}^{2}

as
\dim\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}=m_{k}^{2}
, and the representation
is on
\mathbb{C}^{m}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}
with
m=\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}
. It is in a
way the representation with the smallest possible
m
for the given algebra
\mathcal{A}
.
On the other hand, in the GNS-construction of the representation in Theorem
2.53
,
the
regular representation
is on
\mathscr{H}
with
\dim\mathscr{H}=\dim\mathcal{A}=n
, in the
operator algebra of
\mathscr{H}
with
\dim\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})=n^{2}
.

Hence, comparing the GNS-construction in Theorem
2.53
with the factor representation
in Theorem
2.82
, for the underlying Hilbert spaces one has

n=\dim\mathcal{A}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}^{2}\geq m=\sum_{k=1}^{K}m_{k}
; and as
in this relation equality holds only iff all

m_{k}=1
, this is another instance of
dilation
resp. the “Church of the
Larger Hilbert Space”. For the algebras, the differences are even larger, as

\dim\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{H})=n^{2}>n=\dim\mathcal{A}
.
But one of the advantages of the GNS-construction is the existence of a cyclic
and separating vector, i.e. the “purification”.

It is fairly obvious how to translate this to a von-Neumann-sub-algebra

\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
or a unital *-sub-algebra
\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
,
and on these concrete algebras the
multiplicity
of the representation enters,
and the isomorphism can be refined by
unitary equivalence
.

Theorem 2.83

(Factor Classification)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a
n
-dimensional Hilbert space, and let the von Neumann-sub-algebra

\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
be a factor with centre
\mathbb{C}[I_{\mathcal{H}}]
.
Then
\mathcal{H}
is
unitarily equivalent
to a Hilbert tensor product of
two finite dimensional Hilbert spaces
\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{N}\equiv\mathcal{H}
—

\dim\mathcal{K}=m,\dim\mathcal{N}=\ell
and
n=m\,\ell
—
such that the factor
\mathcal{F}
is
unitarily equivalent
to

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})\otimes\mathbb{C}[I_{\mathcal{N}}]
,
e.g. cf.
[
28
,
71
]
.
Here
I_{\mathcal{N}}
is the identity on
\mathcal{N}
.
The factor
\mathcal{F}
is (as a *-algebra) *-isomorphic to
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
.
The commutant
\mathcal{F}^{\prime}
is unitarily equivalent to

\mathbb{C}[I_{\mathcal{K}}]\otimes\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{N})
.

A factor which has minimal projections (cf. Definition
2.12
) is classed as a
type
\mathrm{I}
factor. There are also type
\mathrm{II}
and
\mathrm{III}
factors, which need
not concern us here. It is clear that any factor of the type
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K})
with a
Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}
is of type
\mathrm{I}
, as the minimal projections are the
one-dimensional ones, namely
\ket{\xi}\bra{\xi}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}))
with a unit
vector
\ket{\xi}\in\mathcal{K}
. More precisely, if
\dim\mathcal{K}=\ell
, then

\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K})
is called a type
\mathrm{I}_{\ell}
factor, as is
\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(\mathbb{C})
.
The Theorem
2.83
holds in a wider context:

Theorem 2.84

(Murray - von Neumann)
.

If the
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathcal{A}
is a factor of type
\mathrm{I}
, it is *-isomorphic
to
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K})
for some Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}
, e.g.
[
88
]
.

As all finite dimensional unital *-algebras are *-isomorphic to a sub-algebra of
some
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
for a finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}
(cf. Theorem
2.53

and Theorem
2.82
), any finite dimensional factor is a type
\mathrm{I}

factor. The factor
\mathcal{F}
in Theorem
2.83
is a type
\mathrm{I}_{m}
factor,
as is the factor
\mathcal{C}
in Theorem
2.81
.

Passing from the abstract Hilbert space case in Theorem
2.83
to matrices
(cf. Remark
2.46
) through a choice of an ortho-normal basis (cf. Corollary
2.55
), one arrives at matrix representations:

Corollary 2.85

(Matrix Algebra Factors)
.

Let the matrix *-sub-algebra
\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be a factor with centre

\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{n}]
, where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{n}
is the
n\times n
identity matrix. Then there is a
unitary matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{\ell}],

where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(\mathbb{C})
is the
\ell\times\ell
unit matrix, and
n=m\,\ell
;
e.g. cf.
[
28
]
. For the commutant
\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
one has

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{m}]\otimes\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(\mathbb{C})
.

The foregoing results are now used for the projections in the centre of a sub-algebra

[
138
,
152
,
28
,
71
]
, to parallel Theorem
2.82
:

Theorem 2.86

(Hilbert Space Factor Decomposition)
.

Let
\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
be a unital von Neumann-sub-algebra on a
finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
. Recall
that the centre
\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{Q})\subseteq\mathcal{Q}
(cf. Definition
2.11
and Example
12
)
is a commutative von-Neumann-sub-algebra, spanned by a PVM
M=\{P_{k}\}_{(k=1,\dots,K)}
of
mutually orthogonal
minimal projections
, cf. Proposition
2.79
,
cf. Definition
2.21
and Remark
2.90
.
Setting
\mathcal{H}_{k}:=P_{k}(\mathcal{H})=\im P_{k}
, one
thus has
\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{H}_{k}
as an orthogonal direct sum.

For each
k=1,\dots,K
, form the von-Neumann-sub-algebras
\mathcal{F}_{k}:=P_{k}\mathcal{Q}P_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{k})
, which according to Theorem
2.81
are all factors.
Then
\mathcal{Q}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{F}_{k}
(cf. Definition
2.69
), i.e. a direct sum
of factor algebras.

From Theorem
2.83
one has that each
\mathcal{H}_{k}\equiv\mathcal{K}_{k}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{k}

is
unitarily equivalent
to a tensor product of two Hilbert spaces, so that

\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{H}_{k}\equiv\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\mathcal{K}_{k}\otimes\mathcal{N}_{k}\bigr).

(2.42)

Further, when considering the factor
\mathcal{F}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{k})
as acting on
\mathcal{H}_{k}
,
from Theorem
2.83
follows that it is
unitarily equivalent
to

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}_{k})\otimes\mathbb{C}[I_{\mathcal{N}_{k}}]
. Thus

\mathcal{Q}=\,\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{F}_{k}\;\equiv\;\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\,\bigl(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}_{k})\otimes I_{\mathcal{N}_{k}}\bigr).

(2.43)

Proof.

The space decomposition is seen quickly from

\mathcal{H}=I_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{H})=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}P_{k}(\mathcal{H})=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\im P_{k}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{H}_{k}.

The algebra decomposition follows from

\mathcal{Q}=I_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{Q}I_{\mathcal{H}}=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}P_{k}\right)\mathcal{Q}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{K}P_{j}\right)=\sum_{k,j=1}^{K}P_{k}\mathcal{Q}P_{j}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}P_{k}\mathcal{Q}P_{k},

as
P_{k}P_{j}=\updelta_{kj}P_{k}
, and one has for
k\neq j
that
P_{k}\mathcal{Q}P_{j}=\mathcal{Q}P_{k}P_{j}=\{0\}
.
It thus reduces to
\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}P_{k}\mathcal{Q}P_{k}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{F}_{k}
.
∎

This is now easily translated into the picture and language of matrices,
e.g. cf.
[
28
]
:

Corollary 2.87

(Matrix Factor Decomposition)
.

Let
\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be a unital *-sub-algebra. Let
\mathcal{Z}=\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{M})
be
its centre, and a PVM (cf. Definition
2.21
) of
minimal projections

M=\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathcal{Z}
, such that
\mathcal{Z}=\spn M
.
According to Theorem
2.81
, each
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
is a factor
and
\mathcal{M}=\oplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
, hence
there is a unitary matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\left(\oplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{M}_{k}\right),

(2.44)

where each
\mathcal{M}_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n_{k}}
is a factor isomorphic to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
,

n_{k}=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
, and
n=\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}
.
From Corollary
2.85
one may glean that one can choose
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}
such that each

\mathcal{M}_{k}=\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{\ell_{k}}],\;\text{ with }\;n_{k}=m_{k}\ell_{k}.

(2.45)

Equivalently, each
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\in\mathcal{M}
has, when transformed, according to
Eq.(
2.44
), the block-diagonal form

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{1}&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{K}\end{bmatrix}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k},

(2.46)

where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k}\in\mathcal{M}_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n_{k}}(\mathbb{C})
, and with
Eq.(
2.45
) one has with certain
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}_{m_{k}}\in\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}_{m_{k}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{\ell_{k}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}_{m_{k}}&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{A}}}_{m_{k}}\end{bmatrix}.

(2.47)

Remark 2.88

(Multiplicity)
.

From Theorem
2.81
and Theorem
2.82
the decomposition
is via
*-isomorphisms
. But observe, from the last two
Eqs.(
2.46
) and (
2.47
) in Corollary
2.87
,
that for a random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\in\mathcal{M}_{sa}
, a value in the spectrum
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}})

— an eigenvalue and hence a possible value in a sample or observation —
has to appear in one
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k})
of the
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k}\in\mathcal{M}_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n_{k}}
in
Eq.(
2.46
). And the Eq.(
2.47
) shows that this
eigenvalue has at least multiplicity
\ell_{k}
.

This multiplicity
\ell_{k}
is established via
unitary equivalence
based on the
underlying Hilbert spaces
\mathcal{H}_{k}
resp.
\mathbb{C}^{n_{k}}
, which is a more refined form of
*-isomorphism, and the multiplicity
\ell_{k}
is a feature of the representation,
here the GNS-representation, cf. Theorem
2.53
, whereas the dimension
m_{k}

is an
intrinsic
property of the abstract algebra
\mathcal{A}
, independent of
any representation.

These analogous decompositions, namely Eq.(
2.43
) in Theorem
2.86
,
in Corollary
2.87
the Eqs.(
2.44
) and (
2.46
),
and Eq.(
2.41
) in Theorem
2.82
,
all indicate, in similar ways, internal symmetries in
the algebra, for further information on this, e.g. cf.
[
58
]

and the references therein. This subject will not pursued further here except
for a few remarks which can be seen in an easy way by looking at
Eq.(
2.41
) and Eqs.(
2.44
)–(
2.47
).
From Eq.(
2.41
) it is seen that each
\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}
in

\mathbb{C}^{m}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}
is an irreducible invariant subspace,
with the decomposition representing the intrinsic symmetries of the algebra
\mathcal{A}
.

In Eqs.(
2.44
)–(
2.47
)
in the transformed form one has
\mathbb{C}^{n}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{C}^{n_{k}}
, and from
Eq.(
2.46
) it is obvious that each of the
\mathbb{C}^{n_{k}}
— which is
the carrier for the representation of one of the factors
\mathcal{M}_{k}
— is invariant under
all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}\in\mathcal{M}
. This is a blown-up version (by a factor
\ell_{k}
) of
the one in Eq.(
2.41
), which results from the
representation resp. realisation as a sub-algebra of some “larger”
full algebra
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
on
\mathbb{C}^{n}
. This is what causes the multiplicity mentioned
in Remark
2.88
, in that Eqs.(
2.45
) and (
2.47
)
indicate that the representation of each factor
\mathcal{M}_{k}
on the corresponding

\mathbb{C}^{n_{k}}
may be further reducible to possibly
\ell_{k}
repeated identical

irreducible
representations or realisations of the factor
\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})
,
as
\mathbb{C}^{n_{k}}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{\ell_{k}}\mathbb{C}^{m_{k}}
.

Note that up to now a possible
state on the algebra, which carries the probabilistic information, has not been used in
these structure results at all.

Remark 2.89

(Probabilistic Structure Interpretation)
.

Recalling the construction Definition
2.68
of the direct product and the equivalent
one of the direct sum in Definition
2.69
, one sees that the above decompositions
are exactly this, direct sums of algebras, in fact factors. Recalling the
interpretation of this construction, following the Definition
2.69
it was
stated that this is what one would call a mixture. It is equivalent to a classical
resp. commutative algebra sampling, and then deciding which of the summands to take
for the further action.

One might also recall, that in Eq.(
2.41
) in the above
Theorem
2.82
, each summand
\mathcal{C}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
is a factor,
produced by one of the minimal projection in the centre of the algebra,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{A})
, cf. Theorem
2.81
. Now, if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})

is the current state of the algebra, then each factor
\mathcal{C}_{k}
in the direct sum is chosen
with probability
\alpha_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})
. Obviously, as the minimal projections in the
centre form a partition of unity,
\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, one has
\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}=1
.

Projective Measurements:

The foregoing shows the importance of the projections when describing a probability algebra,
especially when realising that in the finite dimensional case they are always
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras.
These are generated by their projections, and thus here is the appropriate point to
discuss the extended concept of measurement associated with projective measurements.

In Definition
2.21
the concept of a projection valued measure (PVM) was already
introduced on the special
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
, as well in an abstract
setting in Proposition
2.77
. These turned out to describe the
most basic measurements. This development applies also one-to-one to the
sub-algebra representing
\mathcal{A}
in Corollary
2.55
. This has to
be translated to the Hilbert space representation from the GNS construction in
Theorem
2.53
with a finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathscr{H}
.
It is then generalised to the abstract
setting of abstract
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras in Proposition
2.77
.

Remark 2.90

(Projective Measurement and Projection Valued Measure (PVM) — Hilbert
Space Setting)
.

Considering PVMs, analogous definitions to Definition
2.21
in the Hilbert space
setting can be phrased as follows: every self-adjoint

A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{H})_{sa}
is known from spectral theory (e.g.
[
124
]
)
to have a spectral decomposition analogous to Eq.(
2.38
):

A=\sum_{\lambda_{k}\in\sigma(A)}\lambda_{k}\,P_{\lambda_{k}},

(2.48)

where the
P_{\lambda_{k}}
is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace

\mathscr{H}_{\lambda_{k}}\subseteq\mathscr{H}
; it is given by a polynomial in
A

(cf. Proposition
2.77
). These orthogonal, and also pairwise orthogonal,
projections are a PVM, and generate, just as in Definition
2.21
and Proposition
2.77
,
a commutative sub-algebra which equals
\mathbb{C}[A]
. Each such commutative sub-algebra
can be extended to or embedded in a MASA, by breaking down the projections
in the PVM into
minimal projections
.

As before, possible sharp observations are elements of the
spectrum
\sigma(A)
, e.g.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(A)=\lambda_{k}
with probability

p_{k}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(P_{\lambda_{k}})
for some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[A])
,
called a
projective measurement
or
sharp observation
.
Such a sharp observation is a character
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[A])
,
and thus has to be an extreme point of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathcal{A}])
.
In finite dimensions, these all have the form

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(A)=\tr(\ket{\psi_{k}}\bra{\psi_{k}}A)
of a vector state,
where
\psi_{k}\in\mathscr{H}
is a unit eigenvector of
A
, i.e.
A\psi_{k}=\lambda_{k}\psi_{k}
.
As was mentioned before, the unit vector
\psi_{k}
is often also called the state
or
state vector
, and this is the original meaning of the concept, i.e. the system modelled on
\mathscr{H}
whose observables are described by
\mathcal{A}
resp.
\Upsilon(\mathcal{A})

was measured or is in the state
\psi_{k}
.

As already mentioned, such pairwise orthogonal projections as in Eq.(
2.48
)
are a partition of unity and form a PVM

\Uppi_{H}:2^{X}\ni\{x\}\mapsto P_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{H})),

(2.49)

where
\sigma(A)
has been replaced by a finite set
X
, cf. Remark
2.22
.
If an observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{x}(P_{x})=1
is made, one may say the outcome is
x\in X
.

Remark 2.91

(Abstract Projection Valued Measure (PVM))
.

Consider an observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
, with spectral decomposition as in
Eq.(
2.38
). Possible observations are elements of the spectrum
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
,
e.g.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\lambda_{k}
with probability
p_{k}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}})
for some

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}])
. In this case it is known that for the corresponding projection
from the PVM
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\supset\{\lambda_{k}\}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
one has

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}})=1
and for all other projections
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{j}})=0

for
\lambda_{j}\neq\lambda_{k}
(these are sharp observations).
Hence knowing
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}})=1
— i.e. the
event encoded by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{\lambda_{k}}
is true, or the system is in a state covered
by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
— is equivalent to knowing that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
has the value
\lambda_{k}
.
Such sharp observations of a projection from a PVM
are again called
projective measurements
resp.
projective observations
.

A bit more general PVM is an assignment

\Uppi_{X}:2^{X}\ni\{x\}\mapsto\Uppi_{X}(\{x\})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}),

(2.50)

satisfying the requirements as laid out in Definition
2.21
and Remark
2.22
,
i.e.

\sum_{x\in X}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}},\quad\text{and }\quad\forall x,y\in X:\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{y}=\updelta_{xy}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}.

(2.51)

And, as already described in Definition
2.21
, Proposition
2.77
, and
Remark
2.90
, the PVM generates a commutative sub-algebra

\spn\{\Uppi_{X}(\{x\})\mid x\in X\}=\mathbb{C}[\{\Uppi_{X}(\{x\})\}]\subseteq\mathcal{A}.

Each such commutative sub-algebra
can be extended to or embedded in a MASA, by breaking down the projections
in the PVM into
minimal projections
.

Remark 2.92
.

While in Proposition
2.25
an atomic sharp observation was connected
with a vector state, i.e. a pure state, now this has been generalised to
sharp observations connected to a PVM (cf. Definition
2.21
, Eq.(
2.90
)
in Remark
2.90
, Proposition
2.77
, and the
foregoing Eq.(
2.50
) in Remark
2.91
), i.e. one
may speak about an event represented by a projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))
resp.
P_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathscr{H}))
resp.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
being true or false.
Observing the sharp event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{x}
then means that
x\in X
has certainly occurred.

As a final result connected with both the structure of algebras and PVMs, one may take a
look at Gleason’s theorem. As one might recall from Proposition
2.77
, a finite
dimensional W*-algebra
\mathcal{A}
is generated by its projections
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
. The question
now arises, whether a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is determined by its behaviour
on the projections. This is true in classical probability, i.e. for Abelian algebras.
The question in the general case is answered in the affirmative by Gleason’s theorem,
cf. e.g.
[
37
]
:

Theorem 2.93

(Gleason)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a finite dimensional Hilbert space with
\dim\mathcal{H}>2
,
and consider the algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
of all linear maps, and the lattice

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})))
of all projections
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))

(cf. Proposition
2.25
).

A function
\gamma:\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>[0,1]
which is such that for
any

given PVM

defined on a finite set

and like in Eq.(

\sum_{x\in X}\gamma(\Uppi_{X}(\{x\}))=1
and that
for any subset

it holds that

\gamma(\sum_{x\in S}\Uppi_{X}(\{x\}))=\sum_{x\in S}\gamma(\Uppi_{X}(\{x\}))

(2.52)

— this means that it defines a probability measure on

and on the PVM

\Uppi_{X}
, namely
\mathbb{P}(\{x\}):=\mathbb{P}(P_{x})=\gamma(P_{x})

on the Boolean algebra as in Proposition

—
can be

.

Conversely, a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
gives rise to a

\Uppi_{X}
and on

\mathbb{P}(\{x\}):=\mathbb{P}(\Uppi_{X}(\{x\})):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\Uppi_{X}(\{x\}))\in[0,1]

on the Boolean algebra generated like in Proposition
