.

It should be clear that the theorem holds also for any finite dimensional probability
algebra which has no factor isomorphic to
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
with
\dim\mathcal{K}=2

(factor of type
\mathrm{I}_{2}
) in their factor decomposition,
cf. Theorem
2.86
and Theorem
2.82
)

Structured Representation of States and PVMs:

In the foregoing, the general structure of finite dimensional algebras was shown to
be a direct sum of factors, starting from the fundamental Theorem
2.86
for
sub-algebras of
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, where
\mathcal{H}
is a finite dimensional Hilbert space, and
thus also for matrix sub-algebras of
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
in Corollary
2.87
with explicit
formulas in Eq.(
2.46
), as well as for general abstract algebras in
Theorem
2.82
. The basic results about faithful representations
and the GNS construction Theorem
2.53
and
Corollary
2.55
have been the basis for this.

The two concepts which have emerged so far to describe the probabilistic content
are on one hand PVMs as a general system of “yes-no” questions, as well as states to produce
expectations for these questions. It is important that states can be identified
via the canonical inner product given through the suitably normalised trace — essentially
the unique tracial state (cf. Definition
2.1
) on a finite dimensional space —
with elements in the algebra, the so-called density matrices resp. operators as
detailled in Proposition
2.33
, Corollary
2.37
, and Corollary
2.56
.
The general results on the geometry of states in Proposition
2.48
carry
over to the set of density matrices, cf.
[
17
,
93
]
.

For simplicity, the following discussion is carried out for the matrix representation
of a finite dimensional algebra
\mathcal{A}
in
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
as detailed in
Corollary
2.87
with explicit formulas in
Eqs.(
2.46
) and (
2.47
). It is then a routine task
to translate this into the Hilbert space representation or formulate it for
the abstract algebra formulation.

Corollary 2.94

(Structure of Density Matrices)
.

Let
(\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}})
be a probability algebra.
A density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})
of the sub-algebra
\mathcal{M}

representing the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{M})

can be unitarily transformed to the block-diagonal form

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{1}&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{K}\end{bmatrix}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k},

(2.53)

where each
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}\in\mathbb{M}_{n_{k}}(\mathbb{C})_{+}
. Together with Eq.(
2.45
) from
Corollary
2.87
, one has for each of these the further block-diagonal form
with identical diagonal blocks
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}\in\mathbb{M}_{m_{k}}(\mathbb{C})_{+}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}\otimes{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 2.58334pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 1.07639pt\hbox{\kern-1.50696pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-1.29167pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\textstyle\ell_{k}$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.01385pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.86108pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle\ell_{k}$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle\ell_{k}$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 3.22916pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.73193pt\hbox{\kern-1.93747pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.6458pt\hbox{\kern-1.72218pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle\ell_{k}$}}}}}}}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{\ell_{k}}=\frac{1}{\ell_{k}}\,\begin{bmatrix}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}\end{bmatrix},

(2.54)

with
n=\sum_{k}n_{k}
, as well as for all
k:\;n_{k}=m_{k}\ell_{k}
. Here the scaling
has been performed so that
\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}
.

According to Corollary
2.87
, the form Eq.(
2.53
) comes
from a direct sum of algebras in Eq.(
2.44
),

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\oplus_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{M}_{k}
, with each
\mathcal{M}_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{n_{k}}(\mathbb{C})

a factor unitarily equivalent to
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\mathcal{M}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
, where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{M})
with

n_{k}=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}
is one of the minimal projections in the centre of
\mathcal{M}
.
In Remark
2.89
, the probabilistic interpretation was that this corresponds
to a classical experiment choosing with probability
\alpha_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k})

which of the summands to activate. With the foregoing, we can conclude that

\alpha_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k})=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k})=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{k})=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{k}=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\hat{R}}}_{m_{k}}.

This algebraic structure, which holds for all densities
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})
,
can now be combined with the linear algebra structure shown in Proposition
2.33
.
The set of density matrices was shown to be the disjoint union of the densities of
different rank,
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})=\biguplus_{r=1}^{n}\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})_{r}
, where
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})_{r}

is the density matrices with rank
r
.

This combined structure can now be seen in the light of the geometric structure of

\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})
. In Proposition
2.48

it was stated that the states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{+}\subset\mathcal{A}^{sa}\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
are in the dual positive cone
\mathcal{A}^{+}
. As states are self-adjoint, all
can be played out in the real space
\mathcal{A}^{sa}
. So the normalisation condition

\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\right\rangle=1
specifies a hyperplane
\mathcal{T}\subset\mathcal{A}^{sa}
; and thus

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})=\mathcal{A}^{+}\cap\mathcal{T}
. It should be noted that this hyperplane is orthogonal
to the subspace
\mathbb{R}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}]\subset\mathcal{A}^{sa}
. From Proposition
2.33
is is known that
for the matrix representation for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
there is a unique density matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})_{sa}
. The density matrices have to be positive and normalised, thus

\mathrm{D}(\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}))=\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})_{+}\cap\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mid\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}=1\}
are again on the intersection of
positive cone and hyperplane. Note again that the hyperplane
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mid\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{R}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}})=1\}

is perpendicular to the one dimensional subspace resp. line
\mathbb{R}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}]\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})_{sa}
.

3
Developments from Algebraic Probability

While up to now mainly the algebraic aspects of the subject were in the foreground,
only a minimum of analytic concepts had to be addressed. By concentrating on
finite dimensional algebras, most of the analytical difficulties could be avoided.
It is by now clear that the possible observed valued of an algebraic observable
are elements of its spectrum. Thus to deal with continuously distributed RVs,
the corresponding representation mappings have to be operators on an infinite
dimensional Hilbert space. And to deal with unbounded RVs, one has to address
unbounded operators in an infinite dimensional Hilbert space, with all the
difficulties this might involve. The reader interested
in this area may consult the recent monograph
[
121
]
and the
references therein.

Here we continue the discussion of observations in finite dimensional
probability algebras. The subject of non-commutativity has surprising consequences,
like Heisenberg’s uncertainty relation and the Bell-Kochen-Specker
1
1

1

Often it
is just called the Kochen-Specker theorem. But it turns out that
John Stewart Bell actually proved the theorem in 1966, one year before Simon Kochen
and Ernst Specker.

theorem.

From observations as samples or characters (cf. Definition
2.6
) as well as their
generalisation, the projection valued measures (PVM, cf. Remark
2.20
,
Proposition
2.77
, and Remark
2.91
), we proceed by looking at

valuations
in Section
3.1
. These operations can be seen as examples
of information transmission. Even more generalised measurements or observations,
the
Positive Operator Valued Measures
(POVM)
are touched upon in Section
3.2
. This leads to a brief look on how to model
the transmission of information in general, a concept called

channels
. This is also a way to model input information from a classical system
— a commutative probability algebra — to a general, possibly non-commutative one,
modelling QLB-effects, and transmit this information to other such systems, and finally
read out or output (POVM measurement) in a classical system. Another important
subject is the updating of probabilities and expected values due to information from
observations; this can also be addressed in the picture of channels.

Finally, a subject of classical probability theory is touched upon, where the
methods of algebraic probability can be used, leading to new views on matters
like graphs, reaction networks, random walks, and Markov chains. This is the
so-called quantum decomposition of classical commuting RVs,
which for analysis purposes are embedded in an algebra of non-commuting
operators on Fock spaces in Section
3.3
.

3.1
Observations and Valuations

In Definition
2.6
observations of elements of a
commutative *-sub-algebra
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
were defined,
they turned out to be
multiplicative

states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})
, i.e. *-algebra homomorphisms. As the image range
\mathbb{C}
is commutative,
it is clear that there are in general no non-zero one-dimensional *-algebra homomorphisms
on non-commutative probability algebras.
Thus one might try to have fewer requirements
[
125
]
, and to define
a similar function at least on
\mathcal{A}_{sa}
, leading to the concept of valuation.

Definition 3.1

(Observation and Value)
.

A self-adjoint RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
has a definite value in a certain
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
, which could ideally be observed,
if any one of the following equivalent conditions is satisfied.

1.

\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=0
— the state is dispersion free;

2.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
is pure, cf. Proposition
2.48
;

3.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{2})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{2}
.

That 1.) and 3.) are equivalent is obvious from
\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}((\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})^{2})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{2})-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{2}
, for the equivalence with 2.) see e.g.
[
125
]
.
From 3.) and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
— which follows here from
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
, but
which one would require for any reasonable value assignment — one obtains with the
same kind of argument used in Proposition
2.8
that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
,
i.e. the “values” have to be in the spectrum of the RV.
Recall, cf. Proposition
2.48
, that characters
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{A})
— if

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{A})
is non-empty — satisfy obviously 3.), and thus also the others.

Recalling the action of characters on projections in Proposition
2.18
, one sees that
for a projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{sa}
one has

0\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}^{2})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})^{2}
, and thus
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})
can only
have one of the two values
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})=0
or
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})=1
, just like for characters.
And from Proposition
2.8
it is clear that these two values are the only ones in
the spectrum,
\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})\subseteq\{0,1\}
, of a projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
.

A collection of self-adjoint RVs has jointly definite values in a certain state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}

if the algebra they jointly generate has a state that satisfies Definition
3.1
.
One may then obtain the following theorem
[
125
,
79
]
:

Theorem 3.2
.

A collection of observables / RVs have jointly definite values in a certain state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
— depending on the collection and state —

iff
they are compatible, i.e.
iff
they commute. From Definition
3.1

follows that in that case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}
has to be pure.
On a commutative probability algebra, the pure states are characters.

Another angle on this subject is obtained from the so called
uncertainty relation
,
cf.
[
132
]
; originally due to Heisenberg, it was reformulated by Robertson,
and then extended by Schrödinger
[
123
]
,
to include a second summand in the relation Eq.(
3.1
) on the right hand side,
which is shown here observing Definition
2.64
:

Theorem 3.3

(Heisenberg Uncertainty Relation)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a unital *-algebra. For any state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
and any two self-adjoint RVs
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
one has

\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\var_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\geq\left|\frac{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}([\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}])}{2}\right|^{2}+\left|\Re(\cov_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}))\right|^{2}.

(3.1)

Theorem
3.3
is a consequence of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
As may be gleaned from Eq.(
3.1
), two RVs can not have simultaneously
a definite value in the same state unless
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}([\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}])=0
, e.g. if they commute,
and the real part of their covariance vanishes.
Recall from Definition
2.64
, that if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})

is a character — they exist generally only for commutative algebras — its
covariance vanishes, as does its variance, as well as the value of any commutator,
i.e.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}([\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}])=0
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
. Hence in this case
both sides of Eq.(
3.1
) vanish; this is the classical case.

The last two theorems, Theorem
3.2
and Theorem
3.3
, actually tell
us that states which provide a definite value to a RV, cf. Definition
3.1
,
have to be pure states (Theorem
3.2
), and the RVs to which they apply
have to commute or be compatible. So, to describe observations of a collection of
compatible RVs, one could always regard the commutative probability sub-algebra

\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
which they generate.
On such commutative algebras, characters exist, they are pure, and
they satisfy the uncertainty relation Eq.(
3.1
) from Theorem
3.3

identically, such that both sides vanish. Such a commutative or Abelian probability
sub-algebra
\mathcal{C}
is called a
classical context
, as this describes situations where
all RVs involved can be observed / measured or have a definite value simultaneously
with the uncertainty relations being identically satisfied.

These Abelian sub-algebras can be given a partial order, given by set inclusion.
The poset of Abelian sub-algebras — ordered by set inclusion —
of a probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
are called its
classical contexts
.
As for each such commutative or Abelian probability sub-algebra
\mathcal{C}

it holds that
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime}
, i.e. it is embedded in its
commutant (cf. Definition
2.12
), which, as it is
again Abelian, according to Zorn’s lemma it follows that there are maximal
Abelian sub-algebras (MASAs, cf. Definition
2.12
), and each chain of inclusions
has a maximal element, namely such a MASA. Thus any such classical context, as it is
an Abelian or commutative probability sub-algebra
\mathcal{C}
, can be embedded in a MASA,
and this is in fact its commutant
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
,
cf. Definition
2.12
and Proposition
2.79
.

And obviously it can happen that some Abelian sub-algebra
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{A}
is
a subset of two (or more) different MASAs, e.g.
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{B}

and
\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{C}
, which do not commute,
[\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}]\neq\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\}
.
But the characters which give the observations on each Abelian sub-algebra
(
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})
) (classical context) may be different from each other.

The problem which can therefore arise — as the characters which give the value or
observations on each Abelian sub-algebra may be different from each other —
is that some observable / RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathcal{S}
gets different values depending on in
which larger context (i.e.
\mathcal{B}
or
\mathcal{C}
) the sub-algebra
\mathcal{S}
is considered.
But on the other hand, one would expect that, if the RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}
“has a value”,
that this is the same value, independent of the context.
So more precisely, if say
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{b}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{B})
is one character,
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{c}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})
another one; the question then is whether one
can avoid that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{b}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})\neq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})
for some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathcal{S}
.

But, as characters which could assign definite values to a RV generally do not
exist on non-commutative algebras, one tries with less.
To assign definite values, one needs a functional defined at least on

all
the “real” observables,
\mathcal{A}_{sa}\subset\mathcal{A}
,
satisfying the conditions 1.) or 3.) in Definition
3.1

[
115
]
:

Definition 3.4

(Valuation)
.

A
valuation

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}:\mathcal{A}_{sa}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{R}
is a functional satisfying for
compatible
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
(i.e.
[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
), and
z,w\in\mathbb{C}
:

1.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(z\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}+w\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=z\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})+w\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
;

2.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
;

3.

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=1
.

Essentially, a valuation has to behave like a character, but only on commuting self-adjoint
RVs, but on the other hand it has to be defined on
all
of
\mathcal{A}_{sa}
to be seen
as assigning a definite “value” .
From 1.) and 2.) in Definition
3.4
one can derive easily that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}))=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}))
for any polynomial
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{p}}\in\mathbb{C}[X]
; hence for finite dimensional
algebras this is true for any function and not just polynomials, and under mild conditions
this can be established for almost all reasonable functions also for most
infinite dimensional algebras.

Recalling Definition
3.1
and the discussion following it, it was established there
that the only values a projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
can have are in its spectrum

\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})=\{0,1\}
. And as any self-adjoint
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
is determined
through the spectral decomposition (cf. Proposition
2.77
) by its spectral projections,
the same is also true for any such self-adjoint
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
. Therefore a valuation functional
has to be dispersion free, and one should have
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\upsilon}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
.
Hence such a valuation could assign “definite values” for the all of

\mathcal{A}_{sa}\subset\mathcal{A}
. But alas, this is in general
not possible

[
115
,
36
]
, and that is the content of the next

Theorem 3.5

(Bell-Kochen-Specker)
.

If
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, the bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
,
and
\dim\mathcal{H}>2
,
no valuations exist
on
\mathcal{A}_{sa}
.

This certainly also includes all algebras which contain a sub-algebra isomorphic to

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
with
\dim\mathcal{H}>2
(a factor of type
\mathrm{I}_{n}
with
n>2
), here
it will not be possible to assign definite values to all RVs, the value

depends on the context
.

Although this theorem was derived in the realm of quantum mechanics, its formulation
and proof make only reference to a non-Abelian probability algebra, and it is elementary
linear algebra, although a bit combinatorially involved. But it shows how radically
different commutative and non-commutative probability algebras are.

The proof of the theorem works by constructing a counter-example, i.e. for a
Hilbert space with
\dim\mathcal{H}=3
to construct commutative sub-algebras of

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
which show the impossibility of a valuation. For
\dim\mathcal{H}=3
,
as already mentioned, the counter-example is quite involved. But as an illustration
of the idea, for
\dim\mathcal{H}=4
it is possible to give a much simpler counter-example.

Following a construction originally proposed in
[
40
]
, take

\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{4}
and define 18 vectors
\ket{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{4}\;(j=1,\dots,18)
, in
Tables
1
and
2
, and define the
orthogonal projections onto the one-dimensional subspaces which these vectors span:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}:=\frac{1}{\left\langle j\mid j\right\rangle}\ket{j}\bra{j}.

shown in Table

.
This is done in such a way that each PVM contains four atomic projections. It is easy
to check that the vectors which generate the projections in each PVM are orthogonal,
so that the projections are themselves orthogonal to each other. Each PVM generates,
as was already mentioned several times, cf. Definition

, Proposition

, and

\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{C}^{4})\cong\mathbb{M}_{4}(\mathbb{C})

.

that it can only assume values in the spectrum of a RV. As for any orthogonal

,
