\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{15}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{11}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{13}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{15}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{12}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{16}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{17}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{14}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{18}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{16}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{17}

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{P}}_{18}

Table 3:
PVMs 1 to 9

On the other hand, one checks quickly that in Table
3
each projection
appears
twice
, obviously in different PVMs, i.e. classical contexts. If a
valuation function exists for
\mathbb{M}_{4}(\mathbb{C})
, the value has to be independent of the
fact in which classical context (PVM generated Abelian sub-algebra) the projection is
located. Thus, there should be an
even
number of ones in the
Table
3
, and we have a
contradiction
to the statement in
the previous paragraph. We may therefore deduce that no valuation function exists
on
\mathbb{M}_{4}(\mathbb{C})
, or any algebra containing a sub-algebra isomorphic to
\mathbb{M}_{4}(\mathbb{C})
.

The interpretation is that situations like the one described above with

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{b}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})\neq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{c}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})
can not be avoided if the algebra is sufficiently
large, and thus the RVs can not be given definite values. This means that the value
of a RV
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
depends on its
context
, i.e. in which sub-algebra
it happens to be embedded. These facts, from a classical perspective disturbing,
are on the other hand things to be exploited in quantum information and quantum computing.

3.2
Generalised Observations and Channels

As a motivation for the following, recall that for a projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
representing
an event, in Definition
2.17
it was defined that
\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}):=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}})
was the
probability of sharply observing that event (
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}})=1
). Assume now that the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}

can not be observed exactly or sharply, but that there is a small probability
\alpha
that the
observation of the opposite event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}^{\perp}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}
is mistaken for
an observation of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}
. The event of
registering
the observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}
is
then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{1}:=\alpha\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}^{\perp}+(1-\alpha)\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}
,
while the opposite event is
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{0}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{1}=\alpha\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}+(1-\alpha)\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}^{\perp}
.
For
0<\alpha<1
these are
not sharp
events.

It is not difficult to see that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, so
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{1},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{0}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})

are
effects
(cf. Definition
2.12
), and this is a simple example of a

Positive Operator Valued Measure
(POVM).

Positive Operator Valued Measures (POVMs):

Generalising this little motivation, one defines a more general kind of measurement
by using effects to describe non-sharp events instead of projections for sharp events:

Definition 3.6

(Positive Operator Valued Measure (POVM))
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional probability algebra, and let
(X,\mathfrak{X})
be a
measurable space with base set
X
and
\sigma
-algebra
\mathfrak{X}
.
An assignment
\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}:\mathfrak{X}\ni E\mapsto\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(E):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
, such that

\displaystyle\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(X)

\displaystyle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}},\quad\text{ and for disjoint }\;E_{1},E_{2}\in\mathfrak{X}:

(3.3)

\displaystyle\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(E_{1}\uplus E_{2})

\displaystyle=\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(E_{1})+\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(E_{2}),

(3.4)

is called a positive operator valued measure (POVM).
This implies
\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(\emptyset)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
.

This is a generalisation of the sharp measurements which were considered before, the projection
valued measures (PVM), which can be seen as a special case of a POVM; one can say that
a PVM or a projection is a
sharp
POVM resp. effect.
Events are now described by the positive operators

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\leq\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(E)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
.
The Definition
2.17
of the probability of
observing an event
by a projection
is now generalised to the probability
0\leq p_{E}=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E})\leq 1
of

registering
the observation of the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E}
or outcome
E\in\mathfrak{X}
.

For an observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}
, it was established in Proposition
2.18
that
the only observations or samples of a projection could be
zero or one,
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})\in\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})\subseteq\{0,1\}
, which may be
interpreted as false and true. With a POVM,
the observation can be any probability,
0\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E})\leq 1
. One possible
interpretation is that this is the probability that the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E}
resp. the outcome
E\in\mathfrak{X}

has been registered
as having occurred.

The POVM in turn defines a probability distribution on the
\sigma
-algebra
\mathfrak{X}
by
the assignment

\mathbb{P}_{\text{POVM}}:\mathfrak{X}\in E\mapsto\mathbb{P}_{\text{POVM}}(E):=\mathbb{P}_{\text{POVM}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E}):=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{E})\in[0,1].

(3.5)

This probability assignment generalises the one only for projections
previously established in Definition
2.17
, and may be seen as an
extended Born rule.

As the projections are a special case of effects,
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
,
this makes the PVMs defined in Definition
2.21
, Eqs.(
2.39
) and (
2.49
), and
Remark
2.91
a special case of the abstractly defined POVM here. It should
also be clear on how to formulate this concretely for the two algebras
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})

and
\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})
resp.
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
considered up to now in parallel to the
abstract setting.

Remark 3.7

(POVM on any
\sigma
-algebra)
.

For a PVM in a finite dimensional algebra
\mathcal{A}
it was sufficient to consider finite
outcome sets
X
with
\sigma
-algebra
2^{X}
, cf. Remark
2.22
. This is
different for a POVM, as the outcome space
X
and the
\sigma
-algebra
\mathfrak{X}
may be
infinite. Obviously, also something resembling
\sigma
-additivity has to be included
as well. For the sake of simplicity though, and as it does not change anything in the
presentation here, it will simply be assumed in the following that
X
is a finite
set and that the
\sigma
-algebra is
\mathfrak{X}=2^{X}
as before for PVMs.

Further note that the set of POVMs forms a convex cone in the vector space of
operator valued measures, and the normalisation requirement Eq.(
3.3
)
defines a linear manifold in that vector space. The normalised POVMs are thus
in the intersection of the positive cone and that linear manifold;
this is very similar to the geometry of states, as established in Proposition
2.48
.

This set is clearly convex — hence a convex combinations of normalised POVMs is
again a POVM — and one can show that the
extreme points
are precisely
those POVMs where the outcome space
X
is finite
[
43
]
.
This leads to representation theorems analogous to the representation of density
matrices in terms of pure states.

Also in analogy to the situation with states and functionals in terms of the
Radon-Nikodým derivative (cf. Remark
2.58
), there are similar
possibilities here
[
43
]
, a topic which is outside the present scope.

Gleason’s Theorem
2.93
, which showed that a function which assigns a probability
distribution for every PVM in
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
can be extended to a state, has
an analogue for POVMs, cf. e.g.
[
37
]
:

Theorem 3.8

(Gleason — POVM)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a finite dimensional Hilbert space,
and consider the algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})

of all linear maps, as well as the set of all effects
\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
.

A function
\gamma:\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>[0,1]
, which is such
that for
any
given POVM

\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}:2^{X}\ni\{x\}\mapsto E_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})),

defined on a finite set
X
, analogous to Definition
3.6

in Eqs.(
3.3
) and (
3.4
), it
follows that
\sum_{x}\gamma(\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(\{x\}))=1
—
which means that it satisfies the equivalent of Eq.(
2.52
) and defines a
probability measure on
X
and on the POVM

\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}
, namely
\mathbb{P}(\{x\}):=\mathbb{P}(E_{x})=\gamma(E_{x})
like in Eq.(
3.5
) —
can be
extended
to a state
\gamma\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
.

The converse, that any state induces a probability measure on a POVM,
was already stated in Eq.(
3.5
).

Remark 3.9
.

Generalising Remark
2.92
, one may observe that we started in
Remark
2.90
by tying a sharp observation to an atomic projection,
then generalised this to sharp observations connected to a PVM, and now one
may speak about a
non-sharp
event represented by an
effect

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
,
having a probability
\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}})
to be
registered
as being true.

In case that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is an actual observation or sample,
i.e. a character
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})

of some commutative sub-probability algebra
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
such that

\Uppi_{\text{POVM}}(\{x\})\in\mathcal{C}
, then
\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})\in[0,1]
, not just in
\{0,1\}
as for a PVM,
can be seen as the probability that the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}
(i.e.
x\in X
)

has been registered as being observed
,
whereas
\mathbb{P}_{\text{POVM}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}):=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x})
may be
interpreted as the probability that the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{e}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{e}}_{x}
(i.e.
x\in X
)

will be observed
.

Duality of Effects and States:

As could be gleaned from the foregoing, in a probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
we started
from the duality between observables
\mathcal{A}_{sa}\subset\mathcal{A}
and states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{\star}
, so that for an observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
and a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
the expectation of the observable in the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
was

\mathbb{E}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle
. Here the last expression is
the duality pairing
\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle
on
\mathcal{A}^{\star}\times\mathcal{A}
.
In Example
15
the trace on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
was defined for a finite
dimensional space
\mathcal{H}
, and via the regular representation in
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})

the canonical faithful inner product
\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{c}
on
\mathcal{A}^{2}
was
introduced in Proposition
2.49
. Following the development for density
matrices Proposition
2.24
and Corollary
2.37
, in Corollary
2.56

density elements
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{+}
were introduced, so that for each
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
there is a one-to-one correspondence
with an density element
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
,
such that one may write with the canonical inner product

\mathbb{E}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle_{c}\,\text{ on }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathcal{A}_{sa}\;\text{ resp. }\;\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathcal{A}_{sa}.

(3.6)

When computing probabilities (cf. Definition
2.17
), originally
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

had to be a projection. Generalising this to PVMs, the Eq.(
3.6
)
then displays a duality between state resp. densities and PVMs to produce probabilities:

\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle_{c}\,\text{ on }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})\;\text{ resp. }\;\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}).

(3.7)

Above, this was just further generalised to POVMs, where observations or samples

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}])
don’t produce
sharp results like
1
or
0
, but only a
probability
that an event
has been observed
.
So with the correspondence
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\leftrightarrow\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}
between states and densities —
as well as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\leftrightarrow\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}}
— one can observe the dualities

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})

\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle_{c}\,\text{ on }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})\;\text{ resp. }\;\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\times\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A});

(3.8)

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}})

\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}})=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle_{c}\,\text{ on }\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}])\times\mathrm{E}(\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}]).

(3.9)

Just looking at effects seems to be sufficient to discuss probabilities prior to a sample
or observation in Eq.(
3.8
), as well as the probability
that something has been observed in Eq.(
3.9
).
One might note that in the set of effects
\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
, it is the partial order and
positivity which carries the main information (the structure of an ordered vector space),
preserving the range and ordering of probabilities,
a topic which will be taken up again when channels are shortly discussed.
This structure of the set of effects has been abstracted and generalised to

effect algebras
— e.g. cf.
[
67
,
66
,
24
]

and the references therein — to describe a general kind of observable.
This in turn is the basis for theories of
generalised probability

(e.g. cf.
[
82
,
78
,
113
]
), which start from the
duality structure displayed in
Eqs.(
3.8
) and (
3.9
).

This is that the effects
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}
are in a partially ordered set, usually a subset of an ordered
vector space
\mathcal{E}
, and that they are in the “interval”
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, where

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\in\mathcal{E}
is the
impossible event
and the origin of the vector space, and the
“order unit”
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\in\mathcal{E}
is the
certain event
, and the above interval is a
convex set, so that convex combinations of effects are again an effect. This means in
particular that effects are
positive

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\in\mathcal{E}_{+}
. Additions of effects are
allowed as long as they stay below the order unit, i.e. the sum of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}_{1}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}_{2}

is an effect iff
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}_{1}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}_{2}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
.
The states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
on the other hand live in the dual space
\mathcal{E}^{\star}
of
the effects, and the duality (a bilinear form)
p=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle
is to be interpreted
as the probability
0\leq p\leq 1
of the effect being observed in the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathcal{E}^{\star}
.
Therefore the states have to be positive and normalised, i.e.
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle\geq 0

(geometrically a cone in
\mathcal{E}^{\star}
) and
\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\right\rangle=1
(geometrically a
hyperplane in
\mathcal{E}^{\star}
), so that the probabilities satisfy

0\leq p=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{x}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{x}}\right\rangle\leq 1
, and the set of states is convex, just as for effects.
These few prescription are sufficient to be able to assign probabilities.
Here, however, we shall not go further in this direction and stay within
the setting established so far.

Positive Operator Valued Measures (POVMs) and Positive Maps:

Although the idea of a POVM is a generalisation of the PVM, where the elements are projections
and not just effects, it turns out that these two concepts are very closely related. This is
the content of the following “Neumark(Naĭmark) Dilation Theorem”, another example of the
“Church of the Larger Hilbert Space”, and it is usually formulated in the Hilbert space setting,
cf. e.g.
[
110
,
77
]
.

Theorem 3.10

(Neumark(Naĭmark))
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
be a finite dimensional Hilbert space, and

\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}:2^{X}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
be a POVM as defined in Definition
3.6
.

Then there exists another finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}
,
an isometry
V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K})
(
V^{\dagger}V=I_{\mathcal{H}}
), and
a PVM

\Uppsi_{\mathcal{K}}:2^{X}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
as defined for matrix algebras in
Definition
2.21
, formulated in Proposition
2.77
(cf. Eq.(
2.39
)) in a purely
algebraic setting, and spelt out for Hilbert spaces in Remark
2.90

(cf. Eq.(
2.49
)), such that

\forall E\in 2^{X}:\quad\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}(E)=V^{\dagger}\,\Uppsi_{\mathcal{K}}(E)\,V.

(3.10)

What the Eq.(
3.10
) says is that a POVM, when
dilated
on a
larger space resp. in a larger algebra, is really a PVM, or, in other words,
that a POVM is the
compression
of a PVM.
Another way of saying this is that the POVM has been “lifted” to a PVM.
If the POVM value for
\{x\}\subset X
is the
effect

\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}(\{x\})=E_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
, then there is a
projection

\Uppsi_{\mathcal{K}}(\{x\})=P_{x}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
such that
E_{x}=V^{\dagger}\,P_{x}\,V
.
One may also say that there is a system (
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
) with a sharp observable
P_{x}
,
but one sees only part of it, namely
V^{\dagger}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
.

The form of the representation
E_{x}=V^{\dagger}\,P_{x}\,V
is called the
Kraus
form

[
150
]
, and the map
V
— which doesn’t have to be necessarily an isometry — is
called a Kraus map. Observe that this can also be written as

E_{x}=V^{\dagger}\,P_{x}\,V=(P_{x}\,V)^{\dagger}(P_{x}\,V)=K_{x}^{\dagger}K_{x},

(3.11)

with Kraus operators
K_{x}=P_{x}\,V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K})
, satisfying

\sum_{x\in X}K_{x}^{\dagger}K_{x}=\sum_{x\in X}E_{x}=I_{\mathcal{H}}
.

A POVM may be seen as a mechanism to transfer probabilistic information from a
general probability algebra to a probability distribution on a set
X
as
in Eq.(
3.5
). Such a transfer of information is called a

channel
. To address channels more generally, we start with a
motivating example connected to the preceding Theorem
3.10
.

Example 19

(Observation Channel)
.

Let
X
be a finite set, and
n=\left|X\right|
its cardinality. As
\mathbb{C}^{X}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}
,
consider
\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{C}^{n}
, the commutative Hadamard algebra of Example
2
.
For a given POVM
\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}:2^{X}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
as in the above
Theorem
3.10
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
,
\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}(\{i\})=E_{i}
, define a map

\mathscr{F}:\mathcal{C}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\;\text{ by }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}=(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\,E_{i}.

This is a linear map
\mathscr{F}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
, which maps

•

the identity
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}=(1,\dots,1)\mapsto\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}})=\sum_{i}E_{i}=I_{\mathcal{H}}

onto the identity;

•

adjoint elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star}
to adjoints
\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}}^{\star})=\sum_{i}w_{i}^{*}\,E_{i}=\bigl(\sum_{i}w_{i}\,E_{i}\bigr)^{\dagger}=\bigl(\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{w}})\bigr)^{\dagger}
,
i.e. it is *-linear;

•

positive
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}\in\mathcal{C}_{+}
to positive

0\leq\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=\sum_{i}f_{i}\,E_{i}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})_{+}
;

•

effects
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{0}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}
to effects

0\leq\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}})=\sum_{i}g_{i}\,E_{i}\leq I_{\mathcal{H}}
;

•

and can be written as Kraus form: As
E_{i}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})_{+}
,
it can by definition be written as
E_{i}=G_{i}^{\dagger}G_{i}
with some

G_{i}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
(e.g.
G_{i}=E_{i}^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}
), and thus

\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=\sum_{i}f_{i}\,E_{i}=\sum_{i}G_{i}^{\dagger}\,f_{i}\,G_{i}
.

This map transforms effects (possible measurements) in
\mathcal{C}
to effects in
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
,
where one can evaluate their probability with some state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
:
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{C})
one has
\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}(\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}))=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}},\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})\right\rangle
.
In particular, choosing
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i}=(\updelta_{ij})
, the canonical unit vectors in
\mathbb{C}^{n}
,
one obtains
p_{i}=\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i})
, a probability distribution on
X=\{1,\dots,n\}
.

Thus, defining the dual map
\mathscr{F}^{*}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})^{*},\mathcal{C}^{\star})
as usual for

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})^{*}
via

\left\langle\mathscr{F}^{*}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})},\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}})\right\rangle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}(\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}))=p_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}},

one has transferred the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
to a state

\mathscr{F}^{*}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})})=:\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathcal{H}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{C})
which assigns the probability

0\leq p_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}})\leq 1
to the event / effect
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{g}}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{C})
.
This is due to the fact that
\mathscr{F}^{*}
is also *-linear, positive, and state preserving:

1=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})},I_{\mathcal{H}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})},\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}})\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathscr{F}^{*}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\alpha}}_{\mathcal{H}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}\right\rangle.

In case the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}
is represented by a density operator

R\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}(A)=\tr RA
, one can define the
adjoint map
\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
by use of the Hilbert space structure
on
\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{C}^{n}
and
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, such that for
X\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}
:

\left\langle X\mid\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}})\right\rangle_{c}=\tr\bigl(X^{\dagger}\,\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}})\bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(X^{\dagger}E_{i})x_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(E^{\dagger}_{i}X)^{*}x_{i}\\
=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(G_{i}^{\dagger}G_{i}X)^{*}x_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(G_{i}XG_{i}^{\dagger})^{*}x_{i}=\bigl(\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(R)\bigr)^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}=\left\langle\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(X)\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{x}}\right\rangle_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}.

Hence
\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(X)=[\tr(G_{1}XG_{1}^{\dagger}),\dots,\tr(G_{n}XG_{n}^{\dagger})]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}=[\tr(XE_{1}),\dots,\tr(XE_{n})]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}
.
It is easily seen that this maps density operators onto discrete probability distributions

\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(R)=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}=[\tr(RE_{1}),\dots,\tr(RE_{n})]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tr(RE_{i})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{C})
, and

1=\tr R=\tr(R\,I)=\tr\bigl(R\,\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}})\bigr)=\bigl(\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(R)\bigr)^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}
, i.e. it preserves the trace.

To recap, the map
\mathscr{F}:\mathcal{C}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, its dual
\mathscr{F}^{*}
and its
adjoint
\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}
, are *-linear, positive, and satisfy

•

\mathscr{F}(\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{C}))\subseteq\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
, and
\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}})=I_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})}

(
\mathscr{F}
is unit preserving) (unital);

•

\mathscr{F}^{*}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})))\subseteq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{C})
, i.e.
\mathscr{F}^{*}
is state preserving;

•

\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}(\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})))\subseteq\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{C})
, and
\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}
is
trace preserving (TP).

Preserving the unit for
\mathscr{F}
, and the state resp. trace preservation for

\mathscr{F}^{*}
resp.
\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}
, are two sides of the same coin.
These properties are apparently sufficient to allow assignments of probabilities
to the effects
\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{C})
in
\mathcal{C}
, as just discussed above in the part on
the “Duality of Effects and States”. It is a transfer of probabilistic information,
as embodied in the state, to another system.

So, instead of performing observations on the system given by
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, one now
observes on the system defined by
\mathcal{C}
. The properties of *-linearity, positivity,
and trace preservation were sufficient to achieve this.
In Definition
2.4
in Section
2
we
saw that *-homomorphisms could be used for this, cf. Corollary
3.16
.
But the requirements here are weaker, the map does not have to be multiplicative,
it only has to preserve positivity and the identity. Incidentally, in the extreme
case where the POVM
\Uppi_{\mathcal{H}}:2^{X}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))

above is actually a PVM, the map
\mathscr{F}

does
become a
*-homomorphism
.

Such a map as just described for the general
\mathscr{F}
is called a
channel
.
It transfers information from a system described by
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
to one
modelled on the Hadamard algebra
\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{C}^{n}
, a classical commutative or Abelian
probability algebra. The map
\mathscr{F}
is the channel in the
Heisenberg
picture
— observe that it somehow points backwards — and its dual
\mathscr{F}^{*}
and adjoint

\mathscr{F}^{\dagger}
, pointing forward in the direction of information transmittal, which
transfer states from
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
to
\mathcal{C}
, are the channel in the

Schrödinger
picture.

Now to the formal definitions which are needed for such a channel: In the following, let

\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}
be finite dimensional unital *-algebras.

Definition 3.11

(Positive Map)
.

A *-linear map
\mathscr{P}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
is
positive
,
iff
for all
positive
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{+}
one has that
\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\in\mathcal{B}_{+}
is again positive,
i.e.
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{A}}\;\Rightarrow\;\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\geq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}_{\mathcal{B}}
.

Definition 3.12

(Unit and Trace Preservation)
.

A *-linear map
\mathscr{P}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
is
unit preserving
(UP), or

unital
, or
stochastic
,
iff

\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}
.

A *-linear map
\mathscr{P}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is
trace preserving
(TP),
or
doubly stochastic
,
iff
for all
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}
one has

\tr_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl(\mathscr{P}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\bigr)
.

From this one can show already in general some of the properties which were seen
in Example
19
.

Proposition 3.13
.

Let
\mathscr{P}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
be a *-linear map.
Then the following two statements are equivalent:

•

The Heisenberg picture:
\mathscr{P}
is positive and unit preserving (unital);

•

The Schrödinger picture:
\mathscr{P}^{\dagger}
is positive and trace preserving.

Additionally,
\mathscr{P}
positive implies that it is monotone,
i.e. if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1}\leq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2}
then
\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{1})\leq\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{2})
;
e.g., cf.
[
77
]
.

Completely Positive Maps:

Given two *-linear positive maps
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
and
\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{D}
,
what one would like is to consider the
combined system
\mathscr{P}\otimes\mathscr{Q}:(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>(\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{D})
, cf. Definition
2.71
. It would be desirable for
the map
\mathscr{P}\otimes\mathscr{Q}
to be positive if the component maps
\mathscr{P}
and
\mathscr{Q}

are. For non-commutative algebras this is a non-trivial requirement, and, as counterexamples
show, this is unfortunately
not always
the case;
e.g., cf.
[
46
,
86
,
138
,
150
,
107
,
77
,
152
,
28
,
151
,
114
]
.
More than just positivity is required.
Luckily, it is sufficient to consider
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{D}=\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
and
\mathscr{Q}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{n}

(the identity in
\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
) to check whether this holds in general.
This is tensoring or “interaction” with a “do-nothing” ancilla system.

Definition 3.14

(Completely Positive Maps)
.

A *-linear map
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
induces for every
n\in\mathbb{N}
*-linear
maps
\mathscr{P}_{n}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})

(cf. Example
17
) by setting
\mathscr{P}_{n}=\mathscr{P}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{I}}_{n}
.

A positive *-linear map
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
is
n
-positive
iff

\mathscr{P}_{n}
is positive. It is
completely positive
(CP) iff it is

n
-positive for all
n\in\mathbb{N}
.

Completely Positive Trace Preserving
*-linear maps are often abbreviated
as
CPTP
maps; their adjoints, which are
Completely Positive Unit Preserving
,
are often abbreviated as
CPUP
maps. They satisfy all the requirements for
a successful information transmittal in a channel.
A moment’s thought shows that (e.g. cf.
[
152
]
)

Corollary 3.15

(Geometry of CP Maps and Compositions)
.

The set of CP maps from a *-algebra
\mathcal{A}
to another *-algebra
\mathcal{B}
, as a subset of

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, is a pointed convex cone. Hence, convex combinations of CP
maps are again CP maps. The properties of
unit preservation
(UP) and

trace preservation
(TP) define linear manifolds in
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, and hence
are also preserved under convex combinations.

Let
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
and
\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
be two *-linear completely
positive maps. Then
\mathscr{R}=\mathscr{Q}\circ\mathscr{P}
is a *-linear completely positive map.
If both
\mathscr{P}
and
\mathscr{Q}
are UP resp. TP, so is
\mathscr{Q}\circ\mathscr{P}
.

Some basic results are given by

Corollary 3.16

(Some CP Maps)

Thus every sample

A *-linear positive map

.
