,
152
,
28
,
151
,
114
,
15
]
.

Corollary 3.17

(Cauchy-Schwarz for CPUP-maps)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital *-algebra, and
let
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
be a *-linear CPUP-map.
Then it holds that

\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}:\quad\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star})\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\leq\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}).

(3.12)

e.g., cf.
[
152
,
15
]
. Observe that
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}
is a *-homomorphism

iff
equality always holds in Eq.(
3.12
).

In case that there is a CP-map
\mathscr{R}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
such that

\mathscr{R}\circ\mathscr{T}=\mathscr{I}_{\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
(the identity on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
),
then
\mathscr{T}
is an internal *-automorphism (cf. Definition
2.12
).

Note that these results show that the map
\mathscr{F}
in the above motivating Example
19

is completely positive and unit preserving, and this is also shown by its Kraus form.

Proposition 3.18

(Kraus Form)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
and
\mathcal{K}
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, and let

K\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H})
be a linear map. Then the *-linear map

\mathscr{T}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
, given in Kraus form by

\mathscr{T}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\ni A\mapsto\mathscr{T}(A)=K^{\dagger}AK\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})

(3.13)

is
completely positive
,
cf.
[
46
,
86
,
138
,
150
,
77
,
152
]
.
It is
unit preserving

iff

K^{\dagger}K=I_{\mathcal{K}}
(
K
is an isometry).
It is
trace preserving

iff

KK^{\dagger}=I_{\mathcal{H}}
.
The map
K\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H})
is often called a
Kraus map
or

Kraus operator
.

Note that when both
K^{\dagger}K=I_{\mathcal{K}}
and
KK^{\dagger}=I_{\mathcal{H}}

hold, then
K\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H})
is unitary, the Hilbert spaces
are isomorphic (
\mathcal{K}\cong\mathcal{H})
, and
\mathscr{T}
is a *-isomorphism of the
unital *-algebras
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
and
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
, cf.
[
15
]
.

Together with Corollary
3.15
, one has that the convex combination
of unit preserving Kraus maps is completely positive and unit preserving.
This leads to

Corollary 3.19

(General Kraus Form)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
and
\mathcal{K}
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, and let

X\supseteq\{x\}\mapsto K_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H})
be a collection of linear
maps (
X
a finite set), such that

X\supseteq\{x\}\mapsto\Uppi_{K,X}(\{x\})=F_{x}=K_{x}^{\dagger}K_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))

(3.14)

is a POVM (in particular
\sum_{x}F_{x}=I_{\mathcal{K}}
). Then

\mathscr{T}_{X}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\ni A\mapsto\mathscr{T}_{X}(A)=\sum_{x\in X}K_{x}^{\dagger}AK_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})

(3.15)

is a CPUP-map in
Kraus form
. Its adjoint, a CPTP-map, is given in Kraus form by

\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}_{X}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})\ni B\mapsto\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}_{X}(B)=\sum_{x\in X}K_{x}BK^{\dagger}_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}).

(3.16)

Observe that the effects
F_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
in a POVM
(cf. Eq.(
3.14
)) could be factored in
many ways, given that the Kraus operators
K_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H})
are in no way unique.
If
U_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
are unitary, then the
Q_{x}=U_{x}K_{x}
are also Kraus maps
with
F_{x}=Q_{x}^{\dagger}Q_{x}=K_{x}^{\dagger}U_{x}^{\dagger}U_{x}K_{x}=K_{x}^{\dagger}K_{x}
.
When
\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{H}
, one easy choice is
K_{x}=F_{x}^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}}
, as

F_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))\subset\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})_{+}
.

When bases are chosen in the above Hilbert spaces to represent the algebras as
sub-algebras of matrix algebras, as was discussed in Section
2.2
, the criterion
for complete positivity becomes checking the positivity of a matrix:

Theorem 3.20

(Choi)
.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}:\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C})
be a linear map, and let

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}_{ij}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
be the matrix with all zero entries, except a
1

at position
(i,j)
— the canonical unit vectors in
\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\cong\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C})
. Then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}
is completely positive iff the
Choi-matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{C}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}}=(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{I}}_{n\times n}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}})(\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}_{ij}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}_{ij})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}_{ij}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{E}}_{ij})\in\mathbb{M}_{nm}(\mathbb{C})

(3.17)

is positive, cf.
[
44
]
.

Now finally the result on completely positive maps and tensor products can be stated:

Proposition 3.21

(Tensor Products and CP Maps)
.

Let
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
and
\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{D}
be two *-linear completely positive maps.
Then the combined system map

\mathscr{P}\otimes\mathscr{Q}:(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>(\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{D})

is *-linear and completely positive. If both
\mathscr{P}
and
\mathscr{Q}
are unit preserving,
so is
\mathscr{P}\otimes\mathscr{Q}
.

In case
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{D}
is an Abelian or commutative *-algebra, then the map

\mathscr{R}:(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
defined on elementary tensors

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
by

\mathscr{R}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}):=\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\mathscr{Q}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})

is completely positive, and unit preserving in case both
\mathscr{P}
and
\mathscr{Q}
are;
e.g., cf.
[
138
]
.

The completely positive maps are *-linear operators between algebras, and when
the algebras are represented as (sub-)algebras of operator algebras
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
,
they are maps between these operator spaces, and are therefore sometimes referred to
as
super-operators
. It is thus important to have methods which allow these
super-operators to be represented in terms of normal operators. The Kraus-form
in Proposition
3.18
may be seen as a first important result in this direction,
as it represents the super-operator
\mathscr{T}
in terms of ordinary linear Hilbert space
operators. In the following, a few more such representation results will given.

A complete characterisation of completely positive maps is given by the following
Stinespring Dilation

Theorem 3.22

(Stinespring)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a finite dimensional unital *-algebra,
\mathcal{H}
a finite dimensional
Hilbert space, and
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
a completely positive *-linear map.

Then there exists a finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}
and a unital *-homomorphism

\Phi:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
(cf. Definition
2.4
),
as well as a linear map
V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K})
from
\mathcal{H}
to
\mathcal{K}
, such that

\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}:\quad\mathscr{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=V^{\dagger}\,\Phi(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,V\;\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H});

(3.18)

e.g., cf.
[
46
,
86
,
138
,
150
,
107
,
77
,
152
,
28
,
151
,
114
]
.
If
V^{\dagger}V=I_{\mathcal{H}}
(i.e.
V
is an isometry), then
\mathscr{P}
is unit preserving.

In the special case
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})
, where
\mathcal{J}
is a finite dimensional
Hilbert space, and
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
is CP and *-linear,
there is a finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{E}
,
so that
\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{J}\otimes\mathcal{E}
, and for the homomorphism
\Phi
in
Eq.(
3.18
) one may take

\Phi:\,\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\ni A\mapsto(A\otimes I_{\mathcal{E}})\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J}\otimes\mathcal{E})
. Then

\displaystyle\forall A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J}):\;\mathscr{P}(A)

\displaystyle=V^{\dagger}(A\otimes I_{\mathcal{E}})V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),

(3.19)

\displaystyle\text{and dually }\forall R\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}):\;\mathscr{P}^{\dagger}(R)

\displaystyle=\tr_{\mathcal{E}}(VRV^{\dagger})\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J}).

(3.20)

The map
V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{K})
is often called a
Stinespring map
or

Stinespring operator
.

What the Eq.(
3.18
) says is that a *-linear CP map, when
dilated

on an appropriate larger space resp. in a larger algebra, is really a
*-homomorphism, or, in other words, that a *-linear CP map is the

compression
of a *-homomorphism. Another way of saying this
is that the CP map has been “lifted” to a homomorphism.
This is yet another example of the “Church of the Larger Hilbert Space” theme.
Note also the similarity to Theorem
3.10
. Another view of
Eq.(
3.18
) is that it says that any *-linear CP-map is a combination of
*-homomorphisms (Corollary
3.16
) and Kraus maps (Proposition
3.18
).

Just as in the
discussion following Proposition
3.18
, from Corollary
3.15

it follows that the convex combination of such unit preserving Stinespring
dilations is again CP *-linear and unit preserving.
Here is a kind of converse of Corollary
3.19
:

Corollary 3.23

(Kraus, Choi)
.

Let
\mathcal{H},\mathcal{J}
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, and

\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
a *-linear CP map. Then there are
finitely many linear maps

V_{j}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{J})
, such that

\forall A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J}):\quad\mathscr{Q}(A)=\sum_{j}V_{j}^{\dagger}\,A\,V_{j}\;\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H});

(3.21)

i.e.
\mathscr{Q}
can be brought into
Kraus form
, cf.
[
44
,
152
]
.
Its adjoint may be gleaned from Eq.(
3.16
).

\mathscr{Q}
is unit preserving
iff

\sum_{j}V_{j}^{\dagger}V_{j}=I_{\mathcal{H}}

(i.e.
\{j\}\mapsto V_{j}^{\dagger}V_{j}
is a POVM), and
\mathscr{Q}
is trace preserving

iff

\sum_{j}V_{j}V_{j}^{\dagger}=I_{\mathcal{J}}
.

The importance of this representation in Eq.(
3.21
) is that the
map
\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
between algebras of maps on Hilbert spaces
can be dealt with in the realm of maps on the Hilbert spaces themselves, just as in
Eqs.(
3.19
) and (

).

compares different CP-maps, cf.

Theorem 3.24

(Radon-Nikodým for CP-maps)
.

.

Remark 3.25
.

Here it is worthwhile to point out some general structural similarities which
arise when comparing states and functionals, as well as when comparing POVMs.
Recalling the geometry of states
described in Proposition
2.48
as living in the dual positive
cone
\mathcal{A}^{+}
, a similar pattern was observed for POVMs in Remark
3.7
.
In both cases, this leads to Radon-Nikodým type results — Corollary
2.57
in the
case of functionals, and Remark
3.7
in the case of POVMs — when comparing
different elements of the positive cone. It was already pointed out in
Remark
2.58
that the Radon-Nikodým type statements translate this into
into positive operators resp. elements of the algebra,
i.e. elements in the convex positive cone of the original space.

Here in Theorem
3.24
a similar pattern may be noted. According to
Corollary
3.15
, CP maps form a positive cone, and the above theorem
tells us how the comparison between
\mathscr{P}
and
\mathscr{T}
is translated into a
positive element of the algebra
R\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})_{+}
.

From Theorem
3.22
one can deduce
[
111
,
75
]

some results about the contractivity, as well as on the spectrum
[
152
]

of positive and trace preserving maps. These may be compared with similar
results in the usual Perron-Frobenius theory, which are important
e.g. when considering Markov-chains. First we need

Definition 3.26

(Contractivity)
.

Let
\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}
be vector spaces, equipped with the some norm, and

\mathscr{F}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})
a linear map. If it satisfies

\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{U}:\;\left\|\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})-\mathscr{F}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\right\|_{\mathcal{V}}\leq\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|_{\mathcal{U}}.

(3.23)

then
\mathscr{F}
is
non-expansive
or for short
contractive
, to be precise
in the norm-combination
(\mathcal{U},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathcal{U}}),(\mathcal{V},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathcal{V}})
.

Proposition 3.27

(Contractivity of CP maps)
.

Let
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
be finite dimensional unital *-algebras, equipped with the
trace based canonical inner product, as well as with the
Schatten-
p
-norms
\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{Sp}=(\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right|^{p})^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}}=(\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 2$}}}}}}}}})^{{\mathchoice{{{{\raise 1.80835pt\hbox{{$\textstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.75346pt\hbox{\kern-1.05487pt\hbox{/}}}{\raise-0.90417pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\textstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.1097pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{\footnotesize/}}}{\raise-0.60275pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\scriptsize/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}{{{{\raise 2.2604pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}{\raise 0.51234pt\hbox{\kern-1.35623pt\hbox{\tiny/}}}{\raise-0.45206pt\hbox{\kern-1.20552pt\hbox{{$\scriptscriptstyle p$}}}}}}}}}
for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
,
and similarly for
\mathcal{B}
, cf. Remark
2.52
.
For the sake of simplicity (some statements are true in more general settings), let

\mathscr{T}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
be a CPTP-map. Or equivalently, let its adjoint

\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
be a CPUP-map, cf. Proposition
3.13
.

Then
\mathscr{T}
is
non-expansive

or
contractive
in the Schatten-1- or trace-norm
(i.e. the Schatten-
1
-norm is to be used in Eq.(
3.23
) on both sides),
but
not necessarily
in any of the other Schatten-
p
-norms for
p>1
.
In particular the trace
\tr_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathbb{C}
is Schatten-1-contractive.

Dually, its adjoint, the CPUP-map
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
is

contractive
in the Schatten-
\infty
-norm
(i.e. the Schatten-
\infty
-norm is to be used in Eq.(
3.23
) on both sides),
but
not necessarily
in any of the other Schatten-
p
-norms for
p<\infty
.
In case the map
\mathscr{T}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
is in addition unital, then
Eq.(
3.23
) holds for all
p\geq 1
, i.e.
\mathscr{T}
and its adjoint
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}

are contractive in
all
Schatten-
p
-norms for
1\leq p\leq\infty
.

Proposition 3.28

(Perron-Frobenius Property)
.

With the same notation and assumptions as above in Proposition
3.27
,
assume in the additionally that
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A}
, and further for simplicity that

\mathscr{T}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
is a *-linear CPTP-map. Recall from linear algebra that

\mathscr{T}
and its adjoint
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
— where
\mathcal{A}
is equipped
with the trace-based canonical inner product (cf. Proposition
2.49
) —
have the same spectrum,
\sigma(\mathscr{T})=\sigma(\mathscr{T}^{\dagger})
, and thus equal spectral
radius (cf. Definition
2.7
), which in this case satisfies:

\varrho(\mathscr{T})=\varrho(\mathscr{T}^{\dagger})=1,

(3.24)

i.e. the eigenvalues are all in the unit circle in
\mathbb{C}
, and positivity implies
that they are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs. All eigenvalues

\lambda\in\sigma(\mathscr{T})
on the unit circle — the so called
peripheral spectrum

with
\left|\lambda\right|=1
— are
semi-simple
, i.e. geometric and algebraic
multiplicity agree.

As
\mathscr{T}
is assumed positive and trace preserving, its adjoint
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}
is
positive and
unital
(cf. Proposition
3.13
), this implies that

\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
, and hence
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}\in\mathcal{A}_{+}

is a
positive definite
eigenvector of
\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}
with eigenvalue

\lambda=1\in\sigma(\mathscr{T}^{\dagger})=\sigma(\mathscr{T})
.

As
\mathscr{T}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
is clearly continuous, and as
trace preserving means that for the closed convex set
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
it holds that

\mathscr{T}(\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A}))\subseteq\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
, Brouwer’s fixed point theorem implies that
there is a fixed point (a density)
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}_{+}
with

\mathscr{T}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*}
. This is hence a
positive
eigenvector of

\mathscr{T}
for the eigenvalue
\lambda=1\in\sigma(\mathscr{T})
.

The following two statements are equivalent:

•

\mathscr{T}
is
irreducible
, i.e. if for any projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

one has that if
\mathscr{T}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}})\subseteq\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}
, then either
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}

or
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}
.

•

\lambda=1\in\sigma(\mathscr{T})
is a
simple
eigenvalue,

\mathscr{T}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*}
is the unique fixed point in
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
, and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*}
is
a
positive definite
eigenvector (i.e.
0\notin\sigma(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*})
,
or
\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}^{\star}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=0
only for
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}
).

An irreducible CPTP-map
\mathscr{T}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
implies that

•

All eigenvalues
\lambda
in the peripheral spectrum (i.e.
\left|\lambda\right|=1
) are

simple
, and they are
roots of unity
, i.e. of the form

\lambda_{k}=\gamma^{k}
for
k=0,\dots,m-1
, with
\gamma=\exp(2\uppi\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathrm{i}}{\textstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{i}}/m)

for some
m\in\mathbb{N}
.

•

There is a unitary
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{A})
such that

\mathscr{T}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{k})=\gamma^{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{k}
for
k=0,\dots,m-1
.

Channels

After all this preparation, we are ready to discuss
channels
, cf.
[
150
,
107
,
77
,
152
,
28
,
151
,
114
]
. Channels are the mathematical formalisation of a transfer of
probabilistic information from one probability algebra to another one.

Definition 3.29

(Channel)
.

A channel from the probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
to the probability algebra
\mathcal{B}
is
in the Heisenberg picture is a *-linear, completely positive, and unit preserving map
(CPUP)
\mathscr{P}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, most importantly mapping effects (or POVMs and PVMs)
of
\mathcal{B}
to effects of
\mathcal{A}
.
Dually, the same channel in the Schrödinger picture, the adjoint, is a *-linear,
completely positive, and trace preserving (CPTP) map
\mathscr{P}^{\dagger}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
, essentially
mapping densities on
\mathcal{A}
to densities on
\mathcal{B}
.

Channels are a very versatile object, and can be used to model or describe many concepts
resp. operations in algebraic probability. They are explored in connection
with quantum information and quantum computation. We have already seen some
examples of CPTP maps — which model channels according to the preceding Definition
3.29
—
in Corollary
3.16
. We have also seen ways to construct CP maps in Proposition
3.18

in Kraus-form — closely related to the structure theorems for CP maps, cf. Theorem
3.22
and Corollary
3.23
— as well as through
parallel compositions in Proposition
3.21
and serial composition in Corollary
3.15
.

It is beyond the scope of the present work to discuss further topics connected with
the transmission of information, like coding, entropy, and channel capacities. The
interested reader is advised to consult the literature, e.g.
[
150
,
107
,
77
,
152
,
28
,
151
,
114
]
, and the references therein.

Example 20

(Some Useful Channels)
.

To show the versatility of the concept of channels, some
examples
will be given,
all referring to *-linear CPTP- resp. CPUP-maps between finite dimensional algebras.

Positive Maps and Abelian Algebras:

One example already encountered were positive
*-linear maps involving an Abelian or classical algebra as domain or range, cf. Corollary
3.16
; these are
completely positive
.

States:
as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})\subset\mathcal{A}^{+}
, they are positive unital maps from
an algebra
\mathcal{A}
into
\mathbb{C}
(a commutative algebra, cf. Corollary
3.16
),
and are thus channels.

Classical Output:
observables like
\mathscr{F}
from Example
19
are
another such example; the output —
a classical output
— is not just the
algebra
\mathbb{C}
as for states, but any classical resp. Abelian or commutative algebra

\mathcal{C}
(cf. Corollary
3.16
),
and the map (in the Heisenberg picture)
\mathscr{F}:\mathcal{C}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
can be realised
by a
POVM
. Recall that a
PVM
, sometimes also called
a
von Neumann measurement
, is a
sharp
(extreme) variant of a POVM,
where all the maps in the collection are mutually orthogonal projections.

Classical input:
Similarly, a unital, positive, *-linear map
\mathscr{I}
,
where the image is any classical (Abelian or commutative) algebra
\mathcal{C}
is completely
positive, cf. Corollary
3.16
. Such a channel can be interpreted in the
Heisenberg picture as a
classical input
to a general system
\mathcal{A}
,
i.e.
\mathscr{I}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}
.

*-Homomorphisms:

Some other examples which were already encountered are the
*-homomorphisms (Definition
2.4
), they are unit preserving.
The Stinespring dilation Theorem
3.22
shows that any channel can be
modelled in terms of *-homomorphisms. If such a *-homomorphisms is an *-isomorphism,
it is an
invertible
channel, also possible to be used in the reverse direction
as a channel.

Samples or Characters:
as
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})\subset\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{C})
, these are also
states (Definition
2.6
) and according to Corollary
3.16
they are channels,
but they are also
*-homomorphisms
into the algebra
\mathbb{C}
.

Automorphisms:
A special case of *-homomorphism
are internal
invertible
*-isomorphisms (channels), like
*-automorphisms (unitary transformations or symmetries)
of the form
\mathscr{S}:\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}^{\star}\in\mathcal{A}
,
where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{u}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{u}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{A})
is a unitary.
Such internal *-automorphisms typically indicate symmetries inherent in
the system, where the symmetry group is represented on a subgroup of the unitaries,
a topic which will not be expanded here, e.g. cf.
[
58
]
.
They may also represent a
quantum computation
, cf. Section
4
.

Unitary Equivalences:
Such transformations between Hilbert spaces
are a bit similar. Let
\mathcal{H}
and
\mathcal{K}
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces
with the same dimension, and a unitary
U:\mathcal{H}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{K}
. Such unitaries
establish *-isomorphisms and hence
invertible channels
between
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})

and
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
: for a
A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
one has the
Kraus form

(cf. Proposition
3.18
) of
UAU^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
.
If
\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{K}
, this is a concrete form of an
automorphism
.

Expansion:

The
expansion
is a
tensoring

of a probability-algebra

\mathcal{A}
by a second one
\mathcal{B}
with density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{B})
,
cf. Corollary
3.21
. In the Heisenberg picture,
this is a CPUP-map
\mathscr{E}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}

defined on elementary tensors
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
by

\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
, and extended by linearity.
The adjoint in the Schrödinger picture is a CPTP-map

\mathscr{E}^{\dagger}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
, for a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})

given simply by the tensorisation

\mathscr{E}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})
.

Restriction:

The
restriction
, a CPUP-map
\mathscr{R}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}

in the Heisenberg picture, is simply
\mathscr{R}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}
.
For the adjoint in the Schrödinger picture, which is
a CPTP-map
\mathscr{R}^{\dagger}:\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, this is just
a partial trace, as already indicated in
Eqs.(
2.29
) and (
2.30
) in Definition
2.72
, and in
Eqs.(
2.34
) and (
2.35
) in Remark
2.74
:
if
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B})
is a state on the
tensor product
\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}
, then the corresponding reduced state
on
\mathcal{A}
is given by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{red,\mathcal{A}}=\mathscr{R}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}})=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
.

Combinations:

One possible way of combining CPUP-maps is
convex combinations

of CPUP-maps, cf. Corollary
3.15
.
One may note that CPUP-maps have geometrically a
very similar structure as states: the intersection of a cone with a linear sub-manifold.
The same is true for their adjoints, their geometric structure is similar to that of
density matrices.

Another very important way to combine channels is the
concatenation

of CPUP-maps, cf. Corollary
3.15
; and, as already mentioned above,
all channels can be built up like this, from a few basic building blocks, namely
expansion and restriction and *-isomorphisms resp. unitary transformations.

Conditional Expectation:

This is a simplified discussion, as, depending on the exact requirements,
conditional expectations in
\mathrm{C}^{*}
- or
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebras may not exist, or may
not be unique, e.g. see
[
143
,
142
,
141
,
65
,
68
,
3
,
88
,
116
,
154
,
155
]

and the references therein. Luckily, it is simpler for finite dimensional algebras

[
65
,
68
,
3
,
107
,
152
,
75
]
.

Let
(\mathcal{A},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}})
be a finite dimensional probability
algebra with a faithful state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
,
and
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
a probability sub-algebra.

Definition 3.30
.

A positive unital map
\mathscr{E}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, which satisfies

\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A},\,\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}:\,\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}),

(3.25)

is called a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
-
conditional expectation

[
75
]
,
conditioned on the sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}
. It is sometimes also denoted

\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}
, or even
\mathscr{E}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathcal{B}}
, and often as
\mathbb{E}(\cdot|\mathcal{B})
.

Some authors sometimes use slightly different, but finally equivalent conditions.
What makes the matter simple in the case of finite dimensional algebras is that

\mathcal{B}
is already complete in all vector space topologies. Some of the properties
of
\mathscr{E}
are collected in the following

Theorem 3.31
.

In the case of finite dimensional algebras (and not only then),
the conditional expectation map
\mathscr{E}

exists
and is
unique
;
it is actually the
orthogonal projection

P_{\mathcal{B}}

[
65
,
68
,
3
,
75
]
of
\mathcal{A}
onto

\mathcal{B}
in the associated Hilbert space inner product from
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}
,
cf. Proposition
2.50
. It can also be described as the
adjoint
\mathscr{E}=P_{\mathcal{B}}=\mathscr{J}^{\dagger}
of the natural identity
embedding
\mathscr{J}:\mathcal{B}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}
.

Thus the map
\mathscr{E}
has operator norm less than unity (it is a contraction)
when the algebras are equipped with the Hilbert
\left\|\cdot\right\|_{2}
-norms, and it is
also a contraction (cf. Proposition
3.27
) when the algebras are equipped with the
Schatten-
\infty
-norm (cf. Remark
2.52
). Additionally it is

completely positive
(CPUP), and hence a
channel
.

It also satisfies

\displaystyle\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A},\,\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{B}:\,\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}),

(3.26)

\displaystyle\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}})

\displaystyle=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}.

(3.27)

From this easily follows: The conditional expectation
\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})

minimises the loss function
\Lambda_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}):=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\right\|_{2}^{2}
over
\mathcal{B}
,
and hence one has Pythagoras’s theorem

\displaystyle\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\right\|_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}))\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\right\|_{2}^{2},\;\text{ and the Galerkin orthogonality}

(3.28)

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}-\mathscr{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\right\rangle_{2}\quad\forall\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{B}.

(3.29)

Two particular choices of sub-algebras deserve an extra note:

•

If
\mathcal{B}=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}]
, then

\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mid\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}])=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}}
.

•

If
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A}
, then

\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mid\mathcal{A})=\mathscr{I}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
, where
\mathscr{I}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})

is the identity.

Instrument:

This is a refinement of the
observable
from Example
19
.
There a
CPUP
-map
\mathscr{F}:\mathcal{C}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, where
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathrm{C}(X)
is a
commutative algebra, was considered. According to Proposition
2.79
, any
commutative or Abelian
\mathrm{W}^{*}
-algebra
\mathcal{C}
can be represented in such a way, where

X=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})
is the set of characters resp. samples. This representation will
be used here in the sequel. For
\mathcal{C}
finite dimensional,
X=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})

is a finite set, with
n=\left|X\right|\in\mathbb{N}
; hence

\mathcal{C}\cong\mathrm{C}(X)\cong\mathbb{C}^{X}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}
with unit

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}=[1,\dots,1]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}\in\mathbb{C}^{X}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}
,
and canonical unit vectors
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{X}
with all components zero,
except unity at position
x\in X

— this is the Hadamard algebra from Example
2
.

The observable from Example
19
transmits probabilistic
information from the algebra
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
to the
classical commutative or Abelian algebra
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}
.
To keep track of what happens to the observed system
\mathcal{A}
,
e.g.
[
150
,
107
,
152
,
151
]
, one has
to include the algebra
\mathcal{A}
as part of the output, or even more generally, a
possibly different probability algebra
\mathcal{B}
. In many cases it could be
identical to
\mathcal{A}
, or a sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
, and represents
the observed system after the interaction with the instrument, which,
in the Heisenberg picture, is a *-linear CPUP-map

\mathscr{G}:\;\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}\ni(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\mapsto\mathscr{G}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\sum_{x\in X}f_{x}G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})\in\mathcal{A},

(3.30)

with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}=[\dots,f_{x}\dots]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}\in\mathbb{C}^{X}
, and then expanded by linearity.
Here each
G_{x}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
is a *-linear completely positive map,
and preservation of the unit requires
\mathscr{G}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}
. This also results in

\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}}):=\sum_{x\in X}G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}
,
where the marginal map
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}:=\sum_{x}G_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
, which
is CPUP, displays
the changes to the system when the output on the system on
\mathcal{C}
is ignored.
Observe that these maps define the POVM for the observation:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{x}:=G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}})\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
. In case the POVM is actually a PVM,
the setup is called a
von Neumann
instrument.

The adjoint of
\mathscr{G}
in Eq.(
3.30
), the channel in the Schrödinger
picture, is
\mathscr{G}^{\dagger}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}
, given by

\mathscr{G}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\sum_{x\in X}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{x}\otimes G^{\dagger}_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}),

(3.31)

where
G^{\dagger}_{x}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
is the adjoint of
G_{x}
, and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{X}

is the canonical unit vector.

Without the information from an observation, the interaction with
the instrument leads to state changes, a new state on
\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}
is given
by Eq.(
3.31
)

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}}=\mathscr{G}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\sum_{x\in X}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{x}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},x}=\sum_{x\in X}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{x}\otimes G^{\dagger}_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}).

(3.32)

By taking partial traces
one obtains the
marginal
densities — predicted without knowing the
outcome of the observation. On
\mathcal{C}
it is the vector

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{marg}}\in\mathbb{C}^{X}
with components
\rho_{x}=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},x}=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{x})
, and on
\mathcal{B}
it is

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},\text{marg}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}):=\sum_{x}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},x}
.

On the other hand, assume that the outcome of the observation is
y\in X
,
i.e. the effect
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{y}
has been observed. This means that on
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{C}^{X}

the
posterior
resp.
observed
density is given by the vector

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{obs}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{y}
, the density for the observation / character

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{y}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=f_{y}
. Moreover, this shows that in
Eqs.(
3.31
) and (
3.32
) only the
x=y
term is non-zero.

The marginal density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},\text{marg}}
from above now is not consistent with

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{obs}}
, as it has to be proportional just to

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},y}=G^{\dagger}_{y}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})
; and trace preservation requires a unit trace:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},\text{post}}=\frac{1}{\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},y}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{B},y}.

(3.33)

This Eq.(
3.33
) is called the generalised
Lüders’
or

Lüders-von Neumann
rule.

As can be shown
[
150
]
,
any channel can be built as a
concatenation
(cf. Corollary
3.15
)
from the *-homomorphisms resp. *-isomorphisms —
unitary transformation being a special case — and expansion
and restriction. This is in some way also the content
of the Stinespring dilation Theorem
3.22
.

The idea of channels, i.e. noisy transmission of information, can, among other things,
also be used to describe Markov chains
[
16
,
15
]
; in fact, any Markov
chain can be described with a channel.

Instruments and Observations:

The last example in the list of possible channels, the

instrument
, deserves to be considered a bit more carefully.
There, in the Heisenberg picture, the marginal map which “forgets” about the
observation, was introduced from Eq.(
3.30
)with
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathscr{G}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\sum_{x\in X}G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})
,
where the
G_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A})
are completely positive. It was already
pointed out that these maps define the POVM for the observation:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{x}:=G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}})\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})
. The reverse question is to find
all the possible observations when given a CP map like
\mathscr{T}=\sum_{x}\mathscr{T}_{x}

with all the
\mathscr{T}_{x}
completely positive.
As the Stinespring dilation Theorem
3.22
will be used, things will be
formulated for operator algebras
[
150
]
. The result is in some
sense analogous to the Radon-Nikodým version in Corollary
2.57
, and obviously
related to Theorem
3.24
:

Theorem 3.32

(Radon-Nikodým for sums of CP-maps)
.

Let
\mathcal{H},\mathcal{J}
be finite dimensional Hilbert spaces,
X
a finite set, and

\mathscr{T}_{x}:\;\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),x\in X
, *-linear completely positive maps,
and set
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{T}}}=\sum_{x\in X}\mathscr{T}_{x}
. In the Stinespring form of
Eq.(
3.19
) in Theorem
3.22
, let
V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{J}\otimes\mathcal{E})

be the Stinespring operator for
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{T}}}
, such that

\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{T}}}:\;\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\ni A\mapsto\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{T}}}(A)=V^{\dagger}(A\otimes I_{\mathcal{E}})V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}).

Then there is a uniquely determined POVM,

X\supset\{x\}\mapsto E_{x}\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{E}))
,
such that

\forall x\in X:\;\mathscr{T}_{x}(A)=V^{\dagger}(A\otimes E_{x})V\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}).

(3.34)

An interesting conclusion may be drawn from Eq.(
3.34
) when
\mathcal{E}
is
one-dimensional, as then
\mathcal{E}\cong\mathbb{C}
and thus
(\mathcal{J}\otimes\mathcal{E})\cong\mathcal{J}
.
The Eq.(
3.34
) in this case reads
\mathscr{T}_{x}(A)=V^{\dagger}(p_{x}A)V
,
i.e. it is in Kraus form
(cf. Corollary
3.19
and Proposition
3.18
) with just one term.
The Theorem
3.32
then tells us that
p_{x}\in[0,1]
and
\sum_{x}p_{x}=1
,
i.e. the only decomposition of
\mathscr{T}=V^{\dagger}AV
into CP maps
\mathscr{T}_{x}

is by positive multiples of
\mathscr{T}
, and
