\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{X}=[\dots,p_{x},\dots]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}
is a
probability distribution on
X
. Moreover, in case
\mathscr{T}
is a channel and
thus unital, with its adjoint Eq.(
3.20
) trace preserving, then

V^{\dagger}V=I_{\mathcal{H}}
and
V
is an isometry. Especially in the case

\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{H}
, the identity
\mathscr{I}
and symmetries are of this one term Kraus
form. This leads to

Corollary 3.33

(No Perturbation — No Information)
.

With
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{C}^{X}
and
\mathcal{H}
as before, let

\mathscr{N}:\;\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
be an instrument such that

\mathscr{N}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{C}}\otimes A)=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}(A)=U^{\dagger}AU
with a unitary
map
U\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
. Then
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}^{\dagger}(R)=URU^{\dagger}
is a unitary
global state change. Especially for
U=I_{\mathcal{H}}
it means that
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}
and

\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}^{\dagger}
are the identity, and hence the state is not perturbed through the
interaction with the instrument.

For a decomposition
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}=\sum_{x\in X}\mathscr{N}_{x}
, the Theorem
3.32

in this case says that there
is a
unique
probability distribution
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{X}=[\dots,p_{x},\dots]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}
on
X

such that
\mathscr{N}_{x}=p_{x}\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{N}}}
.
Thus, this probability
p_{x}
is
independent
of
the density operator
R\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))
, and hence can not provide any
information on
R
.

What this says, is that if one insists that the system represented by
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})

is not perturbed, then there is one and only one probability distribution on
X
,
uniquely dependent on the maps
\mathscr{N}_{x}
, no matter what the state resp. density operator
on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
; i.e. no information can be extracted by this kind of observation.

Updating and Conditional Expectation:

In the following Example
21
the connection between the instrument channel
and the conditional expectation channel will be explored. For that purpose we shall
look more closely at a special case of the instrument channel

\mathscr{G}:\;\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, namely for the sake of simplicity at the case
where
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{A}
, and the POVM associated with
the instrument, the observable
\{x\}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{x}=G_{x}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}})\in\mathrm{E}(\mathcal{A})

on
X
for the probability algebra
\mathcal{A}
, is actually a PVM. This
means that the
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{x}\}\subset\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
are actually mutually orthogonal projections
and we have a von Neumann instrument, as well as that
\left|X\right|\leq\dim\mathcal{A}
.

Example 21

(Update from an Instrument)
.

To make this example more concrete, one could assume that a
PVM on
\mathcal{A}
comes from an observation of some observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
,
i.e. from its spectral decomposition
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{c}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{c}}=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}
, with spectral
projections
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
, cf. Proposition
2.77
and Remark
2.91
.
Accordingly, we shall change the labelling of the PVM from
x\in X
to
j=1,\dots,n

with
n\leq\dim\mathcal{A}
. This PVM is combined with one on
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n}
, the canonical
unit vectors
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{j}
as the standard PVM on
\mathbb{C}^{n}
. This translates to starting with

\{j\}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{j}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A})
, a PVM on the tensor
product of the instrument. We also want the CP-maps
G_{x}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
in
Eq.(
3.30
) to evaluate as
G_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{g}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{g}}_{j}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
.
They can be written in Kraus form as
G_{j}:\,\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mapsto G_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathcal{A}
, which produces the correct result.
Such maps are self-adjoint, so that
G^{\dagger}_{j}=G_{j}
in Eq.(
3.31
).
This also makes the marginal maps
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}=\sum_{x}G_{x}
self-adjoint, i.e.
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}
, and both
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}
and its adjoint are
both CPUP
and
CPTP.

These marginal maps
predict
the state / density before the observation,
or without considering the observation. They are given at each position

j\in[n]
by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{marg}}=[\dots,\rho_{j},\dots]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}
, with

\rho_{j}=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left[(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{j}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\otimes\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}^{*})\mathscr{G}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{j}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{i})\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}^{*}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{i}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{i})\right]\\
=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j})=\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}).

(3.35)

The
predicted
marginal density on
\mathcal{A}
after the interaction with the observable
without taking notice of the information provided by the observation is
in the Schrödinger picture

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}G^{\dagger}_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}.

(3.36)

This flow of information for the prediction is depicted in Fig.
1
.

\textstyle{\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}}}
\scriptstyle{{\mathscr{G}^{\dagger}}}
\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{C}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{marg}}}
\scriptstyle{\tr_{\mathcal{A}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}}
\textstyle{{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}}}}
\scriptstyle{{\tr_{\mathcal{C}}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{A}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}}
\textstyle{\mathcal{C}/\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{marg}}}

Figure 1
:
Schrödinger picture / information flow due to interaction

The Heisenberg picture dual to Eq.(
3.36
), the change in the observable

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
, just due to the interaction with the instrument,
without taking notice of or evaluating the information provided by the observation,
follows from Eq.(
3.30
) to be

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{marg}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}.

(3.37)

Observe that both
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}
and its adjoint
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}
fulfil the
assumptions in Theorem
3.32
, which means that each
G_{j}
resp.
G_{J}^{\dagger}

could be described in the Stinespring form with a Radon-Nikodým effect.

Assume now that a certain
k\in[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}
is the outcome
of the observation, i.e. the projection
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=G_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}})\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

has been observed. The observation / sample on
\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{C}^{n}
is thus given by the

pure state
/ rank-one
observed
density

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{obs}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{k}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathbb{C}^{n})_{1}
, the density representation of a
character
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{C})
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{f}})=f_{k}
.

The information from this is that now the predicted density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{marg}}\in\mathcal{C}
in
Eq.(
3.35
) is not consistent with the observation and has thus
to be changed to the
observed
density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\text{obs}}
.
This means that also the predicted marginal density
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}\in\mathcal{A}
in
Eq.(
3.36
) is not consistent with the observation, and has to be adjusted
to incorporate the information from the observation.

Taking into account of this information that
k\in[n]
was observed
means that in Eqs.(
3.36
) and (
3.37
) only the term
j=k
is
non-zero. For the density this means that the
posterior density

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}
on
\mathcal{A}
has to be proportional to

G^{\dagger}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
. Trace preservation requires
that the
posterior
density conditioned on the information of the observation thus
is given by the so-called
Lüders
or
von Neumann - Lüders

rule Eq.(
3.33
)

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}=\frac{1}{\tr_{\mathcal{A}}G^{\dagger}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})}\,G^{\dagger}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\frac{1}{\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k},

(3.38)

by observing that

\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})=\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})
.

One sees directly in Eq.(
3.38
) that the
prior
density from
Eq.(
3.36
),
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
, is changed (by projection)
due to the observation as little as possible — just so much as to be consistent
with the new information contained in the observation — to arrive at the

posterior
density, which connects it with Theorem
3.31
.
As in the Heisenberg picture Eq.(
3.37
) also only the term
j=k
is
non-zero, an observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
is changed to

\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto G_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{post}}\in\mathcal{A}.

(3.39)

What may be noted already here is that the update to take account of the information
that there was either an interaction with the instrument, or both an interaction and
an observation, hast two different forms of being expressed: one is the Heisenberg picture
Eqs.(
3.37
) and (
3.39
) where observables, PVMs, and effects are changed
while the state is kept, and the other is the Schrödinger picture
Eqs.(
3.36
) and (
3.38
) where the state resp. the density is changed.

Both approaches give the same probabilities, both ways are the same
update, e.g. from Eqs.(
3.36
) and (
3.37
) one obtains for all

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}

\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\tr(\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tr(G_{j}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}})\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\\
=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,G_{j}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}))=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}))=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{marg}}).

(3.40)

A bit disturbing is the fact that the change in the observable Eq.(
3.39
)
as a map
G_{k}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
is completely positive, but
not unit preserving

(
G_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
), and thus does not fit under the channel paradigm to cover
the update taking into account the information from the observation.

One way to rectify this is with the concept of conditional expectation discussed above in
the example list of possible channels, by redefining
G_{k}:\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
with a yet
to be defined sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A}
. The
conditioning fact

is here that an observation of the PVM (
\{j\}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}
) is to take place, and this
interaction with the instrument defined by the PVM will lead to new information,
and this new information implies an update on the observables, i.e. Eq.(
3.39
).
In the next Example
22
, this all goes into the definition of the sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}
,
which is needed to apply Definition
3.30
.

Conditional expectation in probability algebras is a lively subject, e.g. see

[
143
,

,
141
,
65
,

,
3
,

,

,

,

]

and the references therein.
One can make the requirements very strict, with the effect that a conditional
expectation only exists under certain circumstances for infinite dimensional
algebras, cf.
[
116
]
; luckily for finite dimensional algebras
they do exist and there is even quite explicit descriptions
[
152
]
.
On the question of whether Lüders’ rule Eqs.(
3.38
) and (
3.44
) is
the right way to formulate conditional expectation Eq.(
3.43
),
see also
[

,

,

,

,

]
and the references therein.

Example 22

(Update as Conditional Expectation)
.

The conditional expectation
\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})
in Eq.(
3.25
) of some
observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
is going to be a function
of that observable and the PVM
\{j\}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
which it
is being conditioned on.
This sub-*-algebra can thus be taken, in case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}
is observed, as the one
generated by expressions of the kind
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathcal{A}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j})=:\mathcal{B}_{j}
for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
. This leaves all
possibilities for such a function for any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
, and at the same times
insures that self-adjoint elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}

are mapped onto self-adjoint elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathcal{B}_{j,sa}
.

Observe that for
j\neq m
the sub-algebras
\mathcal{B}_{j}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathcal{A}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}
and

\mathcal{B}_{m}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{m}\,\mathcal{A}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{m}
are orthogonal. Hence

\mathcal{N}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}\mathcal{B}_{j}\subset\mathcal{A}

would be a candidate sub-algebra, but it is too big. One only wants the
sub-algebra of
\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{N}
generated by expressions of the form

\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}
in Eq.(
3.37
), where each
summand has the same
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}
in the middle. Thus one may set

\mathcal{B}:=\mathbb{C}\left\langle\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\mid\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{b}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{b}}\in\mathcal{A}\right\}\right\rangle\subset\mathcal{N}\subset\mathcal{A}.

(3.41)

Hence it is clear that
\mathscr{J}:\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, where
\mathscr{J}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathcal{A}

is the identity embedding of
\mathcal{B}
into
\mathcal{A}
. From Theorem
3.31
one
may then see that its adjoint
\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}:=\mathscr{J}^{\dagger}
, the orthogonal
projection onto
\mathcal{B}
, is the sought after conditional expectation.

Note that these expressions are identical to
\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}=\,\overline{\!{\mathscr{G}}}^{\dagger}

as used in Example
21
above; they will not be used here as they may lead
to confusion. The reason is that the point of view in Example
21
was that
there is a flow of information from
\mathcal{A}
to
\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{A}

with a trace preserving map, whereas here we use the
unital
conditional expectation

\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}:\,\mathcal{A}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{B}
, and thus the flow of information is in the direction
of the trace preserving
\mathscr{J}=\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}^{\dagger}:\,\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
, as information
from the observation is to be transferred to the whole algebra
\mathcal{A}
.

For an observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}_{sa}
, the expression of the
conditional expectation

\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathcal{B}):=\mathscr{E}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathscr{J}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{marg}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{j}\in\mathcal{B}

(3.42)

contains the information after the interaction with the instrument, and prior to the
information from the observation. It contains all the possibilities which might result
from an observation, i.e. all the possibilities how any
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}
may be updated once some

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
has been observed. Its adjoint in the Schrödinger picture is the already
mentioned embedding
\mathscr{J}=\mathscr{E}^{\dagger}_{\mathcal{B}}=\mathbb{E}^{\dagger}(\cdot|\mathcal{B}):\,\mathcal{B}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{A}
.
The whole situation is shown in Fig.

.

After the observation of some
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
— this means a pure state / character

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}
on
\mathcal{C}
— due to the new information, just the term
j=k

is left in Eq.(
3.41
), and this becomes the projection (cf. Eq.(
3.39
))

\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathcal{B}_{k}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{post}}\in\mathcal{B}_{k},

(3.43)

and in contrast to the conditional expectation in Eq.(
3.42
), this could be
called the
post conditional expectation
, as it is after the conditioning information
has been taken into account. But it usually also called conditional expectation,
sometimes leading to confusion on whether Eq.(
3.42
) or Eq.(
3.43
)
is meant. Note that, as
\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{A}}|\mathcal{B}_{k})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{1}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{1}}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}
, the map
in Eq.(
3.43
) is CPUP.

The new state on the algebra — after the new information due to the
observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
— can then finally be found through the adjoint of
Eq.(
3.43
), it is the embedding

\mathcal{B}_{k}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mapsto\mathbb{E}^{\dagger}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}|\mathcal{B}_{k})=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\in\mathcal{A},

(3.44)

confirming Lüders’ rule Eq.(
3.38
). This
posterior density

then defines a new state on
\mathcal{A}

which is consistent with the new information from the observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
.
Thus Lüders’ rule Eqs.(
3.38
) and (
3.39
) can be seen in
the light of conditional expectation and the updating following an observation.
In classical commutative probability this is connected with Bayes’s theorem and
is often called
Bayesian updating
. One may keep the same term also
in non-commutative probability, although Bayes’s theorem does not hold generally
in this instance
[
42
,
10
,
69
,
112
,
11
,
12
]
, and it is not the basis for the update.

The expectation computed with this new density on
\mathcal{A}
,
with Eqs.(
3.38
) and (
3.39
), is

\mathcal{A}\ni\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mapsto\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}):=\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}]\\
=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}]=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}_{\text{post}}]\in\mathbb{C},

(3.45)

and this could be called the
conditioned expectation
, as it is the expectation

after
the new information of the conditioning event has been taken into account.
The functional
\mathbb{E}(\cdot|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
is the
new state
to reflect this.
Note that in this new state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
is a
sure
event, as
\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}]=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}]=1
.

) is shown in Fig.

One may also observe that according to Corollary
2.57
, the conditioned expectation
state
\mathbb{E}(\cdot|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})

w.r.t. the

, so that for all

one has

.
An explicit form of

may be found in
[
152
]
.

This Example
22
shows how the interaction with the instrument — via the
conditional expectation — and the observation — via the conditioned expectation —
can both be brought under the channel paradigm. One may also note how the flow of
information is from the instrument interaction (in Fig.
2
) resp. the
observation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}
to the original algebra
\mathcal{A}
of observables in Fig.
3
.

One might add that in both instances, i.e. the one in Fig.
2
and the one in
Fig.
3
, the last mapping into the original algebra
\mathcal{A}
is the identity
embedding and thus a purely formal
one. This is due to the fact that according to Eqs.(
3.42
) and (
3.43
)
all the elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}
are updated and mapped into a sub-algebra of
\mathcal{A}
.
This is either just due to the instrument interaction (Fig.
2
) in
Eq.(
3.42
) a mapping into the sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}
, or in case of an additional
observation (Fig.
3
) in Eq.(
3.43
) into the sub-algebra
\mathcal{B}_{k}
.
And as Eqs.(
3.36
),(
3.38
) and (
3.44
) show, the corresponding
densities
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{marg}}\in\mathcal{B}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\text{post}}\in\mathcal{B}_{k}
are also
in the corresponding sub-algebra to provide probabilities according to
Eqs.(
3.40
) and (
3.45
). Hence, any further operation
might just as well proceed from one of the probability sub-algebras, either
\mathcal{B}
or

\mathcal{B}_{k}
, depending on whether the information from the observation has been taken
into account or not, and the original probability algebra
\mathcal{A}\supset\mathcal{B}\supset\mathcal{B}_{k}

is too big and not needed any more.

Conditional Probability:

Like in Definition
2.17
,
conditional probability
will be based on
conditional expectation. It was already mentioned that this concept is still
being debated, e.g. see

[
143
,
65
,
68
,
3
,
88
,
116
,
154
,
155
]
and the references therein.

The question is whether Lüders’ rule Eqs.(
3.38
) and (
3.44
) is
the right way to formulate conditional expectation Eq.(
3.43
),
and conditional probability based on it, e.g. cf.
[
41
,
42
,
109
,
69
,
112
]
.
Like many extensions into a wider realm, often it is not possible to keep all properties of
some construction when extending it.
It is clear that in order to take account of new information in the form of what is in many
instances called
data assimilation
, such a concept is needed, cf. e.g.
[
61
]
, but, on the other hand, Bayes’s theorem does not
hold in the non-commutative case
[
42
,
69
,
112
,
11
,
12
]
. This may be seen as the defining difference
between commutative and non-commutative probability theory
[
10
]
.

Using the analogue to Definition
2.17
, one can define what
might be called
conditional probability

by employing the new state
\mathbb{E}(\cdot|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
from Eq.(
3.45
).
For
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
one can just define a probability as before in Definition
2.17
:

\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}):=\mathbb{E}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}).

(3.46)

And in case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}
commute, it behaves like a classical Kolmogorovean
conditional probability, as

[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}]=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{0}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{0}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}|\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})=\frac{1}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}\,\tr_{\mathcal{A}}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}]=\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})},

and
\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{r}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{r}}_{\mathcal{A}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k})
may be
seen as the
joint probability
of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{q}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{q}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{p}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{p}}_{k}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
.
But in case they do not commute and are not compatible, there is no joint probability,
and some properties are lost;
this is discussed extensively in e.g.
[
69
]
and the references therein.

In this context, it is worthwhile to note that the classical Kolmogorovean
conditional probability has a unique property. To paraphrase

[
41
,
69
]
,
given a classical probability measure
\mathbb{P}
on a
\sigma
-algebra
\mathfrak{F}
, and two
events
A,B\in\mathfrak{F}
, the classical conditional probability, defined as usual by the
ratio
\mathbb{P}(A|B):=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(B)
and using the joint probability

\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)
, is characterised by the fact that it is the
only

probability measure defined on all of
\mathfrak{F}
, such that for
A\subseteq B

the conditioning on
B
just involves a renormalisation of the initial probability
measure; i.e.
\mathbb{P}(A|B)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(B)=\mathbb{P}(A)/\mathbb{P}(B)
.

Now assume that
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, where
\mathcal{H}
is a finite dimensional Hilbert space
with
\dim\mathcal{H}>2
and density operator
R\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{A})
, and let

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}))
be the lattice of all orthogonal
projections, cf. Proposition
2.25
. Further, let
P\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

be an orthogonal projection, and consider the sub-lattice

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\leq P):=\{Q\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}),Q\leq P\}\subset\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A}))
of
all projections less or equal to
P
. Note that, as for
Q\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\leq P)
one
has
Q\leq P
, it follows that
QP=PQ=Q
, and thus all
Q\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\leq P)

commute with
P
. Then it holds that
[
41
,
69
]
:

Theorem 3.34

(Existence and Uniqueness of Lüders Conditional Probability)
.

In the setting just sketched, assume that
\mathbb{P}_{R}(P)=\mathbb{E}_{R}(P)=\tr(RP)\neq 0

(cf. Definition
2.17
).
In an analogous fashion to the classical definition and to the definition in
Eq.(
3.46
), define for any
Q\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{{\mathsf{L}}}}(\leq P)
the function

\Pr(Q):=\mathbb{P}_{R}(Q)/\mathbb{P}_{R}(P)=\mathbb{P}_{R}(QP)/\mathbb{P}_{R}(P)
; obviously this
is just a renormalisation of the initial probability measure
\mathbb{P}_{R}(Q)
.

Then there is a
unique

extension
\mathbb{P}_{R}(\cdot|P)
of
\Pr(\cdot)
to all of
\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})
,
it is derived from the state given by the conditioned expectation
(cf. Eq.(
3.45
))
\mathbb{E}(\cdot|P)\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{A})
on
\mathcal{A}

— it thus satisfies Eq.(
2.52
) — and
whose density operator
R_{P}
is given by Lüders’ rule (cf. Eq.(
3.38
))

R_{P}:=PRP/\mathbb{P}_{R}(P)
, such that for all
Q\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{A})

\mathbb{P}_{R}(Q|P)=\mathbb{E}_{R}(Q|P)=\tr(R_{P}Q)=\frac{\tr(PRPQ)}{\mathbb{P}_{R}(P)}.

(3.47)

It should be clear that the theorem holds also for any finite dimensional probability
algebra which has no factor isomorphic to
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
with
\dim\mathcal{K}=2

(factor of type
\mathrm{I}_{2}
) in their factor decomposition,
cf. Theorem
2.82
and Theorem
2.86
.

This Theorem
3.34
is often taken as reason enough to define conditional probabilities
like in Eq.(
3.46
), based on conditional expectation like in Eq.(
3.45
).
But, as noted already, some additivity properties are lost due to non-commutativity
and Bayes’s theorem does not hold — one reason being that it is not possible to
formulate
joint
probabilities in every case
[
10
,
11
,
12
]

— so that sometimes an extreme sounding position is
argued
[
69
]
, in that there actually is
no
fully viable definition
of conditional probability in the non-commutative case. We will not enter further
into this discussion here.

Channel-State Duality:

The next result, which establishes a one-to-one relationship between channels and
ordinary linear maps on Hilbert spaces themselves, is similar to the ones mentioned
previously; in fact it is closely related to Theorem
3.20
, Theorem
3.22
,
and Corollary
3.23
. Here one of the simpler versions is presented,
for variations on this theme, and different versions
of it, cf.
[
62
]
.

Theorem 3.35

(Jamiołkowski-Choi)
.

Let
\mathcal{H}
(with
\dim\mathcal{H}=n
and orthonormal basis
\{\ket{v_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{n}
)
and
\mathcal{K}
(with
\dim\mathcal{K}=m
) be two finite dimensional Hilbert spaces,
and let
\mathscr{Q}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
be a linear map (a super-operator).
Denote by

\ket{W}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\ket{v_{j}}\otimes\ket{v_{j}}\in\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}

a (maximally entangled) unit vector in
\mathcal{H}^{\otimes 2}
, and by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}=\ket{W}\bra{W}
the orthogonal projector onto it’s subspace. Then

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))\ni\mathscr{Q}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}=(\mathscr{Q}\otimes I_{\mathcal{H}})\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{P}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})

(3.48)

is a linear isomorphism
\mathscr{Q}\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}
between those spaces of mappings indicated.

The inverse mapping
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\mapsto\mathscr{Q}
is given by
mapping a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
onto

\mathscr{Q}:\;\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})\ni A\mapsto\mathscr{Q}(A)=n\,\tr_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}(I_{\mathcal{K}}\otimes A^{\dagger}))\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}).

(3.49)

Observe that the isomorphism of the
Jamiołkowski-Choi-Theorem
3.35
applies
not just to channels, but to any
\mathscr{Q}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
.
The importance of this isomorphism is that it allows to read off properties of the
map
\mathscr{Q}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
by looking at the “normal”
Hilbert space operator
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
of the bi-partite system

\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H}
. These correspondences
of properties are collected in Table
4
.

Operator
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}

Map

Property

\mathscr{Q}(A^{\dagger})=\mathscr{Q}(A)^{\dagger}

Hermitean, *-linearity

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\geq 0

trace preserving (TP)

Table 4:
Correspondence of Properties

One may observe that for a map to be a channel

\mathscr{Q}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
,
it has to possess all the properties in the middle column of
Table
4
. This means that the corresponding Hilbert space
operator
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
has all the properties in the
first column of Table
4
.

Corollary 3.36

(Channel-State Duality)
.

Assume now that
\mathscr{Q}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}),\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}))
is a completely positive
unit preserving map (CPUP), i.e. a
channel
, checking all points in the second
column of Table
4
.
This means that the corresponding Hilbert space operator

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
satisfies all points in the first column of
Table
4
.

First, note that the fourth and fifth row of Table
4
show that
the partial traces
\tr_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}})
and
tr_{\mathcal{K}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}})
are density
operators on
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
and
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, respectively. Moreover,

\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}})=\tr_{\mathcal{K}}(\tr_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}))=\tr_{\mathcal{H}}(\tr_{\mathcal{K}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}))=1.

Together with the other properties in the first column of Table
4
,
it becomes clear that the corresponding Hilbert space operator

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\textstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfbfit{Q}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
is a
density operator
on the
Hilbert space
\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H}
. Thus the Eqs.(
3.48
) and (
3.49
)
implement a
duality
of channels between systems
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K})
and

\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
, and states on the combined system
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{K}\otimes\mathcal{H})
,
represented by density operators, the so called
channel-state duality
.

3.3
Interacting Fock Space and Quantum Decomposition

In this sub-section the idea is to embed an algebra of commuting random variables,
i.e. a classical algebra, into a larger, non-commutative algebra, which can help
in analysing those random variables. For the sake of simplicity, here we only look
at one random variable, a case which still transmits the flavour of the subject.
Connections will come up between the Fock space, orthogonal polynomials, Krylov
subspaces, and the Lanczos method. These methods have led to new views on diverse
classical subjects, like graphs, reaction networks, random walks, and Markov chains.
For a broader survey, cf.
[
102
]
.

Fock Space and Ladder Operators:

The following idea arose in quantum physics to describe the so-called second
quantisation, so to introduce and motivate it, some physical terms will be used.
Given a Hilbert space
\mathcal{J}
to describe
the states resp. modes of some kind of elementary particle,
the Fock space is defined as
\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{J}):=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}\mathcal{K}_{k}
,
with the
sectors

\mathcal{K}_{k}:=\mathcal{J}^{\otimes k}
,
e.g. cf.
[
15
]
.
This is the
full
or
Boltzmannian

Fock space
of
distinguishable
particles resp. modes.
Each tensor power resp. sector in this
non-interacting
Fock space is equipped with
the natural inner product from the tensor power, and similarly then the direct sum.
The one-dimensional space
\mathcal{J}^{\otimes 0}\cong\mathbb{C}
is often modelled as

\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\Psi_{0}
, where the unit vector
\Psi_{0}
is assumed to be orthogonal to

\mathcal{J}
, and is called the
vacuum vector
.
For elementary particles like Fermions or Bosons, one takes the
anti-symmetric tensor product for the Fermionic resp. the symmetric tensor product
for the Bosonic Fock space in order
to accommodate the
Pauli exclusion principle
resp. the

indistinguishability
of individual Bosons.
The symmetric tensor product resp. Bosonic Fock space leads
to Gaussian measures
[
83
]
, cf. also Theorem
3.43
.

As state one can take the vector or pure state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\Psi_{0}}(A):=\left\langle\Psi_{0}\mid A\Psi_{0}\right\rangle

(also called the vacuum state) for
A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{J}))
, giving a probability algebra

(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{J})),\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\Psi_{0}})
with GNS-representation

(\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{J}),\Psi_{0})
.
An important set of operators in that probability algebra are the
ladder operators
,
i.e. the
creation operator

\mathchoice{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
and its adjoint the
annihilation operator

\mathchoice{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=(\mathchoice{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}})^{\dagger}
, and the
number operator

N
.
The latter is the easiest to describe and the same in all variants of the Fock space:
each sector
\mathcal{K}_{n}
resp. tensor power
\mathcal{J}^{\otimes n}
is an eigenspace,
and for
\psi_{n}\in\mathcal{K}_{n}
one defines
N\psi_{n}:=n\psi_{n}
.
In this spectral resolution, other
diagonal
operators
are easily described: Let
\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}
be a sequence of real numbers,
then the
operator function

\mathchoice{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}N^{{\kern-22.96686pt{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\kern 7.08473pt}}_{{\kern-47.31786pt\mathchoice{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 7.08473pt}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}N^{{\kern-22.96686pt{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\kern 7.08473pt}}_{{\kern-47.31786pt\mathchoice{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\kern 7.08473pt}}}{\hphantom{{}^{{{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[15.77101pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}N^{{\kern-20.35336pt{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\kern
