The
creation and annihilation
operators are
ladder
resp.
shift

operators. The creation operator for a new mode
\chi\in\mathcal{J}
is defined on
each sector
\mathcal{K}_{n}=\mathcal{J}^{\otimes k}
for elementary tensors

\psi_{n}=\bigotimes_{k=0}^{n}\varphi_{k}
(with
\varphi_{k}\in\mathcal{J}
and

\psi_{0}=\varphi_{0}=\Psi_{0}
) by

\mathchoice{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\chi):\,\mathcal{K}_{n}\ni\psi_{n}\mapsto\psi_{n}\otimes\chi\in\mathcal{K}_{n+1}
.
Similarly, its adjoint, the annihilation operator, is given by
\mathchoice{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\chi)\Psi_{0}=0

for
n=0
, and for
n>0
by

\mathchoice{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{A^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(\chi):\,\mathcal{K}_{n}\ni\bigotimes_{k=0}^{n}\varphi_{k}\mapsto\left\langle\chi\mid\varphi_{n}\right\rangle\;\bigotimes_{k=0}^{n-1}\varphi_{k}\in\mathcal{K}_{n-1}
.

These ladder operators are defined for some mode or state
\chi\in\mathcal{J}
for each
sector
\mathcal{K}_{n}
in an analogous way, without regard to the number of modes,
using the natural mode-number independent inner
product on the sector
\mathcal{K}_{n}=\mathcal{J}^{\otimes n}
;
explaining the
non-interacting
character.

In case
\dim\mathcal{J}=1
, i.e.
\mathcal{J}=\spn\{\Psi_{1}\}
, all tensor powers resp. sectors

\mathcal{J}^{\otimes n}=\spn\{\Psi_{1}^{\otimes n}\}
are also one-dimensional. Hence one may,
for the sake of simplicity, just take as a unitarily equivalent substitute for
\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{J})

a separable Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
, the closure of
\spn\{\Psi_{0},\Psi_{1},\dots\}
,
where the the
\{\Psi_{n}\}
are an orthogonal sequence, and set
\mathcal{K}_{n}:=\spn\{\Psi_{n}\}
,
cf. e.g.
[
2
,
80
,
108
]
; this avoids unnecessarily
dealing with tensor products.

One-mode Interacting Fock Space:

As stated above, here only the special case of an one-mode interacting Fock space
built from one-dimensional sectors is considered,
but which still is useful when analysing just one random variable,
cf. e.g.
[
2
,
4
,
5
,
8
,
80
,
108
]
, and which shows how the inner product and definition of ladder
operators on each
n
-particle resp. -mode sector is changed such that the
interaction is taken care of.

Definition 3.37

(Jacobi sequence)
.

Let
\{\lambda_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}
be a sequence of non-negative real numbers with

\lambda_{0}=1
, and the property that if for some
m_{0}\geq 0
one
has
\lambda_{m_{0}+1}=0
, this implies
\lambda_{n}=0
for all
n>m_{0}
.
This is called a
Jacobi sequence
.
If such a
m_{0}\in\mathbb{N}
exists, the sequence is called of
finite type
, otherwise
of
infinite type
(
m_{0}=\infty
).

A first Jacobi sequence will be used to define the interacting inner products
on each sector of the Fock sum.

Definition 3.38

(One-mode interacting Fock space)
.

As indicated above, a concrete one-mode interacting Fock space is defined
in the simplest manner by taking a complex infinite dimensional separable Hilbert
space
\mathcal{H}
with inner product
\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
, and a complete orthogonal system

\{\Psi_{0},\Psi_{1},\dots\}
, and letting for
n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
the corresponding summand
resp. sector be
\mathcal{K}_{n}:=\spn\{\Psi_{n}\}
. It is often convenient to extend this by
setting
\Psi_{-1}=0
and
\mathcal{K}_{-1}=\spn\{\Psi_{-1}\}=\{0\}
.

Let
\{\lambda_{n}\}
be a Jacobi sequence as in Definition
3.37
.
The inner product
on the sector
\mathcal{K}_{n}
is defined for
n\geq 0
and
\xi_{n},\eta_{n}\in\mathcal{K}_{n}
as

\left\langle\xi_{n}\mid\eta_{n}\right\rangle_{n}:=\lambda_{n}\left\langle\xi_{n}\mid\eta_{n}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.

(3.50)

It will be assumed that the
\Psi_{n}
in the orthogonal system are
normalised by
\left\langle\Psi_{n}\mid\Psi_{n}\right\rangle_{n}=1
.
Let
m_{0}
be the extended natural number from Definition
3.37
which indicates
for
\{\lambda_{n}\}
a Jacobi sequence of finite or infinite type. Then the
algebraic direct sum

\Gamma:=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{m_{0}}\mathcal{K}_{n},

(3.51)

a pre-Hilbert space
equipped with the inner products Eq.(
3.50
) on each sector,
yields the direct sum inner product
\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\Gamma}
, and
defines the basic
one-mode interacting full Fock space
.

Definition 3.39

Let
\{\omega_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}

\omega_{0}=1

for
n>0

\omega_{n}=\lambda_{n}/\lambda_{n-1}

that in the situation
0/0
one sets
\omega_{n}=0

,
yielding the associated Fock probability space as
\Gamma_{\{\lambda_{n}\}}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}

— a
Qubit
. The Jacobi sequences are explicitly
\{\omega_{0}=\omega_{1}=1,\omega_{2}=\omega_{3}=\dots=0\}
and
\{\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{1}=1,\lambda_{2}=\lambda_{3}=\dots=0\}
, i.e. they are of
finite type
.
With the identification
\Gamma_{\{\lambda_{n}\}}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}
, one obtains

\Psi_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix},\;\Psi_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathchoice{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\
0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad\mathchoice{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\end{bmatrix}.

Theorem 3.43

(
q
-Fock Moments)
.

For the one-mode interacting
q
-Fock probability algebra of Definition
3.42
,
denote the Fock space by
\Gamma(q)
and the ladder operators as functions of
q
:

\mathchoice{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(q)
and
\mathchoice{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(q)
. Now consider the RV

Z(q):=\mathchoice{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(q)+\mathchoice{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}(q)\in\mathcal{L}(\Gamma(q))
,
and the sub-*-probability algebra
\mathbb{C}[Z(q)]
it generates.

In the special cases of Definition
3.42
, the RV
Z(q)\in\mathbb{C}[Z(q)]
is moment
equivalent to some well known distributions:

The Bosonic
q=1
case:

The
standard normal Gaussian
random variable
\gamma

and
Z(1)
are moment equivalent:

\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\uppi}}\;\exp(-x^{2}/2)\;\sim\;\gamma\quad\overset{\text{m}}{=}\quad Z(1).

The Free
q=0
case:

The random variable
-2\leq\upsilon\leq 2
with
distribution according to
Wigner’s semi-circle law
and
Z(0)
are
moment equivalent:

\frac{1}{2\uppi}\;\sqrt{4-x^{2}}\;\sim\;\upsilon\quad\overset{\text{m}}{=}\quad Z(0).

The Fermionic
q=-1
case:

The
Bernoulli (-1,+1)
random variable
\beta

and
Z(-1)
are moment equivalent:

\frac{1}{2}\;(\updelta_{-1}(x)+\updelta_{+1}(x))\;\sim\;\beta\quad\overset{\text{m}}{=}\quad Z(-1).

Orthogonal Polynomials:

This is a classical subject, and some well known
facts are first shortly recalled: Let
\nu
be a Borel probability measure on the real
line
\mathbb{R}
having moments of any order. Using this, define the usual complex

\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R},\nu)
-space with corresponding inner product and norm:

\mathbb{E}_{\nu}(f)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)\,\nu(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x),\quad\left\langle f\mid g\right\rangle_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}(f^{*}\,g),\;\text{ and }\;\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\nu}(f^{*}\,f)}.

Consider the monomial functions
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}},x,x^{2},\dots,x^{n}\dots\in\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{u}})
,
and perform the
Gram-Schmidt
orthogonalisation process starting with the
constant function
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}}
, to obtain

\left\langle\cdot\mid\cdot\right\rangle_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}
-orthogonal polynomial functions
P_{n}(x)\in\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{u}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{u}})
.
They are inductively defined as
P_{0}(x)={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}}
, and for
n>0
by

P_{n}(x)=x^{n}-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\,\frac{\left\langle P_{j}\mid x^{n}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}}{\left\langle P_{j}\mid P_{j}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}}\,P_{j}(x).

(3.60)

It is convenient to set
P_{-1}\equiv 0
.
Similarly to, and following Definition
3.37
, we define

Definition 3.44

(Jacobi-Szegö Coefficients or Parameters)
.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\{\omega_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}
be a pair of real sequences, such that

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\{\omega_{n}\}
is a
Jacobi sequence
according
to Definition
3.37
, and
\alpha_{0}=1
.
If
\{\omega_{n}\}
is of
finite type
with some
m_{0}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
, it is
assumed that
\alpha_{n}=0
for all
n>m_{0}+1
. Such a pair of sequences
are called
Jacobi-Szegö coefficients

or
Jacobi-Szegö parameters
of
finite type
. Otherwise, the

Jacobi-Szegö coefficients
resp.
Jacobi-Szegö parameters
are called
of
infinite type
.

Some well known facts on orthogonal polynomials will be needed in the sequel:

Theorem 3.45

(Orthogonal Polynomials)
.

Given a probability measure
\nu
with all moments as above, and the corresponding polynomials
as in Eq.(
3.60
), define
m_{0}
by
1+m_{0}=\left|\supp\nu\right|

(the extended number
\left|\supp\nu\right|
is the cardinality of the support of the measure);
if
m_{0}\in\mathbb{N}
, the measure
\nu
is called of
finite type
,
otherwise of
infinite type
. Then

1.

All the polynomial functions
{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}},x,x^{2},\dots,x^{n},\dots

are linearly independent for a measure of infinite type,
whereas for a measure of finite type, the polynomial functions

{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}},x,\dots,x^{m_{0}}
are independent, and the Gram-Schmidt process in
Eq.(
3.60
) stops at
m_{0}
.

2.

The polynomial functions
P_{n}(x)=x^{n}+\dots
are monic polynomials of degree

n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
. They are orthogonal, i.e. for
0\leq n,k\leq m_{0}
:

\left\langle P_{n}\mid P_{k}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{L}_{2}}=\updelta_{nk}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\omega_{j}=\updelta_{nk}\lambda_{n}
,
cf. Definition
3.39
.

3.

There exist
Jacobi-Szegö coefficients

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\{\omega_{n}\},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\{\alpha_{n}\}
(cf. Definition
3.44
) of
corresponding type (finite or infinte), such that for
0\leq n\leq m_{0}

\displaystyle x\,P_{n}(x)=P_{n+1}(x)+\alpha_{n+1}\,P_{n}(x)+\omega_{n}\,P_{n-1}(x).

(3.61)

The Jacobi-Szegö coefficients are completely defined by the Gram-Schmidt process
Eq.(
3.60
), and orthogonality relation in the preceding item.

4.

Moreover,
\alpha_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}(x)
and
\omega_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}((x-\alpha_{1})^{2})=\var_{\nu}(x)
. In case
\nu
is symmetric (i.e.
\nu(-\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)=\nu(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x)
), all

odd
moments vanish, i.e.
\mathbb{E}_{\nu}(x^{2k-1})=0
for
k\in\mathbb{N}
.
If all odd moments vanish, then
\alpha_{n}=0
for
n>0
.

Denote by
\mathscr{P}:=\mathrm{P}(\mathbb{R},\nu)\subset\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R},\nu)
the pre-Hilbert space
of all polynomial functions, still equipped with the same inner product as
\mathrm{L}_{2}(\mathbb{R},\nu)
.
Clearly, the polynomial functions
\{P_{n}\}
from above are an orthogonal basis of
\mathscr{P}
.
Introducing normalised polynomial functions
\{Q_{n}\}
, defined by

Q_{n}=P_{n}/\sqrt{\lambda_{n}}
, the three-term recurrence Eq.(
3.61
)
reads (still
Q_{0}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}},Q_{-1}\equiv 0
): for all
n
with
0\leq n\leq m_{0}
:

x\,Q_{n}(x)=\sqrt{\omega_{n+1}}\,Q_{n+1}(x)+\alpha_{n+1}\,Q_{n}(x)+\sqrt{\omega_{n}}\,Q_{n-1}(x).

(3.62)

Corollary 3.46

(
q
-Fock Polynomials)
.

In the special cases of the one-mode
q
-Fock probability algebra considered in
Theorem
3.43
, the orthogonal polynomials
\{P_{n}\}
are well known:

For the Bosonic
q=1
case:

these are the “probabilist’s”
Hermite polynomials
.

For the free
q=0
case:

the
modified Chebyshev polynomials of the
second kind
.

For the Fermionic
q=-1
case:

these are just the constant and linear function, as
the space is only two-dimnsional..

(3.64)

(Probability Algebra — Polynomials)
.

) and (

),
on

The probability algebra

has a GNS representation
(cf. Definition

) on

, and the probability algebra

Now, take the

in Eqs.(

),

Proposition 3.48

(Polynomial Representation)
.

Define an injective map
R:\mathscr{P}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.55554pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\mathscr{R}=\mathbb{C}[X]
by mapping

{\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}}\in\mathscr{P}

(3.67)

Proposition 3.51

(Equivalent Random Variables)
.

The following moment equivalences and equalities between RVs have been established:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}\in\mathcal{A}\;\overset{\text{m}}{=}x\in\mathscr{P}\;\overset{\text{m}}{=}\;X\in\mathscr{R}\;\overset{\text{m}}{=}\;Z:=\mathchoice{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\mathchoice{B^{{{o}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.37514pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.69652pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{o}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.37514pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.69652pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{o}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.37514pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.69652pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{o}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.94722pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.37514pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.69652pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}+\mathchoice{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\in\mathcal{L}(\Gamma)\\
\overset{\text{m}}{=}\;Y_{x}=M_{X}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{P})\;\overset{\text{m}}{=}\;\Upsilon_{X}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{R})\;\overset{\text{m}}{=}\;\Upsilon_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{a}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{a}}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathscr{S}).

(3.79)

The ladder and CAP-operator approach and interacting Fock spaces have been used by
several authors to investigate orthogonal polynomials, also in many and even in an
infinite number of variables,
e.g. cf.

,

The techniques alluded to in the present section, which use the quantum decomposition
in Proposition

and the embedding of a classical RV in a larger non-commutative

,

.

Finite Jacobi Matrices and Favard’s Lemma:

Consider the three-term recurrence Eq.(
3.62
) on
\mathscr{P}
, and take the
basis
\{Q_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n}
in the
n+1
-dimensional subspace
\mathscr{P}_{n}\subseteq\mathscr{P}
,
truncated after
Q_{n}
. Then
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{0}=[1,0,\dots,0]^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{T}}{\textstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{T}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}

corresponds to the
starting vector
Q_{0}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}}
, and the other canonical basis vectors
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{n}

correspond to
Q_{n}
. Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}_{x}
be the matrix representation
of the multiplication operator
M_{X}
Eq.(
3.67
) in that basis.
Then
\mathscr{P}_{n}=\mathscr{K}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}_{x},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{0},n)
is the
Krylov
subspace generated by
the symmetric operator
M_{X}
with starting vector
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{e}}_{0}\equiv Q_{0}={\mathchoice{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.0mul}{\rm 1\mskip-4.5mul}{\rm 1\mskip-5.0mul}}_{\mathbb{R}}

after
n
steps.
Approximating through the truncation — effectively forcing
Q_{n+1}=0
—
one obtains on
\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\equiv\mathscr{P}_{n}
the well known three-diagonal

Jacobi matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}_{x}
, composed from the Jacobi-Szegö coefficients,
representing and approximating
M_{X}
in that basis:

M_{X}\approx\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{M}}_{x}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{T}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{T}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{T}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{T}}_{J,n}=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{1}&\sqrt{\omega_{1}}&&&\\
\sqrt{\omega_{1}}&\alpha_{2}&\sqrt{\omega_{2}}&&\\
&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&\\
&&\sqrt{\omega_{n-1}}&\alpha_{n}&\sqrt{\omega_{n}}\\
&&&\sqrt{\omega_{n}}&\alpha_{n+1}\end{bmatrix}.

(3.80)

This is also in essence the result of the well known Lanczos algorithm — which need
not be reproduced here — for approximating the spectrum of a symmetric operator
(like
M_{X}
), e.g. cf.
[
60
]
. Further, in order to compute the
spectrum of a tridiagonal matrix, there are very effective numerical algorithms,
e.g. cf.
[
60
]
. One may observe that
the Lanczos algorithm, which produces the Krylov subspace and the representation
in Eq.(
3.80
), effectively computes the Jacobi-Szegö coefficients

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\{\omega_{n}\},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\{\alpha_{n}\})
.
The relation between a probability measure with all finite moments
and the Jacobi-Szegö coefficients, in one and many dimensions, is the content of what
is called Favard’s Lemma (only a simple version is stated here), e.g. cf.
[
48
,
1
,
108
,
49
]
and the references therein:

Theorem 3.52
.

(Favard)
To any probability measure
\nu
on the real line with finite moments of any order,
there are associated Jacobi-Szegö coefficients

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\omega}}=\{\omega_{n}\},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\{\alpha_{n}\})
,
the mapping being surjective.

On the other hand, given two such Jacobi-Szegö parameter sequences — or in other words,
given a sequence of polynomials satisfying a three-term recurrence relation like
Eq.(
3.61
), where the coefficients are Jacobi-Szegö parameters as in
Definition
3.44
— there is a state on the algebra of polynomials,
given by a probability measure
\nu
on
\mathbb{R}
with all finite moments, such
that the polynomials from the three-term recurrence are
orthogonal in the inner product induced by the state.

4
Modelling Quantum Processor Units (QPUs)

4.1
Preliminaries

Quantum computing is a new and rapidly developing field that uses the
principles of quantum mechanics to perform computations
[
107
]
.
The idea is that certain types of problems can be solved more efficiently
using quantum computers than with classical computers.
The actual devices — the quantum computers — employed are composed of components
which are such that the algebra of physical observables is non-commutative.
These components are in their basic form quantum mechanical systems with a finite
number of discrete quatum states; usually they have just two states and are
described by
qubits
, or quantum bits, which are the basic units of
information in quantum computing. A quantum computer is then composed of
a number
n\geq 1
of interacting qubits which are operated on by so-called

quantum gates
, which constitutes the actual
quantum algorithm
.

Qubits are similar to the traditional bits used in classical computers,
but they can exist in a superposition of the two states, meaning that they
can represent multiple values at the same time. This kind of inherent parallelism
allows quantum computers to perform certain types of calculations much faster than
classical computers, such as factoring large numbers and searching through
large databases.
Quantum computing has many potential applications, including but not
limited to cryptography, optimisation, simulation, and machine learning.

The current state-of-the-art is defined by
Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.
A NISQ (Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum) computer is a type of
quantum computer that is still under development and lacks some of the
capabilities of hopefully more advanced quantum computers. It refers to the fact
that these early quantum computers are prone to errors, noise and other
issues that can affect their performance and accuracy. These are
noisy qubits

which are subject to decoherence, which means they lose their entangled quantum state
properties over time due to interactions with the environment, such as thermal
fluctuations, electromagnetic noise, or other sources of error, as well as only

limited quantum error correction
, still
slow quantum gates
, a
still quite
limited number of qubits
, and a
lack of quantum algorithms
.

A Quantum Processor Unit (QPU) is a hardware component in a quantum
computer that performs the actual computations. It consists of one or more
quantum processors, which are responsible for executing quantum
instructions and performing calculations based on quantum gates,
which are the basic building of a quantum circuit (also called quantum code).
The QPU is
the
essential component of a quantum computer, as it is
responsible for performing the computations that make quantum computing
possible. It is important to note that QPUs are still under development
and there is ongoing research to improve their performance and capabilities.
But the specific type of QPU is not essential for the quantum algorithms,
as the algorithms reference purely the abstract algebraic properties of the
quantum gates. In this way the representation of quantum algorithms is
independent of the actual hardware implementation of the QPU, similarily as
the representation of classical algorithms is independent of the hardware
implementation of classical computer and CPU (central processing unit).

4.2
From Algebraic Probability to Quantum Computation

In the following Dirac’s
bra-ket
notation explained
at the end of Section
2.1
will be used exetnsively.
From the above very sketchy description of a QPU, one may deduce that according to the
rules of quantum mechanics one qubit will be
described with the bounded operator algebra (cf. Example
15
)
of a complex 2-dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
(
\dim\mathcal{H}=2
) — or more
to the point that the observables are the self-adjoint elements
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})_{sa}

of the full finite dimensional operator algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
— where
one identifies a basis of two orthogonal unit vectors
B=\{\ket{0},\ket{1}\}
,

\spn B=\mathcal{H}
, which are the
states
where the qubit
is set

(
\ket{1}
) resp.
not set
(
\ket{0}
).
Obviously, as described in Example
15

and Corollary
2.37
, these unit vectors resp. more precisely
the corresponding density
operators
\ket{0}\bra{0}
and
\ket{1}\bra{1}
define
pure states

(cf. Proposition
2.24
) in
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}))_{1}
.

It is customary to choose a computational basis identification of
\mathcal{H}
and

\mathbb{C}^{2}
by setting

\ket{0}:=\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix},\quad\ket{1}:=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix}.

(4.1)

As described in Remark
2.35
, this gives a *-isomorphic
matrix representation of the one-qubit algebra
\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
on
\mathbb{M}_{2}(\mathbb{C})
,
where the latter is decribed in Example
14
with its Hilbert-Schmidt inner
product based on the trace and the associated Frobenius state, with more details
in Examples
4
–
6
. The density matrices and
vector states for this matrix algebra are described in Definition
2.23
, and
the set of density matices — which represents all possible states —
in Proposition
2.24
.

In a QPU,
n>1
qubits interact in a
quantum register
when a quantum
algorithm is executed. According to Definition
2.71
the appropriate algebra
for this situation is the
n
-fold
tensor product
of the one-qubit algebra:

\mathcal{Q}:=(\mathbb{M}_{2}(\mathbb{C}))^{\otimes n}=\mathbb{M}_{2^{n}}(\mathbb{C})
, the matrix algebra on the
Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}^{N}
, where
N=2^{n}
. The elements
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{Q}
are often
represented by tensor products of one-qubit matrices
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k}
,
with
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{A}}_{k}\in\mathbb{M}_{2}(\mathbb{C})
.

A quantum algorithm
involves manipulating the qubits in a way that allows
for the solution of certain types of problems and enables the use of
quantum computing for a wide range of applications. The implementation of
this process will depend on the specific problem being solved
and may involve manipulating the qubits using classical electrical signals
or other techniques. From this and the previous remarks regarding NISQ computers,
one may deduce that the whole process involves input from the classical world to
a quantum device (see the Classical Input Channel of Example
20

in Section
3.2
), the computation (a general channel taking account of all
the error sources alluded to above, i.e. a CPUP map, cf. Definition
3.29
),
and an output to the classical world
(see the Classical Output Channel of Example
20
and in more detail
in Example
19
) typically realised as a positive operator valued
measure (POVM) (cf. Definition
3.6
).

But to describe a quantum algorithm, one does not have to deal with a
real

QPU, but one may consider an
ideal
one; here the computation channel can
be considered as an internal *-automorphism (cf. Example
20
) realised
by unitary transformations, a reversible channel according
to the rules of quantum mechanics;
see also in this connection the Stinespring dilation Theorem
3.22
.
Similarly, instead of a general POVM one only need consider the idealised version
of a projection valued measure (PVM) (cf. Definition
2.21

and the part on projective measurements at the end of Section
2.3
);
observe also the Neumark dilation Theorem
3.10
.

Two complementary universality statements are relevant here: (i) exact universality of
two-level embedded
SU(2)
(resp.
U(2)
) subgroups for
SU(2^{n})
(resp.
U(2^{n})
) via
QR/Givens-type factorizations, and (ii) discretization/compilation from a finite dense

SU(2)
gate set lifted through the same embeddings (e.g. via Solovay–Kitaev).
We refer to
[
57
]
for the geometric
embedding-based formulation and the associated universality and discretization results.

The density matrices
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
, which are a one-to-one representation of
the states
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{Q})
, were described in Definition
2.23
.
From Proposition
2.24
, recall Eq.(
2.10
), which shows that
the set of density matrices
is the disjoint union of of densities with ranks of
r=1,\dots,N
:

\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})=\biguplus_{r=1}^{N}\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{r},

with the extreme points of
\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
, also called the
pure states
,
being the rank-one densities (cf. Eq.(
2.11
))

\mathrm{ext}(\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})=\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{1}=\{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}\;:\;\ket{\Psi}\in\mathbb{C}^{N},\;\left\langle\Psi\mid\Psi\right\rangle=1\}.

In the light of the basis choice Eq.(
4.1
) and
Dirac’s bra-ket notation, an orthonormal basis
for
\mathbb{C}^{N}=\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}=(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}
can be generated by the
tensor products of the basis vectors of
\mathbb{C}^{2}
. These are

\ket{00\dots 00}=\ket{0}\ket{0}\dots\ket{0}\ket{0}=\ket{0}\otimes\ket{0}\otimes\dots\otimes\ket{0}\otimes\ket{0};\;\ket{00\dots 01}=\ket{0}\ket{0}\dots\ket{0}\ket{1};\\
\ket{00\dots 010}=\ket{00\dots 0}\ket{1}\ket{0};\quad\dots\quad;\ket{11\dots 10}=\ket{11\dots 1}\ket{0};\;\ket{11\dots 11}.

(4.2)

It is fairly obvious that a basis vector
\ket{x_{0}x_{1}\ldots x_{n-1}}

in Eq.(
4.2
), where
x_{i}\in\{0,1\}
for all

0\leq i\leq n-1
, is the binary representation
(k)_{2}
of
an integer
0\leq k\leq N-1
, where
(k)_{2}=x_{0}x_{1}\ldots x_{n-1}
.
This allows us to associate each integer labeled ket
\ket{k}
with the
canonical vector
\ket{(k)_{2}}\in\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}
from Eq.(
4.2
), as
it is not difficult to see that the set
\{\ket{k}:k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}\}
is
the canonical basis of
\mathbb{C}^{2^{n}}
, literally by interpreting the tensor
product as a
Kronecker product
.

As already mentioned, for the output channel here we want to
use a PVM (cf. Definition
2.21
),
here composed of the projections associated with the unit
vectors in Eq.(
4.2
):

\mathbb{Z}_{N}=\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}\ni k\mapsto\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}:=\ket{k}\bra{k}\in\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{Q}).

(4.3)

It is not difficult to see that the
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}
are commuting
(in fact orthogonal) minimal projections which form a projection
algebra (cf. Example
5
), and even a
N
-dimensional

maximal Abelian self-adjoint algebra
(MASA, cf. Definition
2.12
)

\mathcal{M}:=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}=\mathbb{C}[\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}]\subset\mathcal{Q}
.
This commutative sub-algebra is the
classical context
for the
output / measurement / observation, cf. Section
3.1
.

The projections can be considered as
events

which signify the bit pattern
(k)_{2}=x_{0}x_{1}\ldots x_{n-1}
, and
(cf. Proposition
2.18
) with
probabilities
of being observed
in a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}
with density
matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
given according to the
Born rule (cf. Definition
2.17
)

\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k})=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}=\bra{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ket{k}.

(4.4)

They actually form a

Boolean algebra
according to Proposition
2.19
(the classical output).

Remark 4.1

(QPU — Interacting Fock Space)
.

Now we connect this with the interacting Fock space from Section
3.3
. Define
a
Jacobi sequence
of finite type (cf. Definition
3.37
):

\forall k\text{ with }0\leq k\leq N-1:\,\lambda_{k}=1;\quad\text{and }\forall j\geq 0:\,\lambda_{N+j}=0.

(4.5)

With this Jacobi sequence Eq.(
4.5
), construct the one-mode interacting
Fock space (cf. Definition
3.38
) with the
sectors

\mathcal{K}_{k}=\spn\{\ket{k}\}
for
0\leq k\leq N-1=2^{n}-1
.
This set-up then defines the self-adjoint number operator
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}\in\mathcal{Q}

(cf. Eq.(
3.52
) in Definition
3.39
) with action

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}\ket{k}=k\ket{k}\in\mathcal{K}_{k}
for
0\leq k\leq N-1=2^{n}-1
.
It thus has the spectral decomposition (cf. Remark
2.10
)

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}k\,\ket{k}\bra{k}

(4.6)

and
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}})
generates (cf. Example
6
) the MASA

\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}]=\mathbb{C}[\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}]\subset\mathcal{Q}
.

The ladder operators, i.e. the creation and annihilation operator

\mathchoice{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{+}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.13892pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.81111pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.72223pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},\mathchoice{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{B^{{{-}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.69446pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.63333pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.16666pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}
, defined by Eqs.(
3.55
) and (
3.56
) in
Definition
