, can be seen as increasing resp. decreasing the
binary representation of the quantum register.

Definition 4.2

(
n
-qubits digital quantum computer)
.

An
n
-qubits digital quantum computer is a pair

(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\rho_{0}})
where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{M}_{sa}\subset\mathcal{Q}
is an
non-singular observable that represents the
digital quantum computer and is given by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\sum_{k=0}^{2^{n}-1}\lambda_{k}\,\ket{k}\bra{k},

(4.7)

with distinct non-zero eigenvalues
\lambda_{k}\neq\lambda_{s}
for
k\neq s
,
Such an observable generates (cf. Example
6
) the MASA

\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{C}[\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}]\subset\mathcal{Q}
.

The event
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{k}\}
corresponds to the observable

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{k}\}}=\ket{k}\bra{k}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k},

(4.8)

for each
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
.

Note that the number operator
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{N}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{N}}+\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}})\in\mathcal{M}_{sa}\subset\mathcal{Q}

derived from Eq.(
4.6
) in Remark
4.1
with eigenvalues

\lambda_{k}=k+1
for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
is such an observable.

Observations
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{X}}{\textstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{X}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{X}}(\mathcal{M})
(cf. Definition
2.6
) of the MASA
\mathcal{M}

(cf. Remark
2.20
) can also be represented with the
minimal one-dimensional projections
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}\subset\mathrm{P}(\mathcal{M})
.
This is achieved by realising that they are also
density matrices
\{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\}\subset\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{M})
of pure states, and in
fact multiplicative states, i.e. characters. When the event

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}=\ket{k}\bra{k}
is observed, for a
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{M}

with a spectral decomposition
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\mu_{j}\,\ket{j}\bra{j}

as in Eq.(
4.7
), they have the form

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}})=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}})=\bra{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\ket{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\mu_{j}\,\left|\left\langle k\mid j\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\mu_{k},

(4.9)

as
\left\langle k\mid j\right\rangle=\updelta_{k,j}
. This naturally also gives

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{j})=\updelta_{k,j}
.

Proposition 4.3
.

Let be
\ket{u}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}
be a unit vector and

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{Q})
with density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})

be a quantum state. Then, considering the rank-one
observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\ket{u}\bra{u}
,

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}(\ket{u}\bra{u})=\tr\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\tr(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ket{u}\bra{u})=\bra{u}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ket{u}.

(4.10)

Furthermore, in case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{1}
is a pure state,
where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}
for some unit vector
\ket{\Psi}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}
,
then (cf. Eq.(
4.4
))

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}(\ket{u}\bra{u})=(\left\langle\Psi\mid u\right\rangle)^{2}=\cos^{2}\theta_{\Psi,u},

(4.11)

where
\theta_{\Psi,u}
is the angle between the vectors
\ket{\Psi}
and
\ket{u}
.

This means that the law (cf. Definition
2.27
) of the quantum random
variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\ket{u}\bra{u}\in\mathcal{Q}_{sa}
in this pure state
results in the distribution (cf. Proposition
2.29
) given by Eq.(
4.11
)

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}\left(\ket{u}\bra{u}=1\right)=(\left\langle\Psi\mid u\right\rangle)^{2}=\cos^{2}\theta_{\Psi,u},

(4.12)

and hence

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}\left(\ket{u}\bra{u}=0\right)=\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi,u}.

(4.13)

The following is an easy exercise in linear algebra:

Proposition 4.4
.

Let
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{Q})
be a quantum state represented by the density
matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{r}
for some
r=1,2,\ldots,N.

Then, for any unitary matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})
, it holds that (cf. Example
20
)

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{r}
is a new rank-
r
density matrix
transformed by the channel / internal automorphism given by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}
.

Similarly, in case
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{Q}_{sa}
is an observable,

U\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}U^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
is still an observable.
Furthermore, the probability law of
U\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}U^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
under the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}}
is the same as the probability law of

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
under state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{U\rho U^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}}
.

The above Proposition
4.4

allows one to introduce the next definition.
First, consider the map
\mathscr{N}
to express one step of a QPU:

\mathscr{N}:\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})\times\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})\longrightarrow\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q}),\quad\mathscr{N}(U,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}):=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}.

(4.14)

From Proposition
4.4
,
\mathscr{N}
is well defined.
For each fixed
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})
, the map
\mathscr{N}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}}:=\mathscr{N}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}},\cdot)
is called the quantum channel associated with
the unitary matrix / internal automorphism defined by

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}
, cf. Example
20
.

Definition 4.5

(Quantum Code)
.

For a fixed quantum state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{Q})
represented by
a density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
, a quantum code
or quantum algorithm is
a finite sequence
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1},\ldots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})
, where

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}
is the identity matrix, and
\ell
is the length of the
quantum code. The quantum code is used to perform quantum computations
on the quantum state density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}
using the channel
defined in Eq.(
4.14
) as follows:

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}=\mathscr{N}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell-1}}(\cdots\mathscr{N}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}))\cdots)).

(4.15)

A
n
-qubits digital quantum computer,
given the quantum code
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1},\ldots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})
,
acts as follows:

1.

The quantum computer is initialized in the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}
.

2.

The quantum processing unit
\mathscr{N}
is applied to the quantum
state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}
represented by the density matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
by using the quantum code

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1},\ldots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}\in\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{Q})
, and transforms it
as in Eq.(
4.15
) in Definition
4.5
into a new quantum state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}}
represented by the density matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})
.

3.

The measurement of the observable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{M}_{sa}
from
Definition
4.2
— resp. on the PVM defined by its spectral
decomposition — is performed in
the quantum state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}}
. Thus, the outcome of the quantum
code given by the
n
-qubits digital quantum computer results in
the law of the quantum random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
under the state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}}
:

\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{j})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{j})=\bra{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\ell}\ket{j}=\bra{j}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}\cdots\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\cdots\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}\ket{j},

(4.16)

for each
j\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
. For the observation itself, if the event
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k}

is observed, from Eq.(
4.9
) one has that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\omega}}_{k}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}})=\lambda_{k}
.

Remark 4.6
.

Often a quantum computer uses a pure initial state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}\in\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{S}}{\textstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{S}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{S}}(\mathcal{Q})
given by the density matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{1}
.

The law (cf. Definition
2.27
) of the quantum random
variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\in\mathcal{M}_{sa}
in this pure state is characterised by
the distribution (cf. Proposition
2.29
) given in accordance with
Eq.(
4.11
) (cf. also Eqs.(
4.12
) and (
4.13
) in
Proposition
4.3
) by

\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{k})=\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{P}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{P}}_{k})=(\left\langle 0\mid k\right\rangle)^{2}=\updelta_{0,k},\quad k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}.

(4.17)

Hence, often the first steps of a quantum algorithm have the purpose
of
state preparation
, in order to achieve an appropriate starting
state for the quantum algorithm.

Next, we illustrate a search problem that can be solved by using a
digital quantum computer.

4.3
Grover’s Algorithm

Grover’s algorithm is a quantum algorithm that finds with high
probability the unique input to a black box function that produces
a particular output value, using just
O(\sqrt{N})
evaluations of
the function, where
N
is the size of the function’s domain.
Grover’s algorithm is an example of a quantum algorithm that provides
a quadratic speedup over the best classical algorithm.

Consider the set
\{0,1\}^{n}
of all binary strings of length
n
.
Let
f:\{0,1\}^{n}\>\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\hbox{\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 4.49588pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{{}\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 3.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle{}$}}}\kern 3.0pt}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\kern 14.99176pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise 0.0pt\hbox{\lx@xy@tip{1}\lx@xy@tip{-1}}}}}}\ignorespaces{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}{\hbox{\lx@xy@droprule}}\ignorespaces}}}}\>\{0,1\}
be a function that is constant on all
inputs except for one, which is called the
marked element
.
The goal of Grover’s algorithm is to find a quantum code, namely

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1},\dots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}
, which provides an unitary matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\cdots\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{\ell}
that acts on the quantum state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{1}
such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}}
is
a quantum state that has a high probability of measuring the marked element.

Quantum computers start with a pure state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}}\in\mathrm{D}(\mathcal{Q})_{1}

given by
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}
.
Then, the quantum code
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}
acts on the density matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}
by
the relation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}\ket{0}\bra{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}
. From
Proposition
4.4
we have that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}\ket{0}\bra{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}

is still a rank-one density matrix, and hence there exists a unit vector

\ket{\Psi}
such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}\ket{0}\bra{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}
.
To solve the problem, we will find an unitary matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}
satisfying

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}^{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsf{H}}{\textstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptstyle\mathsf{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{H}}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}
such that
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{f}\ket{0}=\ket{\Psi}
.

Assume that
a\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
is the marked element. Then we would like
to find a unit vector
\ket{\Psi}
such that

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}(\ket{a}\bra{a})=\left|\left\langle\Psi\mid a\right\rangle\right|^{2}=1-\varepsilon

holds for some
\varepsilon>0.

This unit vector
\ket{\Psi}
is the solution of the Grover’s algorithm.
It defines a quantum state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}
such that law of the
random quantum variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
is given by

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=1-\varepsilon\;\text{ and }\;\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi}\bra{\Psi}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\neq\lambda_{a})=\varepsilon.

To proceed, we first take the unitary (and self-adjoint) matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}^{\otimes n}
, where

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1&\phantom{-}1\\
1&-1\end{bmatrix},

is the Hadamard matrix. Then, it is not difficult to see that

\ket{\Psi_{1}}:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\ket{0}^{\otimes n}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}^{\otimes n}\ket{0}^{\otimes n}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\ket{0}+\ket{1})\right)^{\otimes n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^{n}-1}\ket{k}.

Observe, that

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{s})=\left|\left\langle\Psi_{1}\mid s\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\;\text{ for all }\;s\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}.

Now, the law of the quantum random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
under the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}
with density matrix
\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\ket{0}^{\otimes n}\bra{0}^{\otimes n}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}

follows a discrete uniform distribution over the set
\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
.
This is a kind of state preparation.
Observe that

\ket{\Psi_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{k=0}^{2^{n}-1}\ket{k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\ket{a}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}}}{{k\neq a}}}\ket{k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\ket{a}+\sqrt{\frac{2^{n}-1}{2^{n}}}\ket{a_{\perp}},

where

\ket{a_{\perp}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}-1}}\sum_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle k\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}}}{{k\neq a}}}\ket{k},

is a unit vector orthogonal to
\ket{a}
.
Since
\theta_{\Psi_{1},a}+\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}=\frac{\pi}{2}
, we have

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\left|\left\langle\Psi_{1}\mid a\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}=\cos^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a}=\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}},

and

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\neq\lambda_{a})=\left|\left\langle\Psi_{1}\mid a_{\perp}\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{2^{n}-1}{2^{n}}}\right)^{2}=1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}=\cos^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}.

Thus, we can write

\ket{\Psi_{1}}=\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}+\cos\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a_{\perp}}.

Next we consider the unitary (and self-adjoint) matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}-2\ket{a}\bra{a}
, where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}
is the identity matrix.
Then we have

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}\ket{a}=-\ket{a}\;\text{ and }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}\ket{\Psi_{1}}=\ket{\Psi_{1}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\ket{a}=\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}.

In a similar way we take the unitary (and self-adjoint) matrix

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}=2\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}-\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}},
to obtain

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\ket{\Psi_{1}}=\ket{\Psi_{1}}\;\text{ and }\;\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\ket{a}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\ket{\Psi_{1}}-\ket{a}=2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{\Psi_{1}}-\ket{a}.

Geometrically, in the invariant two-dimensional subspace

\mathrm{span}\{\ket{a},\ket{a_{\perp}}\}
the oracle reflection
W_{1}

and the diffusion reflection
W_{2}
compose into a rotation
U_{2}=W_{2}W_{1}
,
which increases the amplitude on the marked state at each iteration;
see Figure
4
.

Finally, the unitary (and self-adjoint) matrix
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}

allows us to obtain

\displaystyle\ket{\Psi_{2}}

\displaystyle:=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}\ket{\Psi_{1}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\left(\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}\right)

\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\left(2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{\Psi_{1}}-\ket{a}\right)

\displaystyle=\left(1-4\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\right)\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}

\displaystyle=\left(1-2\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-2\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\right)\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}

\displaystyle=\left(\cos 2\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-2\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\right)\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}

\displaystyle=\left(\cos 2\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-(1-\cos 2\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}})\right)\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}

\displaystyle=\left(2\cos 2\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-1\right)\ket{\Psi_{1}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}.

Now,

\displaystyle\left\langle\Psi_{2}\mid a\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left(1-4\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\right)\bra{\Psi}\ket{a}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}

\displaystyle=\left(1-4\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\right)\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}

\displaystyle=-4\sin^{3}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}-\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}

\displaystyle=-2\sin\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}(\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}+1).

Thus,

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})

\displaystyle=\left|\left\langle\Psi_{2}\mid a\right\rangle\right|^{2}

\displaystyle=4\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}(\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}+1)^{2}

\displaystyle=4\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})(\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})+1)^{2},

and hence the law of the quantum random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
under the state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}
satisfies

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})>2^{2}\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\frac{1}{2^{n-2}}.

Clearly,

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\neq\lambda_{a})<1-\frac{1}{2^{n-2}}.

In consequence, the quantum code
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}
acts on the matrix density

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}
by the relation
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}
,
providing a quantum state that has high probability of measuring
the marked element.

Since we can write

\ket{\Psi_{2}}=\sin\theta_{\Psi_{2},a_{\perp}}\ket{a}+\cos\theta_{\Psi_{1},a_{\perp}}\ket{a_{\perp}},

where

\sin^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{2},a_{\perp}}=\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})\;\text{ and }\;\cos^{2}\theta_{\Psi_{2},a_{\perp}}=\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}\neq\lambda_{a}),

by taking
\ket{\Psi_{3}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}\ket{\Psi_{2}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\ket{0}^{\otimes n}

and proceeding in a similar way, we obtain a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi_{3}}\bra{\Psi_{3}}}

where the law of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
satisfies

\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{3}}\bra{\Psi_{3}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})>2^{2}\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{2}}\bra{\Psi_{2}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})>2^{4}\mathbb{P}_{\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\frac{1}{2^{n-4}}.

Proceeding in this way, we obtain at step
k
a unit vector

\ket{\Psi_{k}}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\ket{0}
, such that it provides
a state
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{\Psi_{k}}\bra{\Psi_{k}}}
where the law of
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
satisfies

\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})>2^{2k}\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\frac{1}{2^{n-2k}}.

Thus, we can state the following proposition.

Proposition 4.7
.

For
k\geq 1,
consider the quantum code

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1},\overbrace{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2},\ldots,\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}}^{k-\text{times}},

(4.18)

where
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{0}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{I}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{I}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{I}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\textstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol{H}}^{\otimes n}
and
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}=\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{2}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{W}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{W}}_{1}

are self-adjoint matrices in
\mathrm{U}(2^{n})
.
Then the outcome of running the quantum code Eq.(
4.18
) in a

n
-qubits digital quantum computer
(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}},\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\ket{0^{n}}\bra{0^{n}}})

is the law of the quantum random variable
\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}
in the final state

\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{\varpi}}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\rho_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}}
that satisfies

\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\rho_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{2}^{k}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})>2^{2k}\mathbb{P}_{\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}\rho_{0}\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{U}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{U}}_{1}}(\mathchoice{\displaystyle\mathsfit{A}}{\textstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathsfit{A}}=\lambda_{a})=\frac{1}{2^{n-2k}}.

Furthermore, given
\varepsilon>0
, the probability of measuring
a marked element
a\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{n}}
is greater than
1-\varepsilon

for
k=\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil
. This amplification mechanism is the planar rotation depicted in
Figure
4
.

\ket{a}
\ket{a_{\perp}}
\mathrm{span}\{\ket{a},\ket{a_{\perp}}\}
\ket{\Psi_{1}}
\ket{\Psi_{2}}=U_{2}\ket{\Psi_{1}}
\mathrm{Fix}(W_{1})
\mathrm{Fix}(W_{2})
\theta
2\theta

W_{1}=I-2\ket{a}\bra{a}
(oracle phase flip)

W_{2}=2\ket{\Psi_{1}}\bra{\Psi_{1}}-I
(inversion about mean)

U_{2}=W_{2}W_{1}
is a rotation in
\mathrm{span}\{\ket{a},\ket{a_{\perp}}\}
.

Figure 4:
Geometric strategy of Grover’s algorithm in the invariant two-dimensional subspace

\mathrm{span}\{\ket{a},\ket{a_{\perp}}\}
. The oracle
W_{1}
and diffusion
W_{2}
are reflections;
their composition
U_{2}=W_{2}W_{1}
yields a rotation by
2\theta
that amplifies the probability of
measuring the marked state.

5
Conclusion

Here we have glanced a bit on algebraic probability, mainly keeping
to the finite dimensional case and thus avoiding many analytical difficulties.
It was shown that the classical connutative or Abelian case of probability
theory can be covered in the algebraic setting, so that one sees that this
is a more general theory (e.g.
[
26
,
28
,
113
,
118
]
).

This algebraic point of view also allows
a natural approach to random matrices and tensor fields, where the random variables
do not necessarily have to commute, and the interesting object is the behaviour
of their spectra, a distinctly analytic and algebraic concept which is
much more complicated to treat with the usual measure-theoretic background.
Connected with this is one area which was treated only very shortly here,
and this is everything connected with
free probability
. We only
offer the pointers to

[
145
,
74
,
104
,
103
]

for the interested reader.

While this material in Section
2
is essentially mainly linear algebra,
although sometimes not so well known, it is surprising to see what happens
when random variables do not commute, and this gives the striking differences
to the classical case which were explained in Section
3
.
In particular, this section contains the important view on channels,
which are the formal descriptions of information transmission.
Equipped with all this background, in Section
4
a mini-introduction
to quantum computation is given, and it is shown how this relies on the
previous material. As an example of a quantum algorithm, we explain the
Grover algorithm in some detail.

To each and any of the topics much more could be said. We have been a bit more
detailed in the formulation of algebraic probability, and much briefer in the
subjects which build on it, and to continue on the foundational matters

[
10
,
11
,
12
]
are probably good continuation
and starting points for further study. In the applications, it is especially quantum
computation (e.g.
[
107
]
) and quantum information
(e.g.
[
150
,
107
,
77
,
152
,
151
,
114
]
)
where many new developments occur.

We hope that these notes have given a glimpse at the algebraic treatment of probability,
and the differences which come with non-commutativity of random variables. Likewise,
we hope to have sparked some interest among the readers with the small collection of
developments and applications of algebraic probability. Thus they may have an idea now
of what it is, and where to continue in case they are interested in more.
